items.title: ESA's Hera Probe Uses "Superhuman" Vision to Inspect NASA's Asteroid Crash Site
items.blurb: Around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) was by pretty much all measures a resounding success when it struck the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos going more than 22,000 kilometers per hour. However, we still don’t know just how much of a success it actually was - DART was a one-way mission with no real way to track the results of the impact close up. Enter Hera, the European Space Agency (ESA) mission that recently arrived in the binary asteroid system. Now, in a press release, ESA has provided some of the best pictures of the binary system since that fateful day four years ago.

Part of its job is to hunt for strong gravitational lenses, important probes of dark matter. So far it's off to a great start. It found 15,000 strong gravitational lens candidates in its first data relase.

items.blurb: The Simons Observatory is online and surveying the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) in greater detail than ever before. It's looking for tiny fluctuations in the CMB caused by primordial gravitational waves. These waves, if detected, would be as close to slam-dunk evidence for the Big Bang that we can expect to find.

items.title: More than 1,700 bee species are unique to islands, first global assessment finds
items.blurb: More than 1,700 bee species are found only on islands, the first global checklist of island bees shows. If you like bees and island destinations, the best places to visit are in the Mediterranean. Islands like Sicily and Cyprus are where you find the highest diversity of bee species in the world. Bee connoisseurs will also appreciate large tropical islands like Hawaii and Madagascar, where they'll find unique bee species that live only on that particular island.

items.title: This year's humpback whale migration was missing something vital—the calves and their mothers
items.blurb: After centuries of whaling, humpback whales of the Southern Hemisphere were close to extinction. As few as 5,000 animals were left in the oceans. But after efforts to end whaling culminated in a 1985 moratorium, the whales began one of the biggest comebacks in conservation. Around 50,000 humpback whales now migrate along the eastern Australian coastline.

items.title: Data centers damage air quality long-distance, study reveals
items.blurb: The rapid expansion of data centers for artificial intelligence causes negative health and air quality impacts in regions far from where the brick-and-mortar facilities are located, according to a new study by MIT researchers.

items.title: Spirituality and religiosity associated with better quality of life in older adults
items.blurb: Researchers Alessandra Buja and Sohail Akhtar at the University of Padova in Italy conducted a meta-analysis of studies looking at aging adults' quality of life in relation to spirituality and religiosity. Their findings, published Nov. 19 in the open-access journal PLOS Aging and Health, suggested that being religious or spiritual boosts one's view of one's life, and having faith generally confers a greater benefit than turning to it as a means of coping.

items.blurb: In the Federal Court of Australia, applications by self-represented litigants, many using artificial intelligence to research and draft their claims, have skyrocketed.

items.title: Weight-loss drugs could reduce deaths and ease pressure on agricultural land by 2050
items.blurb: New research from the University of Aberdeen suggests weight-loss medications could deliver a double benefit, improving people's health while also helping the environment.

items.title: Neutrons, death metal and a tiny prehistoric dragon: Scans reveal new horned reptile species from 156 million years ago
items.blurb: An unassuming fossil discovery in Wyoming caused quite a stir: Was it a baby dinosaur, a prehistoric snake or perhaps an entirely new species? Neutron imaging at the Paul Scherrer Institute PSI and the trained eye of a paleontologist eventually provided the answer: the 156-million-year-old fossil is that of a previously unknown species of reptile.

items.title: Diplomacy, humor and avoidance—what we found when we investigated friendships across class divides
items.blurb: Several years ago, the U.S. economist Raj Chetty and his team at Harvard University analyzed billions of ties on Facebook in a bid to learn more about social mobility. Their findings highlighted an important link between cross-class friendship and social mobility. Specifically, they found that people from low-income backgrounds who have more friends from wealthier backgrounds tend to have better chances of earning more as adults.

items.title: Newly discovered gut viruses offer clues to the origins of the smallpox virus family
items.blurb: Human and animal digestive systems host vast communities of microorganisms, including bacteria and viruses. Some are harmful, others are beneficial, and many remain poorly understood. In a recent study, scientists found an entirely new group of viruses without even having to go anywhere near anyone's innards.

items.title: Artificial wetland near Valencia traps 36% of incoming microplastics, study finds
items.blurb: The Tancat de la Pipa, an artificial wetland designed as a "green filter" for the Albufera de València, reduces microplastic pollution in the natural lagoon by 36%, according to research conducted by the Institute of Water and Environmental Engineering (IIAMA) at the Universitat Politècnica de València (UPV) and the Faculty of Environmental Sciences and Engineering at Babe–Bolyai University in Romania published in the journal Applied Sciences.

items.title: Black gobies are growing larger despite climate change
items.blurb: Researchers at the Department of Paleontology at the University of Vienna compared fossil and modern ear stones of the black goby (Gobius niger) from the northern Adriatic Sea to reconstruct its growth history over the past 8,000 years. The surprising result: while body size remained remarkably stable in the past, today's black gobies grow faster and reach larger sizes—even as the Adriatic Sea is warming rapidly. The study is now published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

items.title: Huge extinct orca may have eaten other whales
items.blurb: A nearly 8-metre-long species of orca lived in the North Sea over 2 million years ago. Its discovery suggests orcas evolved a diet of marine mammals earlier than scientists thought

items.title: New metal-organic material combines metallic conductivity with promise for light-sensing electronics
items.blurb: In modern electronics and computing, finding advanced materials that can efficiently move electrical charges without losing energy remains a critical scientific challenge. While traditional metals conduct electricity exceptionally well, researchers continually seek innovative hybrid materials that combine the design flexibility of chemistry with true metallic performance.

items.title: Duck-billed dinosaur discovered in Italy had a birdlike beak hidden among its bizarre 'spikes'
items.blurb: For more than 15 years, the Italian duck-billed dinosaur Tethyshadros insularis has been reconstructed with one of the most unusual mouth structures among hadrosauroids. The tip of its upper jaw featured three forward-pointing bony projections on each side, long interpreted as exposed "spikes" or toothlike beak ornaments. However, a new study published in Royal Society Open Science reveals that this interpretation was incorrect.

items.title: Decoding interactomes: Supercomputing predicts bacterial protein links from shared evolutionary patterns
items.blurb: Predicting how proteins interact inside a cell is essential to understanding how organisms function and why they differ from one another, yet experimental hurdles and the computational cost of analyzing millions of protein pairs make it impossible to explore complete interaction networks, particularly in understudied bacteria and organisms.

items.title: Mandatory minimum sentencing oftentimes means 10 more months in prison, study finds
items.blurb: Racial minorities facing federal drug charges have allegations of conspiracy added to their cases at higher rates than their white counterparts, as prosecutors seek to push them over the threshold for a mandatory minimum sentence that then can be used in negotiating stiffer penalties, a new UConn study finds.

items.blurb: An international research team led by geologists from the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences (DEPS) at The University of Hong Kong (HKU) has uncovered new evidence of how the moon's largest impact basin, the South Pole–Aitken (SPA) basin, formed and evolved over billions of years.

items.blurb: Stopover sites are more than just places for migratory birds to rest and refuel. They also help birds adapt to climate change, according to research by Leiden ecologist Yali Si.

items.blurb: Researchers studying brains donated for scientific research stumbled upon the remarkable case of a woman who went through prolonged periods of reduced activity in which her body temperature dropped to as low as 31°C

items.title: From broken circuits to growing graphite: A new role for electromigration
items.blurb: Inside electronic devices, electric current can gradually displace atoms within tiny metal connections, creating gaps or unwanted accumulations that eventually cause circuits to fail. This phenomenon, known as electromigration, has long been regarded as a reliability problem that engineers must work to prevent. Yet the ability of an electric current to move atoms also raises the possibility of putting that movement to constructive use, directing atoms through a material rather than allowing them to migrate uncontrollably.

items.title: Microplastics make up 1 in 100 airborne particles sampled at four Michigan schools
items.blurb: One in 100 of the tiny particles hanging in the air we breathe in Michigan is a microplastic, according to a University of Michigan study. The study tested the air for microplastics in four locations across lower Michigan, all in the parking lots of K-12 schools. It found that microplastics constitute about 1% of particles found in the atmosphere.

items.title: Phantom forests: How low-integrity offsets lead to policy failure
items.blurb: Australia's Safeguard Mechanism (SGM) is failing to reduce emissions and drive decarbonization in the industrial and mining sectors because of an overreliance on cheap, low-integrity offsets, according to a new report titled "Phantom Forests and the Safeguard Mechanism: How Low-integrity Offsets are Obstructing Climate Action."

items.title: Dark personality traits linked to better chance at getting a second date
items.blurb: Some personalities stand out on the first date and end up being asked for a second date, but not the ones we expect. While very few people want to date people with dark traits like psychopathy and sadism, they seem to make a good first impression. Psychopathy involves traits such as manipulation, low empathy and impulsivity, while sadism involves taking pleasure in others' suffering. Yet, on a first date, these traits don't necessarily stop someone from coming across as an appealing romantic partner.

items.title: Hostility in online heat wave discussions shows signs of contagion, study suggests
items.blurb: Anger and frustration can run high in online discussions about climate change. But a new study led by Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU Singapore) suggests that hostility in these conversations tends to follow earlier hostility, hinting that people may pick up uncivil behavior from others.

items.title: Why fierce tropical downpours thrive in a relatively dry atmosphere
items.blurb: Twenty years of weather radar observations around Darwin have helped researchers investigate a surprising feature of tropical rain: the fiercest local downpours tend to occur when the surrounding atmosphere is relatively dry.

items.title: Successful high-purity synthesis of the challenging-to-produce cerium orthoferrite!
items.blurb: A research team including scientists from Ehime University successfully synthesized high-purity CeFeO3, a difficult-to-produce cerium–iron mixed oxide, using hydrogen reduction. By optimizing hydrogen concentration and gas flow rate, they achieved a phase purity of up to 99 mol%. The team also clarified the formation mechanism and identified factors that hinder synthesis. This method, published in the journal Inorganic Chemistry, provides a foundation for future research into applications in magnetic materials and catalysis.

items.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins
items.blurb: A new study has uncovered a surprising concern hiding in popular plant-based foods and drinks. Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk, and soy milk, and found that every single one contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin. Known as mycotoxins, these naturally occurring compounds can contaminate grains, legumes, and seeds during farming and storage.

items.title: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history
items.blurb: A bizarre whale that lived roughly 6 million years ago had a face so dramatically crooked that scientists believe it may have been the most asymmetrical of any mammal. Discovered in Peru, the extinct pygmy sperm whale Scaphokogia huachafo had an enormous downward-curving snout and a skull so distorted that researchers initially thought it had been damaged after death. Instead, its strange anatomy appears to have been an extraordinary evolutionary adaptation for hunting along the seafloor.

items.title: X-rays tear water apart before its electrons can relax
items.blurb: A single X‑ray photon can break both O–H bonds in a water molecule within a few femtoseconds (quadrillionths of a second), creating neutral atomic oxygen. As shown by a study published in the journal Physical Review Letters, this breakup happens before the electrons finish relaxing, revealing an ultrafast pathway for X‑ray–driven chemistry in water.

items.title: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs
items.blurb: Scientists have discovered a strange bacterium hiding beneath the skin of deep-sea creatures known as sea pigs, revealing an unexpected biological partnership. The microbe has an unusually tiny genome, yet more than a quarter of its DNA is devoted to making surface proteins, some of them exceptionally large. Researchers suspect it depends heavily on its host for survival, but what the sea pigs gain in return remains a mystery.

items.title: Cincinnati Zoo trying to shake loose Fiona the hippo after she swallowed a hat
items.blurb: Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo's famed hippo, underwent a colonoscopy this week, and now veterinarians are trying a new way to help her pass a knit cap that she swallowed after it slipped into her enclosure.

items.title: Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible
items.blurb: Hydrogen flames can shift from bright orange to nearly invisible depending on something unexpected: tiny amounts of sodium floating in the air. Scientists say this discovery could help make future hydrogen-powered stoves and ovens safer by replacing visual flame detection with specialized sensors.

items.title: Potatoes grown in simulated lunar soil match Earth-grown performance
items.blurb: Researchers have shown that potatoes grown in simulated lunar soil amended with organic matter are safe to eat and can achieve growth and yields comparable to those produced on Earth. "We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter," said Aymeric Goyer of Oregon State University's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology. "That's an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the moon."

items.blurb: Why do Ozempic and Wegovy produce dramatic weight loss for some people but disappointing results for others? Scientists are investigating whether the body's hidden energy-saving response could help explain the difference and unlock more effective, personalized weight-loss treatments.
