items.blurb: In 2025, 1.16 million people around the world were killed in road collisions. That's 3,178 deaths per day. Up to 50 million were injured.

items.title: The art of success: Study shows arts education benefits students with disabilities
items.blurb: Give students with disabilities greater access to the arts, and good things happen: They come to school more often, face fewer disciplinary problems and improve their writing skills, according to new research from the University of Missouri.

items.title: Climate change and habitat loss could fuel deadly bat-borne disease
items.blurb: Bats carry some of the world's deadliest viruses. Now, as climate change, extreme heat and habitat destruction intensify, so too could the risk of these diseases spreading to humans, according to new Adelaide University research.

items.title: Stonehenge’s six-ton mystery deepens as scientists narrow their search
items.blurb: A major new investigation into Stonehenge’s mysterious six-ton Altar Stone has uncovered fresh clues while ruling out several suspected sources. Once thought to have originated in Wales, the massive sandstone slab is now believed to have come from northeastern Scotland, although researchers have yet to find an exact match.

items.title: Prehistoric ecosystems could hold clues to preventing future wildfires
items.blurb: Could bringing back large herbivores help preserve Europe's rural landscapes and reduce wildfire risk? This is one of the key questions explored by an international study involving the University of Zaragoza, recently published in the journal Ecosystem Services.

items.title: Exquisite X-rays and dynamic compression initiate a new era of physics experiments on plutonium
items.blurb: Scientists at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL), Argonne National Laboratory (ANL) and Washington State University (WSU) have conducted the first dynamic compression experiments on plutonium at a national light source facility, the Dynamic Compression Sector (DCS).

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden hereditary form of aggressive prostate cancer
items.blurb: Scientists have discovered a rare inherited mutation in the CDK12 gene linked to aggressive prostate cancer, with all five identified carriers developing metastatic disease between ages 44 and 62. The finding could lead to expanded genetic testing, helping families uncover hidden cancer risks and potentially detect the disease while it is still treatable.

items.title: Policy changes in Canada had little effect on sales of antibiotics for animals, study finds
items.blurb: Sales of antibiotics for use in food-producing animals have fallen by 11% in Canada since 2018, but not because of federal policy changes.

items.title: Ancient minerals reveal a missing chapter in Türkiye's mountain-building history
items.blurb: A mountain range can bear the marks of events from tens of millions of years ago. The challenge lies in determining when each mark was created. In southern Türkiye's Central Taurides, scientists have developed a method to date some of these ancient movements by examining tiny calcite deposits that formed as faults shifted. This new timeline alters the region's geological history. Researchers discovered a previously unrecognized period during which parts of the crust slid laterally, between the Early Eocene and Early Miocene. They also found that the region's later extension began around 25 million years ago, earlier than previously believed.

items.title: New mixing benchmark could help industry reduce energy use in stirred tanks
items.blurb: Solid–liquid mixing, where particles are dispersed in a liquid, is essential in many industrial processes such as slurry preparation, crystallization, precipitation, adsorption and dissolution. In such cases, effective mixing is critical for contact between particles and liquid, enabling mass transfer. Floating particles often pose a challenge in mixing because they are lighter than the liquid and tend to float at its surface. While impeller agitation does draw them into the liquid, the minimum mixing intensity needed for effective drawdown has been difficult to define.

items.title: Is free will an illusion? New brain research reveals a surprising twist
items.blurb: New research reveals that the brain makes free choices and forced decisions using surprisingly similar neural processes, with activity building toward a decision before we act. The discovery challenges assumptions about free will while suggesting that our personal preferences and experiences still shape what we choose.

items.title: Researchers trace how gut microbes transform dietary plant sterols into circulating sulfated metabolites
items.blurb: Phytosterols are plant-derived compounds found in vegetable oils, nuts and seeds. They are studied for their ability to reduce cholesterol absorption, yet only about 5% enter the circulation and most are excreted. How gut bacteria influence their metabolism and tissue distribution has remained unclear.

items.title: Should we save every old building?
items.blurb: When you visit one of Norway's open-air museums, you can experience a piece of old Norway: log-built timber houses, farmsteads and farm complexes, often situated in a historic cultural landscape.

items.title: Turmeric supplements offer little benefit for knee osteoarthritis
items.blurb: A comprehensive review of clinical trials indicates that turmeric supplements had no meaningful effect on quality of life for people with knee osteoarthritis

items.title: First lunar-specific ground motion model could guide seismic hazard assessments on moon
items.blurb: Civil engineers looking forward to building structures on the moon need to know how ground motion from moonquakes will affect these buildings. But will ground motion models developed for Earth work well for the lunar landscape?

items.title: Watch: Sea level rise isn't just waves—how groundwater threatens coastal cities from below
items.blurb: With El Niño winter storms rolling in, coastal communities will naturally brace for the obvious: surging high tides, pounding waves and seawater spilling over seawalls. Decades of storm coverage have encouraged us to measure climate risk by what crashes onto the shoreline.

items.title: The philosophical reason AI Christmas ads leave audiences feeling cold
items.blurb: It's that time of year when Christmas ads start appearing, and brands offer up a slice of consumerist comfort as you curl up in front of a screen.

items.title: A 115 million‑year‑old 'algae rebellion' in Portugal's sea cliffs pushes back evolutionary timeline
items.blurb: Quite a few scientific discoveries are a product of chance. You set out looking for one thing, but often end up finding something totally unexpected. In micropaleontology, the study of microscopic fossils, this is especially common. You never know what you're going to find until you start examining the samples under the microscope.

items.title: Atoms in sync: Superradiance offers a new kind of frequency comb
items.blurb: When scientists shine a laser beam into a crystal, they typically expect a steady glow as the crystal's atoms are energized and begin to emit light. But in early 2024, while searching for something else entirely, researchers in the lab of Caltech's Andrei Faraon saw a crystal flash in a regular rhythm, like a metronome keeping a beat. The flashes came from billions of atoms embedded in the crystal. Coupled to a tiny superconducting circuit, the atoms had become synchronized and started emitting light together through a special quantum phenomenon known as superradiance.

items.title: Q&A: Schools that ban cellphones see uptick in test scores
items.blurb: We're nearing two milestones in the smartphone era. January will mark 20 years since Steve Jobs first unveiled the iPhone from a stage in San Francisco.

items.title: Sore throat? The brain has surprising control over how ill you feel
items.blurb: Nature, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03774-w The brain might decode pathogens, store memories of previous illnesses and prepare the body for future threats.

items.title: Author Correction: Prospective validation of imaging and serum diagnostic biomarkers of steatohepatitis and fibrosis in MASLD: the LITMUS Imaging Study
items.blurb: Nature Medicine, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41591-026-04803-x Author Correction: Prospective validation of imaging and serum diagnostic biomarkers of steatohepatitis and fibrosis in MASLD: the LITMUS Imaging Study

items.title: Expansion and cytotoxicity of mucosal CAR + T cells in enterocolitis associated with BCMA CAR-T cell therapy
items.blurb: Nature Medicine, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41591-026-04731-w Multimodal profiling of patients with biopsy-confirmed immune effector cell-associated enterocolitis following ciltacabtagene autoleucel shows that CAR T cell infiltrates are concentrated in the duodenum and have a more cytotoxic and clonal phenotype with loss of resident T cells, suggesting that this is a lymphoproliferative disorder with neoplastic characteristics.

items.title: Multicenter characterization of enterocolitis associated with BCMA-directed CAR T cell therapy
items.blurb: Nature Medicine, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41591-026-04783-y In a large multicenter case series, only 32% of patients who developed immune effector cell-associated enterocolitis following treatment with BCMA-directed CAR T cells had achieved disease resolution at last follow-up, with some deaths directly attributable to complications of this disorder.

items.title: Novel selective CDK4-inhibitor ALK-13743: Functional determinants of response in ER+ breast cancer models
items.blurb: Background: Cyclin-dependent kinase 4 (CDK4) and CDK6 are central drivers of cell cycle progression in estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) breast cancer, and pharmacological inhibition of this pair has become a standard-of-care therapeutic strategy. However, currently approved CDK4/6 inhibitors palbociclib, ribociclib, and abemaciclib carry associated toxicities, including myelosuppression and other adverse effects which are associated with inhibition of CDK6 that limits tolerability and combinatorial strategies. Here we describe the preclinical characterization of ALK-13743, a novel, highly selective CDK4 inhibitor. Methods: ALK-13743 was synthesized and characterized biochemically for CDK4 selectivity. Anti-proliferative activity was assessed in wild-type (WT), RB1-deleted and CDK6-overexpressing isogenic ER+ breast cancer cell lines (MCF7, T47D) using live-cell fluorescence imaging. Impact on cell cycle progression was evaluated by immunoblotting. Combinatorial activity was assessed across a 307-drug library. In vivo efficacy was evaluated in T47D xenograft models. Results: ALK-13743 potently inhibited CDK4/Cyclin D1 with an IC50 of 33 nM and displayed selectivity over CDK6/Cyclin D3 (IC50, 99 nM), CDK2/Cyclin E1 (IC50, 1854 nM), and CDK1/Cyclin B1 (IC50, >10000 nM) in biochemical kinase assays. In cellular models, ALK-13743 demonstrated potent antiproliferative activity in CDK4-dependent ER+ breast cancer cells at nanomolar concentrations, while exhibiting limited inhibition in CDK6-dependent cell lines. ALK-13743 exhibited single-agent growth suppression and drug synergy with the selective estrogen receptor degrader giredestrant and PI3K pathway inhibitors but was entirely RB-dependent and blunted by CDK6 overexpression. Single-agent ALK-13743 treatment led to tumor regression in T47D xenografts in vivo. Conclusions: ALK-13743 is a potent, CDK4-selective inhibitor dependent upon RB for its antiproliferative profile in ER+ breast cancer models. Its favorable combinability with multiple clinically relevant targeted agents supports further development, particularly in combination regimens, and positions it as a differentiated CDK4-selective therapy for ER+ breast cancer.

items.title: SHMT1 and SHMT2 inhibition disrupts metabolic adaptation in glioblastoma
items.blurb: Glioblastoma cells adapt to hypoxia and nutrient restriction through metabolic reprogramming. Serine hydroxymethyltransferases 1 and 2 (SHMT1, SHMT2) channel serine-derived one carbon units into folate metabolism, linking biosynthesis, respiration and redox defence. Its contribution to tumour metabolic homeostasis and adaptation to hypoxia and nutrient restriction remains unclear. We combined dual pharmacological SHMT inhibition using (+)-SHIN1 in glioblastoma cell lines, including patient-derived glioma stem-like models, with stable SHMT2 knockdown in LNT-229 cells. Functional analyses assessed clonogenic survival, invasion, migration and susceptibility to metabolic stress. Bioenergetics were measured by extracellular flux analysis and oxygen depletion, redox state by NADPH/NADP; assay, and molecular responses by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry-based metabolomics and 13C6-glucose tracing and tandem mass tag proteomics. Formate supplementation tested the contribution of limited one-carbon availability, three-dimensional co-cultures with human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived embryoid bodies assessed tumour expansion, and in silico analyses of public glioblastoma datasets examined SHMT expression, regional distribution and associations with hypoxia-related genes. SHMT2 was enriched in hypoxic and perinecrotic tumour regions and correlated with hypoxia-inducible factor-1 target genes. SHMT inhibition impaired clonogenic growth, reduced invasion and migration, limited tumour expansion in co-culture, and sensitised cells to death under combined hypoxia and glucose restriction. Under normoxia, it increased respiration and estimates of glycolytic and oxidative ATP production. In G55T2 cells, SHMT inhibition lowered intracellular and extracellular lactate and altered tricarboxylic acid cycle metabolite levels and 13C isotopologue signals. SHMT inhibition increased oxidative stress, reduced the NADPH/NADP; ratio in a cell line- and condition-dependent manner, and reduced extracellular formate accumulation. In G55T2 cells, SHMT inhibition led to a depletion of glutathione. Formate supplementation most prominently restored invasion and partially reversed other antitumour effects of SHMT inhibition, with the extent of rescue varying between cell lines. Under combined stress, SHMT inhibition attenuated hypoxia-inducible factor-1-alpha; accumulation, an effect counteracted by formate supplementation. These findings link SHMT-dependent one-carbon metabolism to redox homeostasis, invasive behaviour and survival under metabolic stress in glioblastoma. SHMT inhibition increases respiratory activity under normoxia while compromising tolerance to combined oxygen and glucose restriction, identifying metabolic adaptation as a potential therapeutic vulnerability in glioblastoma.

items.title: Cerulean Protein Tagging Enhances Immunogenicity and Osimertinib Response of Transplantable Murine EGFR Mutant Lung Cancer Cell Lines
items.blurb: Lung cancers bearing mutations in epidermal growth factor receptors (EGFR) exhibit marked, but incomplete responses to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) like osimertinib. We previously developed genetically-engineered mouse models (GEMMs) for EGFR exon 19 deletion (del19) and L860R (mouse equivalent of L858R). Sequences encoding mC3 cerulean fluorescent protein were included to mark emergent tumor cells. Orthotopic implantation of mEGFRdel19 cell lines into syngeneic C57BL/6J mice yielded tumors that were eliminated upon osimertinib therapy which is not typically observed in patients while mEGFR-L860R cell lines failed to establish tumors. Herein, mEGFRdel19 and mEGFR-L860R cell lines formed tumors in non-induced mEGFRdel19 and mEGFR-L860R GEMMs and green fluorescent protein-transgenic mice, supporting mC3-derived epitopes as mediators of immunoelimination. CRISPR-Cas9 mediated disruption of the mC3 cerulean sequence in established mEGFR cell lines yielded two independent mC3-deleted cell lines that formed orthotopic tumors and exhibited partial osimertinib responses. These studies provide a cautionary tale regarding use of fluorescent proteins in murine cancer models and reinforce host immunity as a participant in anti-tumor TKI responses initiated. These mC3-deleted cell lines serve as improved models to explore mechanisms of incomplete TKI response, acquired resistance and cancer cell interaction with the host immune microenvironment.

items.title: Subtype-specific autophagy profiles in Renal Cell Carcinoma
items.blurb: Autophagy is a highly conserved cellular mechanism essential for recycling intracellular components and providing energy and maintaining cellular homeostasis. The role of autophagy in cancer is double sided, where it can suppress tumorigenesis by degrading damaged organelles and preventing chronic inflammation while supporting survival of existing tumor cells to survive during starvation and stress, and thus support tumor growth. The role of autophagy in renal cell carcinoma (RCC), the most common type of kidney cancer, remains insufficiently described. RCC originates from epithelial cells of the renal tubule and is divided into histological subtypes where clear cell RCC is the most common followed by papillary and chromophobe RCC, showing differences in morphology and molecular features. Recent studies of RCC suggest that mTORC1 and autophagy are involved in kidney cancer development and response to treatment, advocating the need to better understand the role of autophagy in RCC. To this end, we investigated autophagy markers by immunostaining, immunoblotting and quantitative PCR in biobanked fresh-frozen tissue samples of RCC tumor and matched normal tissue. Overall, we found reduced levels of LC3B and GABARAPL1 in clear cell RCC, in stark contrast to chromophobe RCC and benign oncocytoma. This suggests that autophagy levels differ between renal tumor subtypes, indicating that autophagy could play subtype-specific roles. In addition, autophagy modulating drug assays demonstrated autophagy dependencies in metastatic RCC cell line spheroids. This could provide new inroads for therapeutical approaches in RCC.

items.title: Immune Age Acceleration Stratifies Survival in Multiple Myeloma Independent of Chronological Age and Clinical Fitness
items.blurb: Chronological age incompletely explains prognostic heterogeneity in multiple myeloma (MM), particularly among younger patients, whose clinical outcomes vary widely. Existing immune aging clocks are predominantly derived from peripheral blood expression data and thus incompletely reflect the aging of the bone marrow (BM) immune microenvironment in MM. To address this limitation, we developed BM immune aging clocks for ten immune and progenitor cell types trained on single-cell RNA-sequencing data from 1,260 healthy peripheral blood and BM samples and calibrated to BM. We then applied these clocks to BM single-cell profiles from 337 newly diagnosed MM patients enrolled in the CoMMpass study to derive a global immune age acceleration score. In patients younger than 70 at diagnosis, accelerated immune aging was independently associated with shorter overall survival (OS; HR = 2.24, p = 0.003) after adjustment for cytogenetic risk, transplant status, triplet therapy administration, chronological age, sex, performance status, and laboratory deficits, whereas chronological age was not predictive. Subsequent analyses identified CD4+ memory T cell aging as the strongest contributor to overall immune age acceleration and its association with shorter OS. Consistent with this, accelerated immune aging was characterized by terminal effector differentiation of memory T cells, TNF-/NF-{kappa}B-mediated inflammation, and increased lymphocyte-driven TNF, CCL3, and IFN-{gamma} signaling. However, inflammatory signaling alone did not account for survival differences. Longitudinally, changes in monocyte immune age acceleration at first progression were associated with shorter subsequent survival (HR = 3.06, p = 0.005). Together, these findings identify BM immune age acceleration as a prognostic measure of biological fitness in MM, distinct from chronological age and clinical frailty.

items.title: The KMT2A-MENIN complex is a therapeutic vulnerability in SETBP1-mutant leukemia
items.blurb: SET binding protein 1 (SETBP1) is recurrently mutated in high-risk myeloid malignancies, including myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative overlap disorders (MDS/MPNs) and is associated with poor clinical outcomes. Although SETBP1 mutations promote self-renewal and HOX-driven transcription in murine and cell line models, the epigenetic dependencies sustaining these programs in human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) remain poorly defined. Here, we identify the KMT2A-MENIN complex as a targetable dependency in SETBP1-mutant leukemia. Expression of SETBP1D886N enhanced growth and serial replating of human HSPCs and established a transcriptionally permissive chromatin state, with increased H3K4me3, H3K27ac and KMT2A occupancy at SETBP1-regulated loci. Integrated transcriptional and chromatin profiling defined a 94-gene SETBP1 regulome containing HOXA9, MEIS1, MECOM, and MYBand was enriched for transcriptional programs associated with KMT2A-rearranged, NUP98-HOXA9, and NPM1-mutant leukemias. CRISPR-Cas9 disruption revealed a functional requirement for KMT2A, but not for KMT2B or DOT1L in SETBP1D886N HSPCs. Strikingly, deletion of the KMT2A cofactor MEN1 phenocopied KMT2A loss. Disruption of either KMT2A or MEN1 suppressed SETBP1-driven proliferation and leukemogenic transcriptional programs, including leukemia stem cell-associated signatures. We next exploited this dependency pharmacologically. A KMT2A-MENIN inhibitor suppressed canonical SETBP1 target genes and abolished mutant SETBP1-driven serial replating while promoting hematopoietic differentiation and reducing H3K4me3 at leukemogenic loci, despite modest effects on short-term proliferation. Most importantly, three clinically relevant KMT2A-MENIN interaction inhibitors impaired clonogenic growth across primary SETBP1-mutant leukemia patient samples, while inducing myeloid differentiation and suppressing SETBP1 target gene expression. Together, these findings identify the KMT2A-MENIN complex as a key therapeutic vulnerability in SETBP1-mutant leukemia. The consistent activity of multiple MENIN inhibitors across a variety of SETBP1-mutant patient samples and cell models validates the KMT2A-MENIN interaction as an actionable vulnerability and provides a strong rationale for expanding MENIN-directed therapies to SETBP1-mutant myeloid malignancies.

items.title: VPHYL: A Web Application for Converting Emu and EPI2ME wf-16s Nanopore 16S rRNA Abundance Tables into phyloseq and BIOM Objects
items.blurb: Taxonomic abundance data derived from 16S rRNA gene sequencing data are fundamental in microbiome research. To perform downstream statistical analysis and visualization, raw abundance data must typically be converted into standardized data structures, such as phyloseq S4 objects or BIOM files. This conversion requires three input data files: an Operational Taxonomic Unit (OTU) table (count of specific taxa across samples), a Taxonomy table (hierarchical lineage from Kingdom to Species), and a Sample Data table (experimental metadata). For Oxford Nanopore (ONT) 16S data, the two commonly used classifiers, Emu and the EPI2ME wf-16s workflow (Minimap2/Kraken2), generate output files with different formats and column schemas. We found no web-based tool that accepts these classifier outputs directly. Experienced users can reshape them with a script. Researchers who do not program cannot, and for them, this step remains a hurdle. We introduce VPHYL(Versatile PHYLogenetic Standardizer), an R Shiny web application that accepts abundance outputs directly from Emu and EPI2ME wf-16s, splits the lineage into standard ranks, attaches sample metadata, and generates phyloseq objects or BIOM files. VPHYL integrates multi-file aggregation and produces automated HTML reports comprising read statistics, alpha diversity metrics, and taxonomic abundance visualizations. VPHYL output was identical to that of an independently written R script for all nine supported classifier-database combinations. We validated the framework by processing raw abundance datasets processed using the EPI2ME Labs 16S Workflow from a published respiratory microbiome study comprising both porcine and human microbiota composition samples. The published tables were processed by VPHYL without modification, and the resulting alpha diversity indices and taxonomic profiles were consistent with the reported findings; small differences reflect read filtering applied in the original study. The application is publicly available at https://venkat-247.shinyapps.io/VPHYL/.

items.title: Monolith, porous bead, membrane or fibre? A comparative characterisation of four oligo-dT affinity chromatography matrices for mRNA capture
items.blurb: Oligo-deoxythymidine (oligo dT) affinity chromatography is the most widely used capture step for in vitro transcribed mRNA and is now offered in four stationary-phase architectures, yet, to our knowledge, no published study has compared all four. We characterised a monolith, perfusive porous beads, a membrane adsorber and an electrospun cellulose fibre adsorber with a short (eGFP, 930 nt) and a long (SARS CoV 2 spike, S 2P, 4284 nt) mRNA. After screening the loading salt (NaCl or guanidine hydrochloride, Gu HCl), we mapped load flow rate, load concentration and Gu HCl concentration with response surface designs and compared the formats at near-optimal conditions. Gu HCl gave a higher peak recovery than NaCl in seven of the eight matrix construct combinations. At the near-optimal runs, the fibre adsorber recovered 17.9 mg eGFP and 13.3 mg S 2P per mL of bed, 2.3 to 2.6 fold the membrane and 3.5- to 4.8-fold the monolith and beads (p membrane > monolith > beads (0.314 to 0.035 mg/mL/min for eGFP). The membrane and fibre adsorber lost yield sharply above 0.4 to 0.6 M Gu HCl, whereas the monolith and beads declined gradually. In an amortised cost model at baseline cost inputs, the fibre adsorber was the least expensive format per milligram of purified mRNA at every number of device cycles (USD 114 to 140/mg for single use and 78 to 92/mg at 20 cycles), and the membrane the most expensive. A one at a time sensitivity analysis over wide ranges of the mRNA feed cost, the labour and facility rate, the device price and the number of cycles per device left the fibre adsorber the least expensive format in almost every combination examined, with the mRNA feed cost the dominant input. Only the monolith and beads are currently marketed as GMP grade, process scale materials, so the choice of format depends on whether capacity, productivity, cost or manufacturing readiness takes priority.

items.title: Associations between structural and functional hemodynamics in the optic nerve head
items.blurb: Purpose: Glaucoma is characterized by progressive degeneration of retinal ganglion cells axons thought to initiate within the optic nerve head (ONH). Although the precise mechanisms remain unclear, a leading hypothesis suggests that insufficient blood flow and oxygenation may be significant contributors to axonal damage. Measuring ONH oxygenation directly, however, is difficult. Hence, our first goal was to identify associations between structural and functional hemodynamics parameters (flow and oxygenation). We then evaluated whether local tissue oxygenation and hypoxia can be estimated from measurable parameters. Methods: Following previously reported methods, the ONH vasculature of four healthy monkey eyes was reconstructed. Numerical simulations were performed to determine blood flow and oxygen distribution. Structural parameters of each segment, including spatial location, orientation, length, and tortuosity, and functional hemodynamics parameters of each segment, including blood flow, pressure, blood oxygenation, and surrounding tissue oxygenation, were quantified. Results: Structural parameters exhibited no distinct spatial distribution, whereas hemodynamic and oxygenation parameters followed radial patterns. Although blood flow correlated with tissue oxygenation (p<0.001), regional mismatches indicated that flow alone was insufficient to predict accurately local oxygenation. We developed two multivariable mixed-effects models using measurable structural and flow parameters, a quadratic model that predicted continuous tissue oxygenation with high accuracy (R^2=0.75) and a logistic model that estimated local hypoxia risk. Conclusions: Our results provide a framework for estimating local tissue oxygenation and hypoxia risk that currently cannot be measured experimentally from vascular structural and flow parameters that can be measured.

items.title: CT-Derived In Vitro Model Simulating Neonatal Cranial Growth
items.blurb: Purpose: This study presents an in vitro platform for quantitatively simulating cranial growth in neonates from 3 to 6 months of age. Methods: The system integrates a pneumatic-hydraulic actuation unit, multi-camera optical tracking, and a CT-compatible enclosure to replicate and measure intracranial expansion. A phantom head model was fabricated via 3D printing using cranial bones and flexible latex sutures, reproducing neonatal cranial biomechanics. Controlled hydraulic pressure simulates intracranial volume (ICV) growth, while surface and volumetric changes are captured through synchronized imaging. Results: Morphometric parameters - biparietal diameter, occipitofrontal diameter, cranial circumference, and ICV - were measured and compared against published reference data. The system achieved high reproducibility across repeated trials. CT-derived ICV values (R2 = 0.98) closely matched reference trends, with average manufacturing deviations of 0-4 mm between fabricated and reference geometries. Linear morphometric increments confirmed physiologically consistent expansion patterns. Conclusion: The proposed platform provides a quantitatively validated, controllable, and CT-compatible environment for studying neonatal cranial development. It enables biomechanical testing and device evaluation under ethical and repeatable in vitro conditions, with potential future applications in surgical training and pre-operative planning.

items.title: New llama-derived nanobodies enable selective detection and capture of Z-DNA
items.blurb: Z-DNA is a left-handed DNA conformation that forms transiently at susceptible genomic sequences during processes such as negative supercoiling and active transcription. In the cytoplasm, the innate immune receptor ZBP1 senses Z-form nucleic acids (Z-NAs, which could be DNA or RNA), triggering type I interferon production and programmed cell death. Viral infections, endogenous repetitive-element-derived RNAs, and oxidized mitochondrial DNA can generate Z-NAs, nominating them as ZBP1 agonists. Conversely, ADAR1 is proposed to recognize and edit endogenous Z-RNAs, thereby muting inappropriate innate immune responses. Both proteins engage Z-NAs through Z domains, which are evolutionarily conserved across vertebrates. Progress in defining Z-NA biology has been limited by near-exclusive reliance on the Z22 monoclonal antibody, the field's principal detection reagent. To expand the availability of distinct, validated anti-Z-NA affinity reagents, we generated and characterized llama-derived nanobodies. Llamas were immunized with brominated poly(dG:dC) DNA, and four recombinant nanobodies (nZ6, nZ6.2, nZ10, and nZ11) that bound the antigen were identified through affinity enrichment and mass spectrometry-guided discovery. The nanobodies selectively recognized Z-DNA in biochemical assays and displayed nanomolar affinities, while homodimerized nZ6.2 achieved picomolar binding. Unlike Z domains, nZ6.2 does not induce B-to-Z transitions, indicating recognition of pre-existing Z-DNA and immobilized nZ6.2 selectively co-immunoprecipitated ADAR1 and ZBP1 with Z-DNA but not B-DNA. Furthermore, nZ6.2 detected Z-DNA-related structures in a human keratinocyte cell line and in neutrophils from patients with systemic lupus erythematous, producing staining patterns overlapping those of Z22. These renewable, engineerable binders provide orthogonal reagents for investigating Z-NA biology, interferon signaling, and autoimmune disease.

items.title: Generation of a Public Dataset for Etiological Subtyping with the Genomic Cluster Engine
items.blurb: Motivation: Genetic diseases are complex phenomena that are currently defined by their clinical symptoms, rather than by the combinations of variants that give rise to them. Incomplete penetrance and phenotypic variability indicate that the genomic background contributes to the effect of variants. Recent advancements in genomics have produced vast amounts of data and created new opportunities to study genetic diversity across human populations. Much of this variation is inherited as recombination-defined contiguous segments, called haploblocks. We previously introduced a novel methodology for genomic hash encoding, the Genomic Cluster Engine, which groups individuals into clusters using phased haploblock sequences. By encoding each haploblock sequence as a compact hash, the characterization of genomic backgrounds, the subtyping of etiologies and the inference of local ancestry become fast and scalable. Results: We have optimized the Genomic Cluster Engine pipeline for large genomic datasets through parallelization and improved memory management. We applied our pipeline to 2,548 individuals across 26 populations from the 1000 Genomes Project and produced a dataset of haploblock-based genomic hashes for the resulting clusters. The genomic hashes and clusters can be used for investigating variant effects in the context of their haplotype backgrounds or for genotype-phenotype association studies. This comprehensive dataset is now publicly available, providing a valuable resource for both academic and industry researchers worldwide. Availability: The haploblock boundaries, sequences, clusters and genomic hashes for the 1000 Genomes Project are available under the CC0 license at https://data.haploblocks.org and on the Registry of Open Data on AWS https://registry.opendata.aws.

items.title: Disentangling genomic imprinting from indirect parental genetic effects on the human methylome
items.blurb: Imprinted genes regulate development and metabolism and are implicated in both rare developmental syndromes and common diseases. Genomic imprinting is conventionally inferred from parent-of-origin effects (POEs), identified as differences between heterozygotes who inherited an allele from their mother and those who inherited it from their father. However, such differences can also be caused by indirect parental genetic effects, i.e. the fact that the genotype of a parent can be associated with behavioral or environmental changes that affect the phenotype of their offspring. No study of the human methylome has so far accounted for this confounding effect when inferring imprinted loci. Here, we jointly estimate direct, maternal, paternal and parent-of-origin effects at 850,055 methylation probes from whole blood in 2,438 parent-offspring trios from Generation Scotland. Of 5,435 probes with apparent POE signal, 4,974 (91.5%) fall below threshold once parental genotypes are included, suggesting that the vast majority are not attributable to imprinting alone. We treat the 281 remaining probes, 17 on the X chromosome and 42 not previously reported, as a conservative, high-confidence set, map them to 1,118 SNP loci linked to gene expression and protein abundance, and identify 27 probes where imprinting and indirect parental genetic effects both contribute. In a hold-out set of relatives, 250 of the 281 show familial resemblance consistent with a combination of imprinting and parental effects. Our results highlight the importance of accounting for indirect parental genetic effects when interpreting putative imprinting regions.

items.title: Unravelling the role of plant alpha-, beta-, and gamma- chemodiversity in shaping canopy insects of plants within the same species
items.blurb: Plant intraspecific chemodiversity drives plant-herbivore and -pollinator relationships in plots, but whether it also impacts other members of the canopy arthropod community remains unclear. Furthermore, little is known of how different spatial components of plot intraspecific chemodiversity; chemical composition of individual plants within plots (i.e. -chemodiversity); differences in chemical composition among plants within plots (i.e. {beta}-chemodiversity); and cumulative chemical composition of all individuals in plots (i.e. {gamma}-chemodiversity), impact aboveground community assemblage. Using a chemodiversity field experiment containing 84 plots each planted with different combinations of Tansy (Tanacetum vulgare L., Asteraceae) chemotypes (i.e. a manipulated gradient of plot-level chemotype richness), we investigated the effect of plot-level chemodiversity and its components on the diversity and composition of canopy-associated arthropod communities within plots. We found significant impacts of the presence of certain chemotypes on the effective number of common arthropod taxa (Hill q = 1) and the effective number of dominant arthropod taxa (Hill q = 2) within plots. Importantly, the observed pattern was independent of the actual terpenoid (-)chemodiversity of these chemotypes. We also found that plot-level chemotype richness ({beta}-chemodiversity) reduced the effective number of dominant arthropod taxa (Hill q = 2) within plots, driven by impacts on dominance of a nematoceran species associated with Tansy. Cumulative plot terpenoid richness ({gamma}-chemodiversity) did not significantly impact arthropod communities. Instead, we observed that increased terpenoid abundance negatively influenced the effective number of common (Hill q = 1) and dominant arthropod taxa (Hill q = 2) within plots. Our results suggest that within plants of the same species, the chemotypic identity of plants and presence within plots and plot-level chemotype richness ({beta}-chemodiversity) may impact arthropod communities by selecting for specific arthropod taxa making arthropod communities less even. Our results emphasize the nuanced impacts of chemodiversity at different levels and highlight taxon-specific arthropod responses.

items.title: Unravelling the association between non-essential elements and redox homeostasis in wild roe deer
items.blurb: Redox homeostasis, i.e. the balance between oxidative damage and antioxidant defences, is crucial for overall physiological function. Disrupting this balance may lead to oxidative stress. Non-essential elements (e.g. lead, cadmium) exhibit toxicity even at low concentrations and can increase the production of pro-oxidant molecules and impair antioxidant mechanisms. While the adverse effects of acute exposure are well documented, little is known about the impact of chronic, low-level exposure in the wild. Here, we investigated the relationship between non-essential element exposure and redox status in two roe deer populations (Capreolus capreolus), while accounting for the potential modulation by essential elements (e.g. selenium, zinc) and local weather conditions. We measured the concentrations of nine non-essential and thirteen essential elements in hair, and assessed the oxidative status through seven biomarkers in blood samples (n = 649 samples collected between 2016 and 2019). Our findings revealed an elevation of oxidative damage (malondialdehyde and protein carbonyl levels, and reactive oxygen metabolites), and a depletion of an enzymatic antioxidant (SOD activity) but an increase in total antioxidant capacity, with increasing non-essential element content, especially cadmium and mercury. Essential elements showed limited and biomarker-specific associations with redox status, and modulated some of the reported associations between non-essential elements and oxidative stress biomarkers. Finally, individuals that had recently experienced higher temperatures or rainfall exhibited stronger responses. Overall, our study raises concerns regarding the broader consequences of chronic exposure to non-essential elements for wildlife health.

items.title: Relationships between the isotopic signatures of dissolved inorganic carbon and environmental variability in Northern Ireland coastal waters
items.blurb: The isotopic signatures of dissolved inorganic carbon ({delta}13C-DIC) can provide a sensitive tracer of biological and biogeochemical processes in aquatic environments. However, isotopic measurements remain uncommon within routine coastal monitoring programmes. This pilot study investigated spatial variability in {delta}13C-DIC in surface waters across twelve Northern Ireland coastal monitoring stations sampled during July 2020. We tested the relationships between {delta}13C-DIC, dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) concentration, nutrients, chlorophyll-a, temperature and salinity. {delta}13C-DIC exhibited substantial spatial variability, ranging from 1.25 to 2.53{per thousand}. Significant positive relationships were observed between {delta}13C-DIC and temperature (R2 = 0.55, p = 0.009), chlorophyll-a concentration (R2 = 0.38, p = 0.045) and DIC concentration (R2 = 0.52, p = 0.012), while significant negative relationships occurred with dissolved inorganic nitrogen (R2 = 0.53, p = 0.011) and phosphate (R2 = 0.44, p = 0.026). No relationships were detected between {delta}13C-DIC and salinity, suggesting that conservative mixing processes exerted little influence on isotopic variability across the study area. Bulk DIC concentration exhibited comparatively weak associations with environmental variables. The relationships we observed indicate that biological carbon fixation and nutrient use were important controls on spatial variation in {delta}13C-DIC in the coastal waters of Northern Ireland. These findings demonstrate the potential value of {delta}13C-DIC measurements as sensitive indicators of coastal carbon-cycle dynamics and support their inclusion within future coastal monitoring and assessment programmes.

items.title: Ex utero development of mouse embryos from fertilization to mid-gestation
items.blurb: Early mammalian development has largely been studied as two periods divided by implantation: a pre implantation period, when the embryo transits freely through the maternal reproductive tract, and a post implantation period, when it develops within the uterine tissues. Although robust culture methods for mammalian pre-implantation or post-implantation embryos have been established, the continuous transition from the pre implantation zygote to organogenesis has remained recalcitrant to faithful capture in vitro in mammalian species. Here we establish PRE implantation Initiated Ex Utero culture (PRI ExUt), a sequential platform supporting continuous development of natural mouse embryos from the zygote to the E9.5 organogenesis stage, spanning nearly half of gestation without maternal interaction, embedding within exogenous extracellular matrices or co-culture with endometrial organoids. Cultured zygotes developed in vitro into blastocysts, formed egg cylinders, completed gastrulation, and progressed through neurulation, somitogenesis, axial turning and neural tube closure, generating embryonic and extra embryonic tissues with morphology and single-cell transcriptional identity highly similar to those of stage-matched natural embryos developed in utero. We harnessed this platform as a functional benchmark for mouse stem-cell-derived blastoids and found that supplementation with an in vitro-derived OCT4+GATA6+ primitive endoderm-like population substantially extended their developmental potential, enabling bona fide mouse blastoids to reach mid-gastrulation egg-cylinder stages, contingent upon application of PRI-ExUt approach. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that mouse embryos can self-organize faithfully from fertilization to mid-gestation independently of maternal input and establish a continuous experimental window into the first half of mouse embryogenesis. By supporting continuous ex utero development from the zygote to E9.5 in the mouse (corresponding to human Carnegie stages 12/13, 26 to 32 days post fertilization), this platform offers a flexible framework for evaluating the developmental potential of mouse pre implantation embryos and embryo models, and informs ongoing international ethical discussions and legislative efforts to revisit the limits placed on human embryo in vitro culture beyond day 14.

items.title: Mechanical canalization of chiral gut morphogenesis
items.blurb: Chiral organs such as the gut develop complex, stereotyped shapes, despite variability in the molecular and cellular processes that build them. How cell activity specifies tissue-scale handedness and reproducibly shapes whole organs remains unclear. Here, we use the embryonic Drosophila midgut to understand how a symmetric tubular organ reliably coils into a complex loop of alternating handedness, without any known left-right asymmetric gene expression.Through multi-view light-sheet imaging, 3D geometric analysis, and physical modeling, we show that midgut handedness is specified by epithelial cells in a neighboring organ, relayed across all three germ layers, and finally amplified and canalized by the mechanics of confined gut elongation. Myosin 1C expression in the hindgut epithelium controls midgut handedness up to hundreds of microns away, transmitting chiral bias to the midgut through migratory cells that form the longitudinal muscle. As the midgut elongates, a buckling instability then amplifies early left-right asymmetric constrictions, and confinement funnels the organ into a stereotyped coil. Tissue mechanics thus canalizes organ shape into one of two chiral forms, selected by an inter-organ cellular relay.

items.title: A CITE-seq atlas of mouse embryonic hematopoiesis maps endothelial heterogeneity and reveals emerging HSC-associated states
items.blurb: The emergence of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) from hemogenic endothelium during embryonic development is a tightly regulated process in which only a restricted population acquires molecular features associated with long-term hematopoietic potential. Although endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition (EHT) has been extensively characterized, the transcriptional and phenotypic heterogeneity accompanying the emergence of HSC-associated states remains incompletely understood. Here, we generated an integrated single-cell transcriptomic and surface-protein atlas of mouse embryonic hematopoiesis using CITE-seq across E9.5, E10.25 and E11.5 aorta-gonad-mesonephros (AGM) regions and E11.5 foetal liver. Analysis of lineage-associated transcriptional programmes distinguished arterial, venous, hemogenic and HSC-associated states, with HSC-associated signatures occupying a more restricted distribution than broader hematopoietic specification programmes. Hlf expression closely corresponded with HSC-associated transcriptional signatures and CD27 surface-protein abundance, identifying a potentially useful immunophenotypic feature for prospective enrichment of HSC-associated populations. Graph-based connectivity, diffusion pseudotime and RNA velocity analyses revealed heterogeneous relationships among endothelial and hemogenic populations, suggesting an inferred progression from arterial preHSC-HE through arterial HSC-HE towards more advanced HSC-associated states. Notably, analysis of E9.5 endothelial cells identified a restricted subset exhibiting elevated RNA velocity-derived connectivity towards arterial preHSC-HE. These cells displayed distinct transcriptional features with enrichment of pathways associated with cell adhesion, junctional organization and signalling. Differences in selected surface proteins further distinguished endothelial cells with high and low predicted connectivity. In parallel, analysis of arterial hemogenic populations revealed changes in transcriptional programmes and surface-protein expression along inferred developmental trajectories, highlighting coordinated molecular and immunophenotypic remodeling during HSC-associated development. Together, these findings provide a multimodal framework for resolving endothelial heterogeneity and identifying candidate cellular states associated with early HSC emergence. By linking transcriptional signatures to measurable surface phenotypes, this atlas offers experimentally testable strategies for investigating the developmental conditions that precede HSC-associated identity, while distinguishing computationally inferred trajectories from functionally established HSC fate.

items.title: Breastfeeding Enables Systemic Transfer of Functional Maternal Immune Cells to Neonates
items.blurb: Does breastfeeding transfer living maternal immune cells that persist and function in offspring, beyond providing soluble immune factors? Using a foster-nursing mouse model that eliminates prenatal exposure, this study directly tests whether maternal cells can be transferred postnatally through breastmilk. We found that intact maternal immune cells survive neonatal gastrointestinal transit, enter the circulation, and disseminate to peripheral organs. Single-cell RNA sequencing shows that transferred cells span multiple hematopoietic lineages, dominated by monocyte-derived macrophages with a distinct stress-adapted, inflammatory transcriptional state compatible with persistence in the neonatal environment. Interestingly, these maternal cells are detected at sites of neonatal tissue injury, consistent with chemotactic responsiveness. Our findings suggest that breastfeeding may serve as a postnatal route for maternal cellular transfer, potentially extending maternal immune influence beyond gestation.

items.title: Activity-based fluorescence screening uncovers host enzymatic responses to SARS-CoV-2 infection
items.blurb: Transcriptomic and proteomic studies have characterized host responses to SARS-CoV-2 infection, yet changes in endogenous enzymatic activities remain poorly understood. Here, we screened 89 enzyme-activatable fluorescence probes in living SARS-CoV-2-infected Calu-3 cells and identified 18 probes showing enhanced fluorescence, with some exhibiting multiplicity-of-infection-dependent responses. Neither SARS-CoV-2 Mpro nor PLpro activated the tested probes, and several did not exhibit comparable fluorescence enhancements in influenza-virus-infected cells. Target identification and biochemical validation implicated calpain-1 (CAPN1) and puromycin-sensitive aminopeptidase (PSA) as major contributors to probe activation. A PSA-reactive fluorescence probe confirmed that SARS-CoV-2-infected living cells showed enhanced PSA activity, which was suppressed by puromycin. Immunofluorescence analysis revealed a strong positive correlation between PSA and SARS-CoV-2 spike protein signals. Notably, neither CAPN1 nor PSA was included among differentially expressed genes or proteins previously identified in SARS-CoV-2-infected cells. These findings highlight activity-based fluorescence screening as a complementary strategy to expression-based analyses for discovering infection-induced biomarker enzymes.

items.title: New medium for the production of Dermacentor reticulatus and Ixodes persulcatus tick primary cell lines
items.blurb: Background. The increasing prevalence of diseases caused by vector borne infections is an important public health problem. Currently, over 1000 extant tick species have been identified worldwide, and approximately ten percent of them are known to be vectors of pathogens (protozoa, bacteria, and viruses), leading to diseases in animals and humans. Tick cell lines are increasingly being used in research on tick physiology and the pathogens of vector borne infections. To obtain and maintain tick cell lines, traditionally used L-15-based nutrient media. However, obtaining a continuous tick cell line remains a complex and time consuming process. Therefore, it is important to develop new methods that can accelerate the process of obtaining tick cell cultures. Methods. To establish primary tick cell lines, we used, for the first time, a ready-made DMEM/F12 + GlutaMAX culture medium supplemented with 20% fetal bovine serum. Results. In this study, it was shown that DMEM/F12 + GlutaMAX nutrient medium is suitable for obtaining primary cell cultures of two species of ticks from two different genera of the family Ixodidae. Primary cell lines of the tick Ixodes persulcatus were obtained for the first time. We also managed to accelerate the process of obtaining subcultures: the first subcultures were obtained within 1-2 months of tick tissue isolation. Conclusions. This new method, allows us to overcome several existing technical difficulties. It is likely that the DMEM/F12 + Glutamax medium can also be used to obtain and maintain tick cell lines of other species. Thus, an alternative to the traditionally used L-15-based media has emerged, allowing researchers to select the medium most suitable for their tasks. The rapid production of subcultures creates opportunities to conduct certain studies directly on primary cultures, without waiting for their transformation into an immortal culture.

items.title: Tracking the trajectory of individual conjugative plasmids in bacterial communities using CRISPR acquisition-based recording
items.blurb: Horizontal gene transfer mediated by conjugative plasmids is a primary driver of bacterial evolution and the spread of adaptive traits, including antibiotic resistance determinants. Tracking how these plasmids disseminate through complex microbial communities remains a major challenge. Current methodologies often yield static, endpoint snapshots of host identity, overlooking transient transfer events and plasmid encounters with the co-resident mobilome. To overcome these limitations, we introduce SPacer Integration (SPI) plasmids, which turn the mobile element itself into a recorder of its own transfer history. We engineered conjugative and mobilizable plasmids to carry a CRISPR-Cas adaptation cassette (cas1-cas2 and a minimal CRISPR array) and maintain tight repression of cas1-cas2 expression in the donor cell, so that upon transfer they capture spacers from the chromosome and plasmids of new hosts and store them permanently in their own array. Subsequent PCR amplification and sequencing of these expanded arrays provide a molecular record of both the bacterial hosts and the co-resident plasmids encountered. We created SPI plasmids using the backbones of well-characterized mobilizable and conjugative plasmids RSF1010, RP4, F, and R100-1. We tested SPI plasmids in defined laboratory matings and in complex wastewater communities. The analysis of the acquired spacers successfully mapped permissive host ranges and profiled the co-resident plasmids in situ. Requiring only standard cloning, PCR and sequencing, this accessible and cost-effective strategy establishes a new framework for studying plasmid ecology. Because spacers are integrated chronologically, it further offers the potential to reconstruct multi-step transfer trajectories across natural microbial networks.

items.title: Modelling Maternal-to-Zygotic Transition Dynamics to Identify Common Gene Expression Baselines in Zebrafish Development.
items.blurb: We propose a semi-mechanistic ODE-based transcription model for zebrafish embryogenesis that captures common baseline expression dynamics by integrating the maternal-to-zygotic transition mechanism. We fitted this model to a time-course RNA-seq dataset of D. rerio spanning early developmental stages until 120 hpf. Using the inferred model parameters, we identified common gene expression pattern using fuzzy c-means clustering and compared these with clusters stemming from a shape-based approach using smooth trajectories. We show that the ODE-parameter-based approach improves to biological interpretability by linking clusters to underlying regulatory mechanism, such as the timing of zygotic genome activation, thereby generating more precise expression clusters. However, the results also revealed technical biases of the time-course data, originating from the poly(A) enrichment step.

items.title: An atlas of the sRNAs and their targets in Staphylococcus aureus
items.blurb: Staphylococcus aureus is an opportunistic pathogen that causes various diseases in animals and humans. Small RNAs (sRNAs) control major steps in the infection process and acclimation responses, contributing to the architecture of the regulatory networks. However, a large number of putative sRNAs remain poorly characterized. Here we present aureoRNA, an interactive database (https://aurorna.biologie.uni-freiburg.de) that integrates available information for each sRNA, including phylogeny in the phylum Bacillota, public transcriptome datasets for sRNA and mRNA correlation, and permits computational predictions of sRNA functions. The aureoRNA-based analysis of the sRNA RsaD revealed new targets including the oxidative threonine catabolism and the arginine deiminase pathway. A target-centric search identifying potential sRNAs for mRNAs of interest revealed the citZ citrate synthase mRNA as an RsaE target, and two small prophage genes as RNAIII interaction partner. The aureoRNA database facilitates the functional characterization of the entire set of sRNAs and their targets in this major pathogen.

items.title: TRAIT: A Toolbox for Rapid Assembly of Integration Templates for CRISPR/Cas- and Integrase-Mediated Genome Engineering
items.blurb: The generation of genetically engineered mammalian cell models often requires repeated construction of integration donors that differ in their targeting sequences, genetic payloads, or integration strategies. Although modular DNA assembly methods facilitate construct generation, adapting existing expression cassettes to different genome-engineering applications remains labor-intensive. Here, we present TRAIT (Toolbox for Rapid Assembly of Integration Templates), a modular cloning framework that combines direct Golden Gate assembly of targeting elements with Gateway-mediated transfer of genetic payloads. The core vector architecture separates genome-targeting sequences from payload assembly, allowing existing Gateway-compatible constructs to be reused without modification of internal Type IIS restriction sites. We developed vector modules supporting homology-directed repair, homology-independent targeted integration, FrameSelect-compatible donor cleavage, coordinated guide RNA delivery, inducible Cas9 expression, Bxb1-mediated cassette exchange, and conditional transgene expression. An extended MultiSite Gateway workflow enables the assembly of complex integration donors using independently prepared regulatory modules, including components from the Mammalian ToolKit. Functional validation in human cells demonstrated targeted integration, recombinase-mediated cassette exchange, and multiplexed genome editing. We further applied TRAIT to generate human induced pluripotent stem cells carrying functional doxycycline-inducible Cas9 and candidate landing-pad integration constructs. Together, these results establish TRAIT as an interoperable framework for assembling and deploying diverse genome-engineering constructs in mammalian cells.

items.title: Persistence of Non-industrial Gut Microbiota Discriminates Health and Disease States in Industrial Populations
items.blurb: Industrialization has sharply reduced gut microbial diversity, possibly affecting human health. To isolate the effects of industrialization, we assembled 18,075 human metagenomes spanning hunter-gatherer, agro-pastoral, and industrial lifestyles. We confirmed individual-level diversity reductions in industrial populations, but also found that nearly all known human-associated microbes exhibit population-level persistence. Previously hypothesized 'vanishing' microbes are reduced from high prevalence in non-industrial populations to above-median prevalence in industrial populations. Species-level signatures in industrial case-control cohorts suggest that harboring 'vanishing' taxa can be associated with health or pathology, depending on the condition. Controlling for background prevalence, 'vanishing' microbes were more likely associated with cases than controls in obesity, both 'vanishing' microbes and those now 'blossoming' in industrialized populations were associated with glucose intolerance, while 'blossoming' taxa were associated with inflammatory bowel disease. We conclude that most microbes have not gone extinct under industrialization, and that the health effects of lifestyle-associated taxa are context-dependent.

items.title: Persistence of commensal Escherichia coli strains and plasmid transfer in a healthy adult
items.blurb: Little is known about the ecological dynamics of Escherichia coli strains in the healthy human intestinal tract. Here, the composition of commensal E. coli in a healthy adult was tracked over 700 days. 100 E. coli isolates recovered directly from each of 21 faecal samples collected at monthly intervals were characterised. In total 15 strains were recovered; five were resistant to one or more antibiotics. Five "persistent" strains were found in multiple samples spanning 1- to 5-month periods. The relative abundance of persistent strains ranged from 1-100% of E. coli per sample, but they were dominant (>80%) in 14/21 samples and the only strain in 12. Complete genomes were determined for all strains, including isolates of persistent strains from their first and last appearances. Persistent strains belonged to phylogroups B2 (ST1236 and ST420), A (ST10 and ST93), or D (ST362). Single-sample strains were phylogroup A, B1, B2, D or F. Confirming extended survival in the gut, only minor changes were detected in the chromosomes of persistent strains over their residence periods. However, one lost a plasmid and two gained plasmids, providing evidence for horizontal gene transfer in the gut. A Z-type multidrug resistance plasmid moved from one persistent strain to the next and exchanged a small backbone region with a plasmid in the recipient. An M-type arsenic resistance plasmid was acquired by two different strains and transferred to laboratory E. coli with two co-resident plasmids. All persistent strains, but only 2/10 single-sample strains, carried one or more plasmid-borne bacteriocin determinants.

items.title: History of coadaptation to the cag pathogenicity island in Helicobacter pylori
items.blurb: Most Helicobacter pylori strains use genes encoded on the cag pathogenicity island (cagPAI) to inject the CagA oncoprotein into human cells, where it alters cell signalling and morphology to promote bacterial colonization. However, cag- H. pylori strains are found worldwide. Here, we use a global sample of >9,000 Helicobacter genomes to investigate how strains adapt to cag status. We identified variants genome-wide associated with cagPAI presence, including many in vacA and hopQ, as well as in genes not previously linked to cag. We use these variants to construct a cag polygenic coadaptation score, allowing us to systematically explore the dynamics and evolutionary history of the island. Score distribution is bimodal in many populations, showing there is a stable adaptive strategy associated with cag- status. However, these cag- coadapted variants have historically been unavailable to strains in East Asia, providing a potential explanation for the low frequency of cag- strains in this region. We also infer that the cagPAI arrived in H. pylori before the human populations which colonized Australia and Papua New Guinea split from other groups 50,000-70,000 years ago. Adaptation to the island in other populations was achieved in part by using existing variants from the Hardy ecospecies. Our study illustrates how gene coadaptation shapes pathogen evolution after import of a major virulence factor and highlights genetic configurations that may predict increased or decreased disease risk, informing eradication strategies.

items.title: Keratinocyte IL-17RA signaling promotes neutrophil recruitment and clinical lesions in experimental epidermolysis bullosa
items.blurb: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA) is an autoimmune blistering disease (AIBD) characterized by anti-type VII collagen autoantibody-mediated tissue injury. Neutrophils have been identified as essential for dermal-epidermal separation in various in vitro and mouse models of EBA. Although interleukin-17 (IL-17) signaling promotes neutrophilic inflammation, its contribution to EBA and the relevant responding cell types remain poorly defined. We investigated the role and cellular targets of IL-17 receptor A (IL-17RA) signaling using an antibody-transfer model of EBA in mice with global IL-17RA deficiency, combined IL-17A/IL-17F deficiency, IL-17F deficiency, or myeloid cell- or keratinocyte-specific IL-17RA deletion. Complementary in vitro assays assessed IL-17A-induced chemokine expression and neutrophil migration. Global IL-17RA deficiency, combined IL-17A/IL-17F deficiency, and IL-17F deficiency significantly reduced disease severity in vivo. Keratinocyte-specific IL-17RA deletion markedly attenuated EBA, whereas myeloid cell-specific deletion did not confer protection. In vitro, IL-17A increased Cxcl1 mRNA expression in keratinocytes and fibroblasts, and conditioned media from stimulated cells promoted neutrophil migration. These findings identify keratinocytes as key cellular targets of IL-17RA signaling in experimental EBA and support a mechanism linking epithelial cytokine responses to neutrophil recruitment and tissue injury. Our data support investigating the keratinocyte IL-17RA pathway as a potential therapeutic target in EBA and related AIBD.
