items.title: Low serine-glycine-one-carbon pathway activity defines purine salvage dependence in neuroblastoma
items.blurb: MYCN amplification promotes serine-glycine-one-carbon (SGOC) metabolism in neuroblastoma, creating an intrinsic difference in SGOC activity between MYCNamplified and non-MYCN-amplified high-risk tumors. This metabolic distinction provides a model to investigate how SGOC activity shapes purine metabolism. Here, we show that non-MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma cell lines exhibit lower SGOC pathway activity and are more resistant to pharmacologic suppression of SGOC metabolism by SHMT inhibition under serine- and glycine-deprived conditions. Stable-isotope tracing revealed that non-MYCN-amplified cells exhibited lower contribution of serine-derived glycine and one-carbon units to de novo purine synthesis but elevated basal hypoxanthine and adenine salvage. These cells also showed greater preservation of adenylate pools during SHMT inhibition. Genetic depletion of APRT or HPRT1 preferentially impaired proliferation of non-MYCN-amplified cells, demonstrating increased salvage dependence. SHMT inhibition increased purine salvage, providing additional evidence that suppression of SGOC metabolism shifts purine production toward salvage. We also identify methionine salvage as an endogenous source of adenine that supports proliferation during SHMT inhibition through an MTAP-adenine-APRT axis. Together, these findings establish SGOC pathway activity as an intrinsic determinant of whether cells preferentially rely on de novo purine synthesis or purine salvage and identify salvage dependence as a potential therapeutic vulnerability of low-SGOC tumors.

items.title: Combined JAK2 and HSP90 inhibition produces synergistic anti-tumour activity across preclinical glioblastoma models
items.blurb: Background: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains difficult to treat because of tumour heterogeneity and the limited activity of single-target therapies. Our previous phenotypic drug screen identified JAK2/STAT3 signalling and HSP90-dependent protein homeostasis as pharmacological vulnerabilities. We investigated whether combined JAK2 and HSP90 inhibition could produce broader anti-tumour activity across GBM models. Methods: Multiple JAK2 and HSP90 inhibitors were tested alone and in combination across 2- and 3-dimensional patient-derived GBM stem cell models. Drug interactions were quantified using the zero-interaction potency (ZIP) synergy model. Mechanistic studies included RNA sequencing, flow cytometry, western blotting, immunofluorescence and FUCCI live-cell imaging. Activity was also assessed in cerebral organoid GBM co-cultures, non-malignant human neural and glial cells and orthotopic GBM xenografts. Results: Combined JAK2 and HSP90 inhibition produced synergistic interactions in 12 of the 13 GBM cell lines tested, using multiple structurally distinct inhibitor pairs. Gandotinib and NMS-E973 were selected for further mechanistic studies, where the combination reduced spheroid growth and increased caspase-3 activation and PARP cleavage. Combination treatment was associated with G2/M accumulation, altered mitotic regulation, abnormal chromosome and spindle organisation, and increased gamma-H2AX signalling. Anti-tumour combination activity was maintained in cerebral organoid co-cultures, where tumour burden was reduced as assessed by imaging, histological and luciferase-based measurements, while the drug combination had relatively limited effects on non-malignant human neural and glial cell types tested over the same concentration range. In vivo, combined Pacritinib and NMS-E973 treatment significantly reduced tumour burden in orthotopic G7 xenografts compared with vehicle or either single agent. Conclusions: JAK2/HSP90 co-inhibition produces reproducible anti-tumour activity across heterogeneous GBM models and disrupts cell-cycle and mitotic progression. These findings support further evaluation of this combination strategy in GBM.

items.title: Investigating the critical role of serine in antimicrobial peptide binding to lipopolysaccharide
items.blurb: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a major component of the Gram-negative bacterial outer membrane, is a potent endotoxin responsible for triggering severe host immune responses and sepsis. Understanding the atomic-level mechanisms governing how antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) recognize and neutralize LPS is essential for designing effective anti-endotoxin therapeutics. Here, we present an in silico investigation of the single-molecule interaction between Escherichia coli O111:B4 LPS and the cationic antimicrobial peptide GL13K, alongside two single-point mutants at position 9 (GL13KS9A and GL13KS9T), using all-atom molecular dynamics and umbrella sampling simulations. Consistent with experimental trends, mutating SER9 into alanine significantly alters peptide binding affinity to LPS. Surpisingly, removal of the polar character of serine leads to substantial changes in the interaction of the N-terminus with LPS via the loss of hydrogen bonding to stabilize a hook shape at the C-terminal end. In specific, while wild-type GL13K exhibits the strongest unbinding free-energy barrier, the S9A substitution changes the conformational landscape in such a way as to redirect the peptide's N-terminus from lipid A toward the core oligosaccharide and substantially reduces the unbinding barrier, whereas S9T maintains an similar affinity. Our work demonstrates the effects of distal mutations even in peptides on their binding and lays important groundwork for the development of peptide-based LPS inhibitors.

items.title: From DNA Helicity to Structural Twist: An Undergraduate Laboratory Module for DNA Origami Design
items.blurb: Precise control of nanoscale architectures makes DNA origami a promising platform for biomedical applications such as drug delivery, biosensing, and bioimaging. A key constraint in DNA origami design is that crossover placement must account for the helical pitch of DNA. For new learners, however, it can be difficult to understand how a DNA helical pitch affects assembled structures. Here, we report a hands-on laboratory module to teach undergraduate students about this fundamental helical pitch/structure relationship. A rectangular DNA origami tile is designed as a model system with its helical pitch varying from 10.5 to 10.84 base-pairs per turn. When the tiles are linked into a ribbon, the small mismatch-driven deformations of individual tiles accumulate into a global twist. The twist appears as characteristic kinks under atomic force microscopy (AFM). In a five-day pilot, three engineering students designed the DNA origami tile and used CanDo finite-element simulations to predict its deformations at different helical pitches. They assembled ribbons and used an intercalator, ethidium bromide (EtBr), to vary DNA helicity without changing the crossover layout. With increasing EtBr concentration, all three participants observed the ribbon chirality transition from right-handed to flat to left-handed conformations. By comparing predictions with their own observations, students gain a practical understanding of how DNA helicity governs DNA structure design.

items.title: Prediction and Dissection of Nitrogenase Activity Based on Protein Sequences using Dual Descriptor
items.blurb: Nitrogenase reduces N2 to ammonia at ambient temperature and pressure, but its activity differs markedly among natural sequences, and conventional wet-laboratory screening suffers from low throughput and long turnaround times. Existing computational methods have partially alleviated this bottleneck, yet most of them rely on protein embeddings obtained from protein language models together with features such as gene expression, and their interpretability analyses mostly stop at the level of feature contribution. Here we present CarmnaDD, a purely sequence-driven framework built on the dual descriptor (DD): two learnable components, the composition weight map (CWM) and the position weight function (PWF), jointly generate a position-resolved description N(k), so that activity can be predicted without any prior knowledge beyond the sequence. On the same dataset used by Carmna, CarmnaDD attains R2 = 0.60 for regression and AUC = 0.94 and F1 = 0.86 for classification, better than our previous Carmna, which integrates multiple features. Interpretability analysis shows that the amplitude of the periodic terms of the PWF decreases as the rank increases, indicating that the positional encoding strategy adapts to the rank; the high-weight 3-mer fragments in the CWM are significantly enriched in polar uncharged residues, which corroborates the SHAP-based conclusion of Carmna; sliding-window scanning identifies fragments significantly associated with activity (FDR < 0.05), and the strongest window displays a D-X-E pattern with conserved flanks and a polymorphic center, sequences carrying R at the central position showing the highest activity; conservation is significantly negatively correlated ({rho} = -0.30) with description intensity. Mapping the key windows onto the protein structure shows that four highly correlated windows converge on the nucleotide-binding interface and the conformational-transmission/protein-docking interface of NifH. These results provide a purely sequence-based framework for nitrogenase activity prediction that balances performance and interpretability.

items.title: Localizing Unsampled Regions in Partially Sampled Pathogen Phylogenies Using Machine Learning
items.blurb: Motivation: Pathogen phylogenies are useful for monitoring the evolution of pathogens and for detecting new variants, as it provides information that can aid public health decisions and outbreak response. Since not all infections are sequenced, certain pathogen lineages may be missing or only poorly represented in reconstructed phylogenies. Identifying these gaps could help to determine where additional data collection is required. Results: We developed a computational method to locate regions of missing samples from the observed tree alone, without sequences from those samples. A machine learning model predicts which branches lead toward the missing region. Beam search then identifies three representative paths and estimates a candidate most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of the missing region for each path. We tested this framework on 5,000 simulated phylogenies where we controlled which tips were deleted. On an independent test set, the best candidate recovered an average of 89.9% of deleted tips, increasing to 90.7% when all three candidates were combined. Predicted and true MRCAs lay on the same ancestral-descendant lineage in 91.3% of cases. We further evaluated the approach on an empirical SARS-CoV-2 phylogeny with introduced missingness. By identifying potentially underrepresented lineages, this framework could help real-time identification of missing infections and improve outbreak response.

items.title: Machine Learning-Assisted Raman Spectroscopy for Quantitative Prediction of Multicomponent Mixtures
items.blurb: Machine Learning (ML)-assisted Raman spectroscopy that can efficiently analyze molecularly specific fingerprints is well suited for quantitative analysis of complex chemical mixtures. However, developing accurate predictive ML models for multicomponent systems remains difficult because collecting sufficient experimental calibration data is slow, expensive, and limited. In this work, we present a ML-assisted Raman spectroscopy framework for predicting the quantitative composition of multicomponent lipid mixtures (consisting of 15 lipids). To reduce the experimental burden of generating extensive multicomponent spectral datasets, we computationally constructed a large spectral library using experimentally measured pure-component Raman spectra from 15 lipids, including triglycerides, medium- and long-chain fatty acids, and fatty acid methyl and ethyl esters. Mixture compositions were sampled across a constrained compositional space and used to generate training spectra from weighted combinations of the pure component spectra. Experimentally prepared mixtures were then used to evaluate the model under real measurement conditions. To reduce the mismatch between library-generated spectra and experimental mixture spectra, a linear correction strategy was applied to account for systematic spectral differences caused by mixing effects, intermolecular interactions, and measurement variability. The corrected experimental spectra were then used for concentration prediction with an uncertainty-aware workflow. The compositions of the 15 lipid mixtures were successfully predicted using the ML model trained solely on a simulated dataset, achieving R^2 values exceeding 0.95 for each lipid. By combining scalable, library-based model training with experimental validation on physical multicomponent mixtures, this approach minimizes the need for exhaustive calibration datasets while maintaining high quantitative accuracy. The proposed framework offers a practical path for quantitative Raman analysis of chemical mixtures and can easily be extended to quality control applications across the food, pharmaceutical, nutraceutical, and chemical industries.

items.title: Sparrowhawk: harnessing WebAssembly for private microbial genomics, and beyond
items.blurb: Computational methods are a growing component of every scientific discipline, but the pace of training and expertise for using these methods has not kept up with their widening usage. Researchers expect state-of-the-art methods to be able to independently explore their results, and do so dynamically and interactively. Producing such an application which implements a new algorithm, even though it would access a much wider audience, is typically beyond the expertise and time constraints of computational method developers. Here, we show our Sparrowhawk framework can rapidly create an interactive web application to run interactive analysis on a user's machine, across a wide range of algorithms. Focusing first on genomic epidemiology, a domain with a specific need for such methods, we created novel lightweight methods for genome assembly, antimicrobial resistance gene annotation, and taxonomic identification. Our results exceed performance of previous lightweight methods, and produce results that reproduce or closely match previous analysis pipelines. By using WebAssembly, our framework benefits from not requiring installation, command line knowledge, or transferring sensitive data over an internet connection. We show how algorithms from other researchers, and spanning fields from machine learning to physics, can rapidly be ported to web tools using our framework. We demonstrate an immediate impact on microbial bioinformatics, but expect that uptake of Sparrowhawk by developers of other tools broadly will help other researchers, and create new tools for teaching and public engagement. Thanks to the broad availability and familiarity with web browser tools across society, Sparrowhawk has the potential to significantly lower the barrier to entry to advanced computational methods.

items.title: Dual photoresponsive hydrogel surfaces enabling integrated single-cell analysis of morphology and gene expression
items.blurb: Integrated single-cell analysis linking time-resolved cellular phenotypic dynamics with gene expression is essential for understanding cellular heterogeneity but remains technically challenging. Here, we report a dual photoresponsive hydrogel that combines a photoactivatable cell-trapping material with a photodegradable hydrogel, enabling light-directed single-cell capture, time-resolved imaging, and the on-demand release of selected cells for downstream gene expression analysis. This approach allows cells to be arrayed at a high density with uniform spacing, facilitating high-throughput monitoring of morphological dynamics. Cells exhibiting phenotypes of interest can be precisely retrieved by localized hydrogel degradation induced by secondary light irradiation and subsequently subjected to single-cell gene expression analysis. Using this workflow in combination with high-throughput real-time image processing technology, we directly link dynamic morphological features to gene expression and demonstrated the ability of the workflow to examine transcriptional alterations associated with invasive cancer cell behavior.

items.title: Towards an understanding of injury in aortic tissue prior to actual failure: quantification of mechanically induced collagen damage using collagen hybridizing peptides
items.blurb: The development, validation, and optimization of endovascular aortic devices require quantitative assessment of tissue damage occurring during surgical interventions. Until now, this assessment--before complete failure--has been largely unfeasible for lack of a suitable methodology. Recently developed collagen hybridizing peptides (CHPs) allow selective detection of damage to collagen, the primary load-bearing constituent of the aortic wall. However, their application in large, mechanically loaded arteries has not yet been established. Therefore, we optimized an experimental workflow for large arteries that accounts for their energy-storage function and geometrical constraints; furthermore, we have characterized the tissue's autofluorescence and selected a suitable CHP fluorophore. Specimens from a single porcine aorta were examined using uniaxial tensile testing, histological analysis, fluorescence spectral analysis, confocal microscopy, and quantitative image analysis to present collagen damage as a function of tissue stretch. The workflow detected load-induced collagen damage before tissue failure, whereas histological evaluation showed no obvious load-induced disruption. Damage scores were comparable between the undeformed control and the specimen stretched by a factor of 1.2, while specimens stretched beyond 1.2 exhibited elevated scores. This pattern corresponded to higher complication rates with excessive stent oversizing. Furthermore, the proposed protocol can be adapted for ex vivo stent deployment experiments to compare collagen damage resulting from various aortic device designs and deployment conditions. Quantitative damage metrics could inform structurally motivated constitutive material models for computational simulations of endovascular interventions. Combined with histological and structural analyses, this workflow could also help link tissue composition--or organization--to individual susceptibility to damage.

items.title: Pseudo-Central Retinal Blood Vessel in Pig, Sheep and Goat
items.blurb: Humans and non-human primates have central retinal blood vessels (CRBVs) through their optic nerve head (ONH). The collagen of pig, sheep and goat ONHs also forms structures that look like CRBVs. We aimed to determine whether the CRBV-like structures in pig, sheep and goat are true CRBVs or if they should instead be called pseudo-CRBVs. Coronal sections through the ONHs of human, monkey, pig, sheep and goat eyes were imaged for collagen. We then used DAPI, multicolor DiOlistics and GFAP immunostaining to visualize nuclei, astrocytes and other ONH constituents. CRBV-like structures were classified into three types: true CRBVs if the structure was only a blood vessel; fully pseudo-CRBV if the evidence indicated only neural tissues or cells other than erythrocytes within; or partial pseudo-CRBV if some of the region appeared as a vessel and other parts did not. All eyes exhibited CRBV-like structures in the collagen. In human and monkey eyes they were all true CRBVs. Conversely, the CRBV-like structures were fully or partially pseudo-CRBVs in 80% (4/5) of pig, 50% (3/6) of sheep and 100% (2/2) of goat eyes. In majority of pig, sheep and goat eyes, CRBV-like structures were actually pseudo-CRBVs. Often, what appeared like a vessel lumen, was instead filled by neural tissues reminiscent of pores. The mechanisms that lead to CRBV-like structures that are not actually CRBVs in these three species, but not in humans and monkeys, remain unknown.

items.title: Monoclonal antibodies for detecting collagen IV α3α4α5 in basement membranes
items.blurb: The collagen IV 345 trimer forms a specialised network within basement membranes that is essential for normal kidney, inner ear and ocular function. Variants in COL4A3, COL4A4 or COL4A5 disrupt this network and cause Alport syndrome. Yet, current antibody tools detect individual collagen IV chains rather than the assembled 345 trimer. Here, we generated a recombinant human mini-COL4A345 trimer and used it to produce mouse monoclonal antibodies that recognise native collagen IV 345. We screened hybridomas using biolayer interferometry, native dot blotting, denaturing western blotting and immunofluorescence, followed by characterisation of selected purified antibodies using surface plasmon resonance. Three clones, Ms5, Ms44 and Ms72, detected native, folded collagen IV 345. We validated antibody specificity using Col4a3, Col4a5 and Col4a6 knockout mouse tissues, and assessed their utility for human kidney immunofluorescence and immunoprecipitation from mouse kidney. The antibodies detected conformationally intact collagen IV 345 in tissue, with no detectable cross-reactivity with collagen IV 112 or 556 networks under the conditions tested. Clone Ms72 provided the strongest and most consistent tissue signal, localising collagen IV 345 to the glomerular basement membrane, cochlear basement membranes and retinal pigment epithelium-associated basement membrane. Ms72 also immunoprecipitated endogenous collagen IV 3, 4 and 5 from wild-type kidney tissue, confirming recognition of the native complex. These monoclonal antibodies provide a resource for detecting collagen IV 345 in basement membrane networks. Their potential applications include assessment of the 345 heterotrimer in patient biopsies and evaluation of gene therapies and other interventions aimed at modulating 345 deposition in Alport syndrome.

items.title: Social compensation changes predicted effects of individual loss in animal societies
items.blurb: Animal populations globally are suffering significant declines; many species are social, and individuals are likely to adjust their social behaviour as they lose associates. Therefore, social networks may respond to population decline as individuals adjust their social connections in response to changing social environments. Our understanding of how individual responses to loss of their associates alters the structure of their social networks is rudimentary. To quantify how social responses to individual loss can alter network structure, we simulated individual loss and compensatory formation of new social ties across 268 empirical animal social networks. Compensation changed the structural effects of individual loss, though these effects often depended on which individuals were removed. Loss of central, peripheral or random individuals produced different network responses, while social compensation had similar effects regardless of compensation strategy. Together, these results suggest that compensatory social behaviour can reorganise social networks as populations decline, even if departing from the original structure. Accounting for these responses may improve predictions of how demographic change affects social structure, particularly when losses are socially patterned and without knowing the compensation strategy. Broadly, our findings highlight compensation as a potentially important process linking individual social behaviour to the reorganisation of animal societies.

items.title: Spatial and epigenetic programs underlie heterogeneous cellular senescence in the aging liver
items.blurb: Aging is a complex biological process leading to tissue dysfunction, and driven in part by progressive epigenetic drift, widespread transcriptional dysregulation and cellular senescence. Senescent cells (SnCs) accumulate across tissues in a heterogeneous and cell type-specific manner, yet their molecular signatures and spatial organization within native tissue have not been systematically mapped. Here we combined single-nucleus transcriptomic, epigenomic, three-dimensional (3D) genome and spatial profiling to systematically characterize aging of the mouse liver and associated cellular senescence. Aging was marked by hepatocyte loss, immune cell expansion, erosion of repressive H3K9me3 heterochromatin, alteration of 3D genome organization, and activation of stress-response pathways known to promote senescence. Age-associated SnCs were spatially colocalized within discrete inflammatory microenvironments termed SenSpots. Different SenSpots were dominated by distinct hepatocyte senescence states (senotypes), driven by unique transcription factors, and exhibited distinct lobular zonation. Single-cell DNA methylation profiling revealed a subset of immune cells in aged livers with loss of DNA methylation at constitutive heterochromatin and elevated senescence signatures. AAV-mediated, p21-promoter driven Stat1 deletion in the aged liver selectively suppressed interferon-responsive senescence programs while pharmacological inhibition of MDM2 attenuated senescence-associated inflammatory signatures. Together, these findings reveal that hepatic senescence is not a uniform state but a set of diverse epigenetically reprogrammed, spatially organized, and pharmacologically modifiable inflammatory niches.

items.title: Quantum-assisted genomic prediction of blast resistance in rice (Oryza sativa L.) using SNP and haplotype representations
items.blurb: Rice blast caused by Magnaporthe oryzae threatens rice production, and genomic prediction may accelerate identification of resistant germplasm. We evaluated classical machine-learning and simulated quantum-kernel models for binary and three-class prediction of leaf blast (BL) and panicle blast (PB) resistance in 204 rice accessions with 2,120 repeated phenotypic observations. Models used 328,597 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), 104,068 phased haplotypes, or 49,451 unphased haplotypes. Binary prediction outperformed three-class prediction. The highest binary macro-F1 scores were 0.87 for BL and 0.73 for PB. Phased and unphased haplotypes reduced predictor dimensionality by 68.3% and 85.0%, respectively, while retaining broadly comparable performance. Quantum support vector classification achieved competitive results in selected binary tasks but did not consistently exceed the strongest classical models. These findings establish a benchmark for SNP- and haplotype-based prediction of rice blast resistance and for evaluation of quantum machine learning in crop genomics.

items.title: Ecotypes matter: photoperiod and site of origin underlie the onset of leaf senescence in Eriophorum vaginatum, an Arctic foundation species
items.blurb: The rapid warming of the Arctic is causing the growing season to expand and the climate to become more unpredictable. This scenario is intensifying a crucial trade-off arctic plants face: maximizing growth during the short growing season while avoiding freezes at the shoulder seasons. In response, ecotypes have evolved phenological behaviors that are finely tuned to their local climate, which often involves the use of photoperiod cues, especially in the fall. Under the rearrangement of temperature and light regimes, however, such phenological adaptations might prevent native plants from taking advantage of longer growing seasons. To test this phenological mechanism of local adaptation we used a decade-long reciprocal transplant experiment in Northern Alaska and observed the effects of seasonal light and temperature regimes on the leaf phenology of an arctic foundation species, Eriophorum vaginatum. We found that ecotypes rely heavily on site-specific photoperiod cues, but may also use temperature cues. These results indicate that local adaptation of this widespread species to local climates required the evolution of diverging phenological responses to seasonal changes in light. Because light cues will remain stable as the shoulder seasons expand, these adaptations are increasingly maladaptive, and could leave Eriophorum vulnerable to more competitive species.

items.title: Evolution of sex-specific hormesis in a toxic niche specialist
items.blurb: Ecological specialists often exploit toxic niches that can exclude competitors, predators and pathogens. Whether such specialization has intrinsic fitness benefits remains unclear. We address this question through study of Drosophila sechellia, a specialist on noni fruit, which is toxic for other insects. A noni diet did not affect innate behaviors but increased female reproductive fitness, lifespan and stress resistance, and biased offspring sex ratios towards females. These traits were linked to female-specific lipid accumulation upon noni consumption. Strikingly, noni's principal toxin, octanoic acid, reproduced these female-specific phenotypes, exhibiting a dose-dependent, biphasic - or hormetic - effect. The beneficial effects of octanoic acid require Alkbh7, a conserved mitochondrial protein involved in fatty acid metabolism. Finally, modelling showed fecundity and female bias can jointly maximize population growth. These results reveal how evolution of hormesis, to confer nutritious value upon a toxin, yields sexually-dimorphic fitness benefits, including an unusual uncoupling of reproductive fitness and lifespan.

items.title: Limitations of gene-dense datasets for inferring relationships in rapid radiations: An example from the Ice Plants
items.blurb: Premise: Aizoaceae (ice plants) are among the most rapidly radiating plant families on Earth, making them among the most difficult clades in the tree of life to resolve. Large, gene-rich datasets have been a powerful tool for exploring contentious relationships, and the Aizoaceae are an ideal model for testing the limits of gene-rich datasets for inferring the tree of life. Methods: In this study, we assembled a phylotranscriptomic dataset comprising 28 newly sequenced and 11 publicly available transcriptomes to infer relationships within the Aizoaceae. We inferred gene trees from 4,845 putative orthologs extracted from 15,818 homologous gene families, which we also used to infer gene duplications. We tested whether gene-tree filtering approaches could identify gene subsets that resolve relationships within the clade. Results: We found that, regardless of the gene-filtering approach or species-tree estimation, relationships among the Aizoaceae were largely congruent. Relationships within the subfamily Ruschioideae still showed little gene tree concordance. Our simulations show that inferring relationships within rapid radiations may be impossible because of short internodal branch lengths, regardless of the number of genes sampled. Gene duplication analysis at the base of the radiations provides candidates that potentially contributed to adaptations driving the radiation. Conclusions: This study highlights that rapid radiations can be difficult to infer because of pervasive incomplete lineage sorting and noise, and that limited information within individual genes may make methods that rely on gene trees unsuitable for these relationships. This appears to be the case in Aizoaceae; however, these limitations suggest that synteny-based analyses will play an important role in future investigations of the tree of life.

items.title: Continuity, not accuracy: how canopy approximations shape competition and selection in size-structured vegetation models
items.blurb: Light competition drives ecological and evolutionary processes in forests. Real canopies are too complex to simulate in full, so stand models approximate them. We assessed three canopy approximations, the Perfect Plasticity Approximation (PPA), Flat Top and Deep Crown, in two stages. First, we compared their instantaneous light interception with a high-resolution reference model (MAESPA), focusing on competition among individuals and on vulnerability to self-shading. Second, we embedded them in a dynamic vegetation model and traced effects on stand development, demographic equilibrium and invasion fitness, the basis of evolutionary prediction. Deep Crown, which allows leaf area to overlap between individuals, reproduced MAESPA's continuous response of light capture to height. The PPA, and the Flat Top in stands of uniform height, instead produced a stepwise response around the point where a focal tree becomes taller than its neighbours. In the dynamic model, the PPA's discontinuities were tolerable for stand development but shifted demographic equilibrium by an order of magnitude. Every runnable representation produced a continuously stable strategy (CSS), but under the PPA it was reached through a stepped, erratic selection gradient and was not robustly located. All approximations overestimated light capture under self-shading, increasingly so at realistic leaf area. Our results show that continuity of the shade each plant casts as a function of height, rather than average accuracy or assimilation detail, determines whether an approximation can support evolutionary inference. Approximations adequate for stand-level light interception can mislead for competition and selection among individuals.

items.title: Unravelling the Role of Uterine-Derived Estrogen in Establishing Endometrial Receptivity and Supporting Embryo Implantation and Decidualization in the Golden Hamster
items.blurb: The mammalian embryo implantation is generally regulated by ovarian estrogen and progesterone in laboratory animals so far studied. In some animals, like golden hamsters, the process of implantation is reported to be independent of ovarian estrogen. Other studies, however, suggest that estrogen-related events do exist for implantation. We also observed the complete absence of implantation in letrozole-treated uterine horns (an inhibitor of the key enzyme for estrogen biosynthesis). However, the vehicle-treated horn bear has a normal implantation site in D6 of pregnancy. Hence, there must be an involvement of estrogen that may come from a source other than the ovary. It may be either non-ovarian or locally synthesized (non-systemic, uterine). But the involvement of non-systemic estrogen is not well documented. So, in the present study, the de novo synthesis of estrogen in the uterus and its role in early pregnancy is described. For this, letrozole-treated and control uterine horns were further studied using the tools of proteomics and genomics to know the exact cause of failure of implantation. Using IHC, it was observed that there is a presence of cytochrome P450 aromatase, a rate-limiting enzyme in the estrogen biosynthesis pathway, in the uterine horn of pregnant hamsters at the time of implantation. The expression profile of this enzyme and their mRNA was further checked by western blot and real-time PCR, respectively. It also corroborated earlier IHC observations. We found that their expression is markedly induced at the implantation site and in stromal cells around the day of implantation and decidualization, respectively. This aromatase is responsible for de novo synthesis of estrogen in association with other steroidogenic enzymes, which was also observed to be present in the uterus during early pregnancy. This locally synthesized estrogen is sufficient to elicit other implantation-specific physiological factors required for successful embryo implantation and decidualization in the absence of ovarian estrogen. Since embryo implantation in human beings is also ovarian estrogen independent and much more similar to hamster, so, this study may help in managing issue concerning to infertility in women due to early loss of pregnancy.

items.title: Development of a high-throughput protein array to discover selective dsRNA binding domain interactions
items.blurb: Endogenous double stranded RNAs (dsRNAs) function as signal transduction molecules through interactions with host proteins. These interactions can induce signaling cascades implicated in normal homeostasis and diseases such as cancer. Therefore, the discovery of interactions between dsRNAs and dsRNA binding proteins (dsRBPs) is critical for comprehensive elucidation of signal transduction cascades. Discovery of dsRNA-dsRBP interactions remains hindered due to technical limitations that can include a lack of reliable reagents to enrich a given dsRBP or enrichment techniques that cannot identify direct dsRNA-dsRBP binding. As an alternative, we report the development of protein domain arrays to enable high-throughput discovery of direct interactions between dsRNAs and dsRBP reader domains. We establish a modular antibody-independent approach coined dsRBP-seq to identify putative dsRNAs. Validated dsRNAs are subsequently used to probe dsRBP domain arrays to discover multiple dsRNA binding domains that bind the same dsRNA. The establishment and application of this new technical approach reveals a domain-specific interaction of the dsRNA transcript encoding 26S proteasome complex subunit, Sem1, that binds with double-stranded RNA binding motif 3 of Staufen Double-Stranded RNA Binding Protein 2 (STAU2). Altogether, our workflow establishes a high-throughput approach to discover direct dsRNA-dsRBP interactions and the protein domains required for dsRNA binding.

items.title: Single-cell transcriptomics of human astrovirus VA1-infected intestinal organoids reveals cell-type-specific responses and a requirement for cholesterol biosynthesis during infection
items.blurb: Human astroviruses are prevalent but understudied enteric viruses that cause gastroenteritis and neurological disease, particularly in children and immunocompromised individuals. No vaccines or antivirals are available, partly because their biology and pathogenesis remain poorly understood. Here, we used single-cell RNA sequencing to characterize transcriptional responses to VA1, a non-classical human astrovirus associated with the majority of extraintestinal disease cases, in fetal ileum-derived human intestinal organoids. VA1 altered epithelial cell-type proportions and progressively spread through the organoids. Differential gene expression analysis of enterocytes and progenitor cells, the cells most prevalent in the organoid model, revealed shared antiviral responses, including interferon signaling, as well as cell-type-specific responses. Enterocytes exhibited a broader early transcriptional response and specifically upregulated cholesterol metabolism and biosynthesis pathways at 1 dpi. By 3 dpi, progenitor cell-specific genes suggested inflammatory and epithelial-defense responses. In two different intestinal epithelial cell lines, T84 and Caco-2 cells, limiting extracellular lipid availability did not alter replication but increased VA1 binding in Caco-2 cells. Pharmacologic inhibition of cholesterol biosynthesis and 25-hydroxycholesterol treatment reduced VA1 replication, while disrupting intracellular cholesterol transport had no detectable effect. Together, these findings expand our knowledge on HAstV biology by defining shared and cell-type-specific epithelial responses to VA1 infection and identifying cholesterol biosynthesis as an important host pathway for successful VA1 replication.

items.title: Exploitative competition among different dormancy strategists shapes community diversity, recovery from perturbations and response to dispersal
items.blurb: Dormancy is a reversible physiological state of reduced metabolic activity that occurs in plants and animals, but is particularly common among microorganisms. Microorganisms can switch into dormancy spontaneously or in response to environmental cues. While previous work has investigated the ecological and evolutionary consequences of the switching mechanism, it is unknown how different dormancy-switching mechanisms within a microbial community interact to shape composition and community-level response to environmental changes. Here, we used mathematical modelling to investigate how different microbial strategies for entering and existing from dormancy shape community dynamics under stable conditions, following perturbation, and after dispersal. We modelled strategists that had no dormant state (non-switching), those that employed spontaneous switching, those that switched given a cue (triggered switching), and those that used a combination of spontaneous and triggered switching (mixed switching). We also examined how competition and the costs of switching influence activity dynamics within the community. Our simulations revealed the importance of exploitative competition among dormancy strategists in shaping the community response to perturbation and dispersal. In a mixed community containing different dormancy strategists, spontaneous switchers maintained a dormant pool, but suffered an implicit competitive disadvantage. Meanwhile, triggered switchers were more competitive under favourable conditions but could be pushed into dormancy by exploitative competition from other strategists. Interestingly, dispersal events could intensify competition, induce dormancy in resident populations and alter the relative activity of different strategists, while also restoring community members lost during perturbation. To evaluate these predictions, we then analysed an existing dataset of soil mesocosms that experienced heat perturbation and subsequent dispersal. The data showed a stable dormant pool, consistent with the presence of stochastic switchers, and the observed dormancy dynamics following dispersal supported competition-driven inactivation among triggered switching strategists. However, we found no evidence that dormancy provides general protection against the heat perturbation. Instead, the results suggest that survival may depend on the inherent tolerance of community members, while subsequent recovery reflects the interplay between dormancy, immigration, and competition. Our work shows how dormancy not only impacts community-level resilience to perturbations but also alters, and is altered by, exploitative competition among community members.

items.title: Constructing value on the fly from episodic memory supports flexible decision-making
items.blurb: Value-based decisions often require people to flexibly draw on and combine information from past experiences to evaluate novel stimuli and adapt to changing demands. Although numerous studies have highlighted the involvement of episodic memory in value-based decision-making, whether and how a common episodic mechanism can support diverse decision-making scenarios remains poorly understood. Here, we introduce GENESIS-Value, a computational framework that constructs value on the fly by retrieving and integrating episodic memories, rather than relying on stable, precomputed value representations. The model combines generative stimulus representations with a flexible query-key-value retrieval mechanism, allowing the same memory store to support different valuation and choice strategies. Across five simulations, we demonstrate that GENESIS-Value can use episodic sampling to reconstruct the values of experienced stimuli, generalize to novel stimuli based on shared features, estimate feature values, guide both individual and sequential choices, and select among multiple offers involving different rewards and levels of risk. We further show that retrieval can be guided by stimulus features, temporal proximity, reminders, and reward outcomes, as well as combinations of these factors, enabling adaptation to different decision demands without requiring separate value functions. The model also captures qualitative behavioral signatures reported in empirical studies of episodic decision-making. Together, these findings establish a unified computational account of how episodic retrieval can support diverse forms of value-based inference and choice. Rather than replacing stable value representations, episodic retrieval may provide a complementary mechanism that allows decision-makers to flexibly address a variety of choice scenarios by reconstructing the value of available options on the fly.

items.title: Targeting Heparan Sulfate 3-O-Sulfation Enhances Acetylcholine Receptor Clustering and Stabilizes Neuromuscular Junctions in Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
items.blurb: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a severe neuromuscular disease caused by dystrophin deficiency, leading to progressive muscle degeneration and neuromuscular junction (NMJ) instability. Using rat models of DMD, we identified a dysregulation in heparan sulfate (HS) biosynthesis at the NMJ, characterized by reduced expression of Hs6st2 and Hs3st5 genes that encode sulfotransferases required for the production of rare 3-O-sulfated heparan sulfate (3S-HS) forms. These genes act synergistically to enhance agrin signaling: their co-expression in myotubes potentiates acetylcholine receptor clustering, and HSPG mimics bearing tetrasulfated 3-O-sulfated motifs reproduce this effect and promote Agrin-LRP4 interaction. In DMD rats, muscle co-transduction of Hs6st2 and Hs3st5 prevents NMJ fragmentation and improves muscle strength. These findings identify 3S-HSs as novel regulators of NMJ stability and support HS modulation as a complementary therapeutic strategy in DMD.

items.title: The mechanical nature of injury shapes the composition and temporal dynamics of inflammation after traumatic spinal cord injury
items.blurb: The pathophysiology of traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) is a complex, evolving process that begins with a mechanical trauma. Progressive secondary damage then occurs, in which neuroinflammation plays a pivotal role. Much has been learned about the persistent inflammatory response during the chronic phase of SCI. However, variations in lesion models, animal species, strains, and the post-lesion intervals investigated make it difficult to conclude on how inflammation contributes to recovery or to exacerbation of damage. Here, we systematically compared two preclinical rat models of thoracic SCI: contusion and bilateral dorsal hemisection (bDH), that produce severe injuries leading to comparable initial locomotor deficits. We present a detailed analysis of neuroinflammatory temporal dynamics from acute (1-7 days), subacute (14 days), and chronic stages (> 4 weeks). The two models shared some inflammatory patterns, but specific cellular and molecular responses differed in magnitude, composition, and temporal evolution. These signature inflammatory dynamics were associated with differences in endogenous axonal plasticity, astroglial remodeling and progressive lesion maturation, and with distinct functional recovery rates. As the lesion gradually became chronic, inflammatory activity was remodeled, but persisted. These results reveal the interplay between the mechanical cause of SCI, the corresponding immune response, and the ensuing tissue remodeling processes. They highlight the importance of injury context and subsequent evolution. We discuss them as contributions to our understanding of the physiopathology of spinal cord lesions, with the broader goal of designing therapeutic strategies aiming to appropriately modulate inflammation

items.title: Dissociated network and cellular remodeling in the hippocampal-cortical circuit after induction of neuronal hyperexcitability
items.blurb: Neuronal hyperexcitability (NHE) can leave lasting consequences in neuronal circuits. It is often assumed that hyperexcitable neurons give rise to hyperactive networks. Here we asked how a single injection of kainic acid, which induces NHE without seizures, reshapes the hippocampal-cortical circuit at the cellular and network levels two months later. Using high-density microelectrode arrays in acute slices, we found a long-lasting reduction in spontaneous firing and bursting across the hippocampal regions, a lower proportion of active electrodes throughout the circuit, and weaker coupling from CA1 to the entorhinal cortex. In contrast, whole-cell recordings revealed region- and cell-type-specific changes in intrinsic excitability. CA1 and CA3 pyramidal neurons and CA3 interneurons exhibited increased evoked firing, whereas CA1 interneurons exhibited reduced evoked firing. Deep-layer entorhinal neurons, however, received less excitatory synaptic input and fired less. Thus, network and cellular alterations were dissociated after NHE. Finally, a pharmacological challenge with the GluK1 agonist ATPA revealed region-specific changes in network responsiveness, with a blunted response in CA3 and enhanced response in the non-entorhinal cortex, with no differences in DG, CA1 or entorhinal cortex. These findings suggest that, after the induction of NHE, region- and cell-type-specific neuronal remodeling coexists with reduced network activity ex vivo, and that the state of the circuit cannot be inferred from the properties of its individual neurons.

items.title: Early life stress reduces prefrontal dendritic spine density in adult male mice
items.blurb: Early life stress (ELS) is a major risk factor for anxiety, depression and substance use disorders later in life, and it is thought to act in part by changing how emotion-regulating circuits develop. The prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) cortices exert top-down control over the basolateral amygdala (BLA), and this circuit is still maturing during early postnatal life. Stress in adulthood removes dendritic spines from prefrontal neurons, but it is less clear whether ELS causes lasting spine changes across this circuit, and the IL in particular has rarely been studied. Here, we asked whether ELS alters dendritic spine density in the PL, IL and BLA of adult male mice. From postnatal day (PND) 10 to 17, ELS pups were separated from the dam for 3 h per day and individually isolated from their littermates, and their home cage had reduced nesting material until PND21. Control pups were separated together with their littermates for only 15 min per day and kept standard nesting. In adulthood, brains were processed for Golgi-Cox staining, and spines were counted on proximal apical and basal dendrites of layer II/III pyramidal neurons in the PL and IL, and on dendrites of principal neurons in the BLA. ELS reduced spine density by approximately 30% in the IL and PL dendrites, with the largest losses concentrated on proximal apical dendrites. The BLA showed a smaller reduction of about 12%. These preliminary findings suggest that ELS leads to an important and lasting loss of dendritic spines in prefrontal regions that regulate emotional responses.

items.title: Tonic dopamine regulates cell-type-specific PKA activity and motivated behavior
items.blurb: Dopamine in the striatum fluctuates on fast ``phasic`` and slow ``tonic`` timescales. Although disruptions in tonic dopamine have been implicated in the pathophysiology of neuropsychiatric disease, the effect of slow, minutes-long fluctuations in dopamine on neuronal activity and behavior remain unknown. Here we use two-color fluorescence lifetime photometry at high temporal resolution (FLIPR) and calibrated optogenetic and chemogenetic manipulations to determine the impact of tonic dopamine on motivated behavior and downstream signaling in vivo. We establish a method for tracking tonic dopamine using FLIPR and determine that dopamine release fluctuates across short (100s of milliseconds) and long (10s of minutes) timescales. We find that dopamine type 1 (D1R) and type 2 (D2R) receptor expressing spiny projection neurons (SPNs) are differentially affected by changes in tonic dopamine in vivo, confirming long-standing hypothesis on tonic dopamine function in the striatum. Finally, we show that accumbal tonic dopamine levels predict and causally mediate an animal`s motivation to work for reward by regulating the rate of reward-motivated actions and engagement in a progressive ratio task. Altogether, we show that tonic dopamine affects downstream signaling and motivated behavior, and establish a new set of methods that allows for careful capture and manipulation of tonic dopamine in vivo.

items.title: Semaglutide quiets "food noise" in mice by impairing the wanting, but not the liking, of glucose
items.blurb: Semaglutide and other GLP-1 receptor agonists are transforming obesity treatment, and patients often describe a quieting of intrusive food thoughts that motivate overconsumption of ultra-palatable foods, referred to as "food noise," yet it remains unclear which components of feeding behavior they act upon. Here, we designed a battery of behavioral tasks that separate the perceptual, hedonic, and motivational components of glucose intake in mice. Semaglutide impaired sweet taste categorization (in a psychophysical task) and induced conditioned taste avoidance not aversion, and thus left palatability intact. Its largest effect, however, was on motivation: it selectively disrupted the active pursuit of glucose and, to a lesser extent, lipids, sparing passive intake. In a novel lick-triggered taste alternation task, two fixed sippers delivered either glucose or a second tastant (e.g., saccharin or lipids), with the tastants swapping positions after a set number of licks. This design separated effortless consumption, when the swap brought glucose directly to the mouse (passive hit), from effortful pursuit requiring crossing to the opposite sipper (active hit). A single dose of semaglutide left passive hits intact, but markedly reduced active hits: mice readily exploited glucose that came to them, yet often failed to go after it. As the drug's effect waned, mice regained body weight by selectively overconsuming standard chow over glucose, and glucose over lipids, a shift in diet choice that persisted through the end of the experiment. Thus, semaglutide impairs the wanting, but not the liking, of glucose, providing (in mice) a behavioral correlate of the quieting of "food noise" reported by patients.

items.title: Reading the temperature fingerprints of electrocatalytic reactions
items.blurb: Electrocatalysis is key to turning renewable electricity into fuels and chemicals, and industrial electrolyzers typically operate at moderately elevated temperatures. Measuring how reaction rates change with temperature is also a powerful, yet underexplored, way to probe what controls them. Such measurements yield two quantities: an apparent activation enthalpy, reflecting the energetic cost of the reaction, and a prefactor, which is linked to the activation entropy.

items.title: Even AI thinks it's a man's job: Models reveal gender bias in resumes and hiring assessments
items.blurb: The first hurdle may arise even before an application is submitted. A woman asks artificial intelligence to help her write her resume: The system chooses words, highlights qualities and builds a profile. Then another system, perhaps based on the same model, evaluates that text. If both reproduce gender stereotypes, the risk is a double filter: Bias enters the application and is reinforced by the person selecting it.

items.title: Archaeology students find Roman treasures on first excavation
items.blurb: The discoveries include gold jewelry, inscriptions and a finely carved gemstone, and were made at a site in Redesdale, Northumberland.

items.title: This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs
items.blurb: More than 300 million years ago, long before dinosaurs roamed Earth, the Chicago area was a steamy, swampy landscape teeming with bizarre creatures. Now, scientists at the Field Museum have identified a previously unrecognized species of ancient amphibian ancestor, revealing new clues about the evolution of frogs and salamanders.

items.title: Webb confirms first-of-its-kind merger of a supergiant and smaller sun-like star
items.blurb: Researchers recently identified a first of its kind: A star slightly less massive than the sun spiraled into and merged with a puffy supergiant star on the outskirts of our neighboring Andromeda galaxy. They nicknamed the newly single, potentially "rejuvenated" star Bao. Their discovery was then bolstered by quick-turn observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope that were carefully cross-referenced with extensive data from telescopes in space and on the ground.

items.title: Protecting wild bees in Europe through calcareous grassland management and connected habitats
items.blurb: Calcareous grasslands are wildflower-rich ecosystems that develop on shallow, alkaline, nutrient-poor soils over chalk or limestone bedrock. They are rare and important habitats for wild bees and other pollinators—yet how well they can support these valuable communities depends on how they are managed. An international research team, led by the University of Göttingen, has shown that long-term abandonment or intensive management threatens the diversity of wild bees. Extensive management of these areas, together with appropriate nature conservation measures in the surrounding landscape, is crucial. The findings were published in the Journal of Applied Ecology.

items.title: Who's to blame for a rogue AI? New legal framework maps accountability
items.blurb: Cyberattacks and other harms caused by artificial intelligence challenge the ability of laws to determine who is liable. Product liability law would point to the company that built the AI model, but AIs are trained on data the company didn't produce, and the legions of people who have used them also played a role. Free speech and social media immunity laws that treat an AI agent as responsible for its own actions could imply the AI agent deserves the same rights as a person.

items.title: Gen Z men more likely than boomers to hold traditional views
items.blurb: A report published today from the King's Global Institute for Women's Leadership has found that young men in Britain are more likely to misperceive society's views on gender compared to other generations. Researchers found that Gen Z males are more likely to think society holds traditional views about them and therefore may be conforming to social expectations most Britons have left behind.

items.title: Switching off cellular recycling gene increases yields of hard-to-make drug target proteins
items.blurb: With an unusual genetic modification that disabled cells' recycling systems, researchers found a way to make cells produce significantly larger amounts of the proteins used to discover and develop new medicines. The findings could help speed up drug development while reducing research and development costs.

items.title: One unusual tooth suggests Homo erectus shared southern China with another human species
items.blurb: One of the most important ancestors to humans was around for much longer than previously believed. That is the conclusion of a new international study published in Nature in which researchers, including scientists from the University of Copenhagen, analyzed nine fossil teeth discovered in two caves in southern China. The teeth are between 324,000 and 184,000 years old, extending the known timeline of Homo erectus by around 200,000 years.

items.title: Midsize mussels fared the worst during the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome
items.blurb: During the record-breaking Pacific Northwest heat dome in 2021, a mussel's life depended on its size and location on the shoreline at Cattle Point on San Juan Island.

items.title: Shrinking ruthenium catalysts boosts ammonia production rate up to 57-fold
items.blurb: Ammonia is drawing renewed attention as a "magic container" for safely storing and transporting hydrogen, a promising clean energy source of the future, as well as a carbon-free fuel that does not emit greenhouse gases when burned. However, for ammonia to be widely used as a key fuel, improving the efficiency of its production process is essential.

items.title: Scalable photonic quantum computer provides new insights into the fundamentals that shape its performance
items.blurb: Photonics-based quantum computers open up new possibilities for investigating highly complex problems in mathematics and have the potential to revolutionize fields ranging from energy and chemical research to secure communications. By utilizing the unusual properties of light particles, they can perform calculations that pose enormous challenges even for the most powerful supercomputers—or remain entirely beyond their reach. At Paderborn University, researchers are now investigating a fundamental question using Germany's first scalable photonic quantum computer, a 'Gaussian boson sampler': which quantum resources are most important for the performance of these devices?

items.title: Tropical plantations reshape biodiversity in ways species counts alone cannot reveal
items.blurb: The conversion of tropical rainforests into intensively farmed rubber or oil palm plantations threatens global biodiversity. However, this does not necessarily lead to the increasing similarity of the remaining species in every case, as might be expected. An international research team led by the University of Göttingen discovered that organisms react very differently to intensive agriculture. The results are published in the journal Nature.

items.title: Newly described South China Sea crab suggests relatively recent shift from shallows to deeper waters
items.blurb: A newly described crab species from the South China Sea suggests a relatively recent shift in one crab lineage from intertidal habitats to deeper waters. Found at depths of about 100–300 meters (330–980 feet), Macromedaeus putrimanubriatus is closely related to the intertidal species M. orientalis.

items.title: Where in Europe could electric‑powered ferries create cleaner travel routes?
items.blurb: Electric battery-powered ferries use electricity from the shore to charge batteries on board. These batteries supply electric motors that propel the ship. On suitable routes, low-carbon electricity could make sea travel substantially cleaner and strengthen its potential as an alternative to flying.

items.title: Spectral clues suggest hollow-core magnetic jet in brightest-ever gamma-ray burst
items.blurb: A China–Italy joint research team has reconstructed the time-resolved spectrum of GRB 221009A, the brightest gamma-ray burst (GRB) ever observed, and proposed that the burst may have produced a magnetically dominated jet with a hollow core. This is presented as a possible interpretation of the emission line's rise-then-fall evolution rather than a direct detection.

items.title: Today's Thanksgiving holiday was invented amid the Civil War to unite a divided country
items.blurb: It is hard to imagine a more American holiday than Thanksgiving. Every year, elementary schoolers learn about the first celebration: that after surviving a terrible year, New England's first European immigrants, the Pilgrims, invited their Indigenous neighbors to a feast in gratitude for their help and God's providence.

items.title: Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive
items.blurb: Exercising too much without adequate recovery may disrupt brain chemistry in surprising ways. Scientists found that mice subjected to prolonged, intense training had elevated dopamine levels in a brain region linked to memory and emotions, even 48 hours after exercising. The discovery could help explain why overtrained athletes sometimes struggle with insomnia, anxiety, and persistent fatigue, although these symptoms were not directly measured.

items.title: Smart lighting technology enables remote color control
items.blurb: Lighting has evolved from simply illuminating objects to changing their perceived colors. A smart lighting technology has been developed that changes how objects appear in color by adjusting only the light shining on them, without repainting the objects or modifying their surfaces. The technology can change the perceived color of specific objects while maintaining natural white illumination in the surrounding space. Visitors will be able to see how the same object appears in different colors at an exhibition to be held at the National Science Museum in Daejeon, South Korea, in November.

items.title: Young emperor penguins encounter industrial krill fishing during first year at sea
items.blurb: New research has revealed young emperor penguins encounter industrial krill fishing in their epic first year at sea, strengthening the case for proposed new marine protected areas. The study was co-led by France's CNRS, the Center Scientifique de Monaco and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution. The international research team tracked 48 juvenile emperor penguins from three colonies around the Weddell Sea: Snow Hill Island, Jason Peninsula and Atka Bay.

items.blurb: The headlines of recent weeks and months have been dominated by men accused of doing terrible things to women.
