items.blurb: When alpha-gal syndrome first emerged, it was a baffling medical mystery. Today, diagnoses are rising, yet much about this potentially life-threatening condition remains unexplained.

items.title: Why do farts smell so bad? The secret is brewing in your gut
items.blurb: The secret behind truly terrible-smelling farts lies in tiny amounts of sulfur-containing gases produced by gut bacteria as they digest food. Scientists reveal why some foods make farts smell worse, why loud farts aren't always the stinkiest, and how our noses evolved to detect these powerful odors.

items.title: Rac1-Abi-1 Signaling Links DNA Repair to Tumorigenesis
items.blurb: The DNA damage response governs genomic integrity, and abnormal DNA repair can drive tumorigenesis. We previously identified a Rac1-Abi-1 signaling pathway in which Rac1 activates protein phosphatase 5, leading to Abi-1-S323 dephosphorylation and enhanced non-homologous end joining (NHEJ). Given the error-prone nature of NHEJ and its potential to promote genomic instability, we sought to determine whether Rac1-Abi-1-mediated regulation of NHEJ contributes to tumorigenesis. Here, we demonstrate the tumorigenic role of Abi-1-S323 dephosphorylation in nonmalignant cell models and multiple tumorigenesis models established using a newly generated genetically engineered Abi-1 mouse model. We first found that the dephospho-mimetic Abi-1-S323A mutant promoted transformation-associated phenotypes in nonmalignant human cells and enhanced orthotopic glioblastoma growth under unperturbed conditions. To further investigate its tumorigenic potential in vivo, we generated CRISPR/Cas9-mediated Abi-1-S296A knock-in mice, in which S296 corresponds to human S323. Abi-1-S296A mouse embryonic fibroblasts exhibited increased proliferation, while mutant mice developed spontaneous tumors involving lymphoid tissues and organs under unperturbed conditions. Furthermore, Abi-1-S296A increased susceptibility to tumorigenesis following DNA damage. In a low-dose whole-body irradiation model, Abi-1-S296A mice showed a trend toward shortened survival and increased tumor development, with lesions including Harderian gland papillary cystadenomas, round-cell neoplasms, and anaplastic sarcomas. In addition, in an azoxymethane/dextran sulfate sodium (AOM/DSS)-induced colorectal tumor model, Abi-1-S296A mice developed significantly more tumors and had a greater tumor burden. These findings identify Abi-1-S323 dephosphorylation as a previously unrecognized regulator of tumorigenesis and establish a new mouse model for investigating the physiological and pathological consequences of constitutive activation of upstream NHEJ-regulatory signaling.

items.title: The Caenorhabditis elegans pangenome elucidates hyper-divergent region gene content to reveal extensive gene copy-number variation and a novel anthelmintic resistance locus
items.blurb: Caenorhabditis elegans has been a keystone model in biological research since the early 1970s, and it was the first metazoan to have its genome sequenced and assembled in 1998. Over the last few decades, the genetic and genomic resources developed for C. elegans made it one of the most powerful models for understanding metazoan biology. Recently, the C. elegans community has collected over 2,000 globally distributed wild strains, which after whole-genome sequencing, were found to contain punctuated regions of extreme genetic variation, called hyper-divergent regions (HDRs). HDRs have been described in organisms across the tree of life, including plants and humans, and genes in HDRs appear to be involved in adaptation, such as environmental response genes, parasitism genes, or immunity genes. However, the extreme genetic divergence at these loci complicates short-read alignments, and the genomic content of these regions in non-reference strains is largely uncharacterized. To define the gene content in HDRs, we de novo assembled and annotated genomes of 140 genetically diverse strains. These data enabled the construction of the first gene-based pangenome for the species. Among these strains, we characterized the landscape of structural variation and developed novel methods to quantify gene content diversity. We found that both variable copy-number and stable-copy environmental response genes were enriched in HDRs. These results further suggest that these regions have an important evolutionary role in adaptation to heterogeneous environments. We leveraged this pangenome to elucidate gene content in previously identified quantitative trait loci associated with adaptive traits. In one HDR, we found large deletions, spanning multiple genes, that are correlated with resistance to the anthelmintic drug abamectin. The C. elegans pangenome provides novel insights into genome and gene family evolution in a genetically diverse animal species, and empowers deeper investigations of genotype-phenotype relationships underlying adaptive traits, particularly in the context of structural and gene copy-number variation.

items.title: A near-infrared fluorescent genetically encoded calcium ion biosensor with a direct response
items.blurb: Near-infrared genetically encoded calcium ion (Ca2+) indicators (NIR GECIs) enable Ca2+ imaging at longer wavelengths than green or red fluorescent GECIs, providing reduced autofluorescence and phototoxicity, and improved compatibility with deep-tissue and multiplexed imaging applications. We have previously reported biliverdin (BV)-binding phytochrome-based NIR GECIs such as NIR-GECO2G that exhibit inverse fluorescence responses. Although inverse response GECIs can effectively report Ca2+ dynamics, their high baseline fluorescence in the resting apo state causes faster photobleaching and substantial out-of-focus background fluorescence, complicating signal interpretation. Here, using the inverse response NIR-GECO2G as the starting scaffold, we developed a direct response Ca2+ indicator, designated dNIR-GECO1.0, through iterative rounds of protein engineering and screening. dNIR-GECO1.0 exhibited greater molecular brightness than NIR-GECO2G, robust fluorescence in mammalian cells without exogenous BV supplementation, and a high dynamic range for reporting Ca2+ changes. A detailed mechanistic investigation identified the key mutations within the Ca2+ binding domain that were necessary to convert the inverse response indicator into a direct response indicator. Resonance Raman spectroscopic analysis provided insight into the specific changes in the BV chromophore resulting from the Ca2+-dependent conformational change.

items.title: Metabolic transitions reprogram translation through sequence-dependent regulation
items.blurb: Cells suppress protein synthesis during starvation, but how translation recovers upon nutrient repletion remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we followed translational recovery in budding yeast after repletion of glucose, nitrogen, or phosphate, combining time-resolved metabolomics, structural proteomics, transcriptomics, and spike-in-calibrated ribosome profiling. Nutrient addition rapidly altered ribosome occupancy in distinct, transcript-specific programs. To identify their sequence determinants, we developed RiboNet, a deep learning framework that predicts ribosome load and positions along transcripts from mRNA sequence. RiboNet-guided in silico mutagenesis revealed reduced pausing at serine codons upon glucose repletion and transiently increased pausing at leucine codons following nitrogen repletion. These responses coincided with altered cognate tRNA charging and metabolite-associated structural changes in aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases. RiboNet also identified a conserved 5' UTR motif, GAUY, that increased reporter protein output following glucose repletion. Our findings reveal how metabolic state alters the contributions of mRNA sequence features to translation initiation and elongation.

items.title: Native architecture of a mitochondrial oxphosome
items.blurb: Mitochondrial cristae are the primary bioenergetic units of eukaryotic cells, yet the molecular principles that dictate their morphologies remain largely unknown. Using in situ cryo-electron tomography and integrative modeling, we resolve the native organization of the respiratory machinery in the diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum. Unlike previously studied animals and green algae, diatoms possess tubular crista, a conserved membrane architecture found in diverse and globally relevant species. We identify several native supercomplexes assemblies, including an oxphosome comprising the entire respiratory chain. Our results, together with molecular dynamics analyses, reveal that these supercomplexes assemble through a lipid-mediated mechanism. We propose that tubular cristae are shaped by the interplay between membrane-bending ATP synthase oligomers that bud the hemispherical crista tips and supercomplexes that act as molecular roadblocks to constrain ATP synthase propagation, thereby balancing membrane curvature and allowing cristae body extension. Furthermore, we show that the diatom Complex I retains ancestral subunits related to fatty acid synthase. Beyond illuminating diatom bioenergetics, our findings reveal a fundamental principle of mitochondrial morphogenesis where ATP synthase-driven membrane curvature is spatially fine-tuned by respiratory supercomplexes.

items.title: LANCE-seq: Live-tissue Analysis via Needle-encoded Capture Extraction for Spatial Transcriptomics
items.blurb: Spatial transcriptomics enables the resolution of spatial heterogeneity in gene expression within tissues, yet most existing sequencing-based methods rely on ex vivo tissue processing, making it difficult to track dynamic molecular changes in the same living individual. We developed LANCE-seq (Live-tissue Analysis via Needle-encoded Capture Extraction sequencing), a live-tissue spatial transcriptomics platform based on encoded microneedle arrays that enables high-density spatial RNA capture through poly(amidoamine) (PAMAM) dendrimer-functionalized interfaces and microfluidic orthogonal combinatorial encoding. In frozen mouse brain tissue, LANCE-seq detected an average of 6,399 genes per spatial spot and reconstructed the spatial distribution of major brain regions and representative marker genes. Furthermore, in the acetaminophen (APAP)-induced acute liver injury model, LANCE-seq enabled repeated sampling from the same living animal at different time points. At 6 h after APAP treatment, injury-related genes such as Hmox1, Ddit3, Atf3, and Fgf21 were significantly elevated, and transcriptional programs associated with stress, inflammation, and cellular injury were broadly enhanced. Meanwhile, liver zonation-related transcriptional signatures were remodeled, with different relative zonation states all exhibiting activation of injury programs. By integrating high-throughput spatial encoding with minimally invasive in vivo sampling, LANCE-seq provides a platform for longitudinal spatial transcriptomic studies of drug responses and disease progression.

items.title: PYTHOCHEMICAL COMPOSITION AND ANTIMICROBIAL ACTIVITY OF LEPIDIUM SATIVUM SEED EXTRACTS AGAINST SELECTED HUMAN PATHOGENS.
items.blurb: This study evaluates the antimicrobial activity of Lepidium sativum (Garden Cress) seed extracts against Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, Fusarium oxysporum, and Candida albicans using methanol and acetone as solvents. The antimicrobial effects were assessed through the zone of inhibition and minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) using serial dilution. The methanol extract exhibited the highest inhibition zones, measuring 23.6 mm for S. aureus and 21.5 mm for E. coli, while the acetone extract showed 22.9 mm and 18.3 mm, respectively. C. albicans exhibited moderate susceptibility, with inhibition zones of 16.2 mm (methanol) and 14.8 mm (acetone), whereas F. oxysporum showed weaker inhibition at 12.4 mm and 10.7 mm, respectively. MIC values ranged from 10-1 to 10-4 dilutions, with methanol extracts maintaining higher efficacy at lower concentrations. These findings validate Lepidium sativum as a potential natural antimicrobial agent, particularly against gram-positive bacteria, and suggest further exploration of its bioactive compounds for pharmaceutical applications.

items.title: Cumulative antibiograms: effects of isolate selection and stratification order on susceptibility estimates and resistance representation
items.blurb: Cumulative antibiograms depend on how isolates are selected and how data are stratified. Different selection strategies may affect both the number of isolates included and the susceptibility estimates reported. We retrospectively analyzed routine microbiology records from a tertiary-care hospital in Barcelona, Spain (2022-2025). Within each patient-organism-calendar-year unit, we compared three isolate-selection strategies: first-isolate, resistance-phenotype, and susceptibility-profile. We assessed the number of isolates retained, susceptibility at standard or increased exposure, the identification of resistance-phenotype profiles, and the effect of de-duplication before versus after stratification. Annual differences in susceptibility were estimated using paired cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals. For Pseudomonas aeruginosa, susceptibility-profile selection retained 16.9% more isolates than first-isolate selection, with differences exceeding 5 percentage points in 10 of 44 annual antimicrobial comparisons. No annual susceptibility differences exceeding this threshold were observed for the other species. Resistance-phenotype and susceptibility-profile selection criteria identified 468 MDR and 278 XDR P. aeruginosa isolates. Of these, 90 (19.2%) of the MDR and 53 (19.1%) of the XDR isolates were not captured by first-isolate selection. In the broader stratification dataset, stratification-first processing increased first-isolate retention by 21.2% for blood specimens and 11.2% for inpatients. These findings show that modest changes in cumulative susceptibility can coexist with incomplete representation of resistant phenotypes. In conclusion, phenotype- and AST-profile-based selection capture additional resistance information beyond first-isolate selection, despite modest differences in cumulative susceptibility. Clinical validation is needed before their use to guide empirical therapy.

items.title: Region-Specific Changes in the Aging Enteric Nervous System
items.blurb: As human life expectancy increases, understanding the physiological changes that accompany aging becomes increasingly important. Gastrointestinal (GI) dysfunction is common with age, and age-related changes in the enteric nervous system (ENS), which regulates GI motility, may contribute to this decline in function. Studies of the aging ENS have reported contradicting results, potentially reflecting the substantial regional heterogeneity of the ENS and the fact that most studies focus on only one or two areas of the GI tract. Neurons in the myenteric plexus, which regulate intestinal contractions and motility, are organized into ganglia that form circumferential stripes along the length of the gut. Here, we systematically compare neuronal and glial density and organization across all five regions of the small and large intestine in young (3-4 month-old) and aged (22-26 month-old) mice. We find that neuronal density remains unchanged with age across all regions, despite localized changes in ganglia organization. Although the overall stripe-like arrangement is preserved, ganglia are less aligned with stripes in the duodenum and ileum, while those in the ileum and distal colon are smaller, contain fewer neurons, and have a greater proportion of neurons located outside the ganglia. Glial cell numbers vary regionally with age, increasing in the duodenum and distal colon but decreasing in the proximal colon. The proportion of Calretinin+ neurons, meanwhile, remains stable across the small intestine. Together, these findings reveal that aging is associated with selective, region-specific remodeling of myenteric plexus cytoarchitecture rather than uniform structural decline across the GI tract. This comprehensive regional analysis may help reconcile conflicting reports of age-related changes in the ENS.

items.title: The global geometry of optimal neural representations
items.blurb: Efficient coding hypothesizes that neural activity optimally represents information under resource constraints. The global structures of such optimal population codes are difficult to study theoretically, and previous works have usually resorted to either focusing on local properties like fine discrimination or placing restrictions on the parametric forms of neural tuning. We address the general problem by analytically deriving the neural representation that minimizes the all-pairs average classification error of a one-dimensional circular variable under various forms of neural response noise. Our method is based on formulating the space of neural response distributions as a statistical manifold whose geometry can be simplified through a generalized version of variance-stabilizing transformations. The theory fully characterizes the complete family of optimal population codes and allows us to make two novel predictions. First, an optimal code should allow the existence of oppositely peaked bimodal tuning curves. Second, there should be a correlation between spike count variability and tuning sharpness. We validate both of these predictions in the mouse head direction system.

items.title: Energetic costs of osmo- and ionoregulatory responses to desiccation and recovery in a model insect
items.blurb: Climate change is expected to increase the frequency, duration and intensity of weather events that cause desiccation stress to small-bodied terrestrial insects. Whether a desiccation event may cause mortality depends on the time-dependent osmo- and ionoregulation responses of insects to desiccation and their recovery. Yet these responses and their associated energetic costs are not always clear for a range of mesic species. Here, we characterised the ability of house crickets (Acheta domesticus) to physiologically resist and recover from desiccation. We measured water loss from different tissues, changes in haemolymph volume and in haemolymph ion concentration as well as stored macromolecules (lipids, carbohydrates and proteins) use over a time-course of desiccation (0, 3, 6 or 18 h) and recovery with access to water and with or without access to food (18 h desiccation and 6 h recovery). During 18 h of desiccation, crickets regulated haemolymph ion concentration, avoiding hyperkalaemia and hypernatraemia, despite losing up to 14.5 and 21.1% of their body water for female and males respectively, across all body compartments. Recovery represented a distinct physiological phase to acute stress with a restoration of ion concentrations and body water with significant energetic contributions from stored macromolecules. We conclude crickets employ a general two-phase physiological strategy to withstand and recover from a short-term acute desiccation stress, establishing a physiological baseline to evaluate potential desiccation stress, and providing key insight into the time-dependency of osmoregulation and ion regulation for insects encountering fluctuating desiccation stress under climate change.

items.title: Myeloid mDIC Deficiency Remodels Adipose Macrophages to an Efferocytosis-Associated State and Improves Metabolic Homeostasis During Obesity
items.blurb: Obesity-associated adipose inflammation contributes to metabolic dysfunction, yet the mechanisms linking mitochondrial metabolism to macrophage efferocytosis remain incompletely understood. The mitochondrial dicarboxylate carrier (mDIC), encoded by SLC25A10, regulates adipocyte function, but its role in macrophages remains unclear. Here, we investigated how myeloid mDIC deficiency affects mitochondrial function, macrophage heterogeneity, and metabolic homeostasis during diet-induced obesity. We observed reduced mDIC protein expression in subcutaneous white adipose tissue from individuals with obesity, whereas palmitate increased mDIC expression in mouse and human macrophages. Myeloid mDIC deletion preserved mitochondrial respiration under palmitate stress. Single-cell RNA sequencing of adipose stromal vascular cells from high-fat diet (HFD)-fed mice revealed an expanded efferocytosis-associated macrophage population and reduced proportions of inflammatory and lipid-associated macrophages. Consistently, mDIC-deficient macrophages exhibited increased Mertk expression and greater association with apoptotic cells. Pharmacological inhibition of mitochondrial ATP synthase or electron transport markedly suppressed apoptotic cell uptake, including the quenching-resistant fraction, without substantially affecting macrophage viability. In vivo, myeloid mDIC deletion attenuated HFD-induced weight gain, improved insulin sensitivity, and increased CD11c-CD206 adipose macrophage abundance, accompanied by elevated expression of alternative activation-associated markers. Together, these findings identify myeloid mDIC as an important regulator of macrophage mitochondrial function and adipose immune remodeling during obesity, suggesting a novel mechanism by which mitochondrial bioenergetics contribute to macrophage apoptotic-cell handling and metabolic homeostasis.

We got through to the very end of Quentin Tarantino’s previous film Once Upon a Time in Hollywood without finding out exactly how, why or if Brad Pitt’s stuntman character Cliff Booth murdered his wife. It was an issue only addressed in Tarantino’s novel based on the movie. And throughout the 140 minutes of this outrageous sugar-rush sequel – scripted by Tarantino and directed by David Fincher – this subject is tactfully passed over in silence, the one point that damages our perception of Cliff’s amiable-cowpoke good nature.

Cliff is the guy who climaxed the previous picture by helping with a dramatic rescue; after, that is, gallantly refusing an age-gap relationship with Margaret Qualley’s jailbait teen. Well, we may not get the complete picture of Cliff’s matrimonial circumstances until Tarantino’s forthcoming crossover Cliff Booth novel, with which this film is to form a kind of multimedia narrative event. But there is nonetheless such a huge amount of energy, fun, scabrous black comedy, provocative bad taste and film-making style to be had here.

items.title: ‘In our lands the rain is made of bullets’: Palestinian artists look back in anger, melancholy and defiance
items.blurb:
IMMA, Dublin
From massacre locations painted on to basalt slabs to photocollages of bulldozed airports, artists from across the Levant address their traumatic history

In 2006, Simone Fattal painted on to basalt slabs the names of places indelibly associated with massacres in the Levant since 1948: Deir Yassin; Jenin; Qana; Sabra. Through the names, in the same Arabic script, runs a line of poetry by Etel Adnan: “In our lands of drought the rain forever is made of bullets.”

Fattal’s work, which documents atrocities on a material that burst from the earth as lava before settling into stone, introduces a show that likewise combines the recording of history with anger both hot and cold.

The last named of those massacres, perpetrated by a Lebanese Christian phalangist militia during Beirut’s occupation by Israeli forces in 1982, also inspired the poem Praise for the High Shadow by Mahmoud Darwish, a line from which this show takes as its title. Writing in exile in Beirut, Darwish riffed on the sea as a symbol of Palestinian displacement and memory, connecting people dispersed around the eastern Mediterranean to each other and to their homeland. The angry, melancholy, defiant work of these (mostly) Palestinian artists also weaves a traumatic national history into the cosmopolitan culture of the Levant and the interlinked world in which we now live.

items.title: Grand Theft Auto would be a huge TV series – here’s why it will never happen
items.blurb:
It is the biggest game of the decade, but there are a billion reasons why GTA shouldn’t be adapted for television. It joins a list of wildly popular titles that won’t see the light of day on streaming platforms

You probably aren’t going to see a Grand Theft Auto TV show anytime soon. Speaking on a recent podcast, Strauss Zelnick, the CEO of the game’s parent company Take-Two Interactive, said that a film or television adaptation of GTA would only happen if its team thought that it would “somehow engage and delight our consumers. It’s a high bar to do that. And, of course, there’s always a risk of failure. So we don’t rule it out, but we’re very, very selective.”

And, well, good. There are a billion reasons why a small screen version would be a terrible idea. Creatively, the thrill of a GTA game is that no two players have the exact same experience. While you might spend your days mowing down civilians and bazookaing police helicopters out of the skies, someone else might take that time to go hiking or explore the waterways. The game is so open-ended, and so moulded to a player’s sensibility, that trying to reduce it to a scripted linear narrative would make it feel uncomfortably thin.

items.title: Abandoning a Cat by Haruki Murakami review – an intimate meditation on family and memory
items.blurb:
The author explores the life and legacy of his estranged father, from adoption and abandonment to his horrific experiences of the second world war

When Haruki Murakami was a child living in Nishinomiya, Japan, his father announced they were getting rid of their cat. He put his son and the cat on his bike and cycled along the Shukugawa river to a beach 2km from their house. There, they put the box with the cat in it on the ground among some trees and cycled away “without a backward glance”. When they got home, they opened their door to find the cat they’d just left “greeting us with a friendly meow, its tail standing tall. It had beaten us home.”

Murakami always wondered how the cat got home so quickly, and why his father had wanted to banish her. These are just some of the unanswered questions that surface in Abandoning a Cat, an essay that first appeared in the New Yorker in 2019, and which is now being published as a book and audiobook. Translated by Philip Gabriel and read with gentle warmth by Kotaro Watanabe, it finds the author telling the story of Murakami Sr, from whom he was estranged for 20 years and who remained a mystery to him in his lifetime.

items.title: ‘Sam-Bankman Fried messaged me from prison’: rising star Anthony Boyle on playing the disgraced tech bro – and a zero-hours bike courier
items.blurb:
The actor’s latest roles see him go from a delivery guy on £40 a day to the notorious crypto scammer who stole more than $10bn. His sympathies are clear: ‘I wasn’t brought up to care about money,’ he says

In the spring of 2019, Anthony Boyle went to see Cillian Murphy in Grief Is the Thing with Feathers at St Ann’s Warehouse in Brooklyn. Afterwards, the 24-year-old actor hung around the stage door. “There were 500 people queueing up for Cillian, but I was the only one who wanted to meet Enda Walsh,” says Boyle, laughing. When the Dublin-born writer Walsh finally appeared, Boyle introduced himself. He was from west Belfast, he’d read Walsh’s plays at drama school, and it was his dream to work with him one day. He asked if Walsh would like to come and see him on Broadway, where he was playing Scorpius Malfoy, son of Draco, in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. How did he respond? Boyle grins. “He was sort of like: ‘Oh.’”

Since Walsh never went to see The Cursed Child, Boyle assumed the writer had immediately forgotten about him. Then, a few years later, he received a letter from Walsh explaining that he was adapting Keiran Goddard’s 2024 novel I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning, about five close friends from a council estate in Birmingham who find themselves questioning everything about their precarious lives as they hit 30. He had scripted the part of Patrick, a politically outspoken graduate working as a zero-hours bike courier to support his young family, with Boyle in mind. Clio Barnard was on board to direct.

items.title: The Hill by Harriet Clark review – distinctive debut of growing up with a mother in prison
items.blurb:
This unusual portrait of a young girl whose prison visits are interweaved with her grandmother’s war-weary reminiscences rewards attention

American author Harriet Clark’s first novel, partly inspired by her own life, is narrated by a girl whose mother is in prison. Suzanna is being raised by grandparents while her mother serves a life sentence for driving the getaway car for a botched bank robbery intended to fund revolutionary political activism. Although Suzanna refuses the narrative, in some ways this is a coming-of-age story, but with a protagonist whose overwhelming need is to go nowhere and change nothing.

The Hill is shaped by the tension between the novel’s need for a plot and Suzanna’s rejection of her own role in the Bildungsroman. Prison visits structure Suzanna’s life, their rituals and repetitions at once marking and resisting the passage of time. At first, her grandfather drives her from their shabby urban apartment to the hilltop prison and escorts her to the entrance to the children’s centre, where on a good day the prisoners are allowed to play with their children under close surveillance. Later, the grandfather dies, activities in the centre are restricted and Suzanna’s visits take increasingly constrained forms. Abjuring ordinary teenage activities, she takes the train towards the hill every Saturday, submits to searches, and follows rules about how to move and what and whom she may not touch.

Good holiday movies are an exercise in knowing silliness, and so it is a relief when the first 10 minutes of this movie, directed by Elizabeth Allen Rosenbaum, strikes the rare December balance between hearth-like warmth (the twinkle in Meester’s chocolate eyes when her Hannah Brooks lands a verbal punch) and complete lunacy (she lands that punch in an argument with her ex about … cuddling … literally seconds after thwarting an assassination attempt in Times Square). items.blurb: Erin Ogunkeye welcomes Reed Brody, Member of the International Commission of Jurists, Human Rights Lawyer and veteran war crimes prosecutor. The International Court of Justice's ruling on Myanmar marks, according to Brody, "a historic victory for the Rohingya, but also a landmark for international justice." He explains how the court assessed evidence of genocidal intent, rejecting Myanmar's justification of its military operations as counterterrorism. He argues that "the existence of an armed conflict or a security objective doesn't exclude genocidal intent," a finding he believes will have "far-reaching implications in future genocide cases," including South Africa's case against Israel over Gaza. Brody also discusses the Gambia's role in bringing the case and growing challenges to international accountability, warning that "we're in a very dangerous moment."

Li believes that Xi Jinping has the most to gain from the meeting, as it allows him to demonstrate China's global status and its role as a diplomatic convener. Putin may also benefit from the opportunity to meet the two leaders despite Russia's international isolation following its invasion of Ukraine.

items.title: Outages, spies, and trillion-dollar IPOs: is this our AI future? – Stateside with Kai and Carter
items.blurb:
It has been a wild few weeks in the world of tech. First, Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy, forced an unimaginable leadership change at Nvidia – arguably the most consequential company in AI development. Then, chaos erupted as a rolling set of IT outages disrupted flights, banking, tech companies and the federal government. And now, Anthropic is blowing minds with a trillion-dollar IPO – one of the largest in stock market history. The Atlantic’s tech writer Charlie Warzel tells Kai Wright that these events are linked: they’re all examples of the ways in which we shoulder unprecedented risk today, in order to bet on AI’s future reward. It’s a convoluted logic that keeps the AI race speeding forward, no matter how many warning signs it blows past. Charlie Warzel is also host of the Atlantic’s podcast Galaxy Brain.

items.title: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras
items.blurb:
We can’t make AI safe for humanity if tech bosses are allowed to run their companies like autocracies

Over the past two years, a troubling pattern has emerged across the world’s leading AI laboratories. Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. Last month, the person who oversaw safety reports for OpenAI’s product releases said he was quitting the ChatGPT creator because the company’s culture was “broken” and the entire AI industry was too careless in developing the technology. The previous month it was a researcher at OpenAI’s rival Anthropic who quit, warning that he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.

As a society we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle – and then we move on. But we miss the deeper institutional failure those resignations reveal: as the great political scientist Albert Hirschman made clear, exit is not voice.

Isabelle Ferreras is accelerator fellow at the University of Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI, FNRS research director at the University of Louvain, Belgium and co-founder of DemocraticIntelligence.org

items.title: The Altruists review – two of TV’s best actors light up this chaotic crypto tale
items.blurb:
Julia Garner and Anthony Boyle play the FTX founders behind ‘the greatest fraud ever committed’ in the US. It’s a mind-boggling story – just make sure you don’t miss a single moment

What happens when you put really stupid clever people in charge of the world? Not as presidents (they currently trend mostly towards the merely stupid) or prime ministers (generally neither really stupid nor really clever), but in charge of the real world, which is to say the online world, the one that really governs us? We are watching that play out day by day, but if you have enough slack left in your dread-system, a cortisol spike yet to execute, why not add a warning from history to your consumption of horrors?

Welcome to The Altruists, a breakneck breakdown of the brief career of Sam Bankman-Fried (played by Anthony Boyle) who, with his on-off girlfriend Caroline Ellison (played by Julia Garner), set up the cryptocurrency exchange FTX with the belief that it would revolutionise finance and – as the increasingly absurd/dishonest/knowingly satirical Silicon Valley mantra has it – make the world a better place. A very few years later, FTX – worth $36bn (£27bn) at its peak – collapsed and in 2023 the pair were convicted of various charges deriving from what the trial judge called “the greatest financial fraud ever perpetrated in this country”. Ellison was sentenced to two years in prison after testifying against Bankman-Fried. Bankman-Fried is serving 25 years and was ordered to forfeit $11bn (£8.3bn). He says he is innocent and is applying to the supreme court to review his conviction.

Fils arrives first, chewing gum, and looking very calm … and now here’s Zverev, dressed also in black but channelling his inner Federer with a gold bag. He’s ditched the jacket he wore the other day with 1 on the back. Perhaps he feels as if he doesn’t need to remind people of his new status given the supremacy of his two performances so far this week.

Jamie Murray is talking on Sky Sports and says Zverev was “smoking the ball” in practice earlier. Which is ominous for Fils. He’s then asked which players are most likely to close the gap on Zverev/Sinner/Alcaraz next year. He thinks Fils has got as good a chance as any, given he doesn’t have many points to defend at the grand slams in 2027, having missed this year’s Australian Open and French Open through injury and lost in the US Open first round. It shows how brilliant the 22-year-old’s been away from the slams that he’s still managed to climb to a career-high ranking of No 7. While online carjackers are busy exploring a “most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world”, football’s real-life power brokers are gearing up for a March showdown in the actual city of Rabat.

When I first saw the photo in yesterday’s Football Daily, I thought Mauricio Pochettino had opted for a short back and sides, presumably to pre-empt him tearing his luscious locks out in frustration at forthcoming poor results/terrible January transfer window/petulant sniping from sulky squad members. items.title: Danny Kelly loved football and never forgot the absurdity of earning a living talking about it | Max Rushden
items.blurb:
The journalist and broadcaster who died last week aged 69 knew the enduring power of radio, even as the landscape changed so quickly

It’s injury time at the Emirates on 29 October 2008, Arsenal are 4-3 up against Tottenham. Tom Huddlestone cushions a ball to Luka Modric, whose strike takes a deflection. It loops over Manuel Almunia and off a post into the path of Aaron Lennon, who prods it home and starts skipping towards the Spurs supporters before diving on to the ground and being enveloped by Modric, Benoît Assou-Ekotto, Darren Bent and a couple of pitch-invading fans. Pandemonium, for once, seems the apt way to describe it.

But the real entertainment is happening in a radio studio at 18 Hatfields, London SE1; the old home of TalkSport. As the goal goes in, a guttural voice makes an indecipherable but very loud noise. It’s hard to transcribe – perhaps “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH”, or maybe “OOEEERRAAGGH”. It’s just a noise, but it’s unmistakably Danny Kelly. He regains the power of speech and follows it up with: “Gooooaaaal … Goalll Stan, Goalll at the Emirates.” Reporter Ian Abrahams and Stan Collymore join the excitement, before Danny comes back: “I LOVE FOOTBALL, STAN, I LOVE IT.” It is such a brilliant piece of radio. From one of the absolute greats.

Continue reading...

items.title: Gonzalo García: ‘I love Craven Cottage – the fans can reach out and touch you’
items.blurb:
Spain Under-21 striker admits the pace of the Premier League has surprised him but says he must stay calm over goal drought at Fulham

The first thing Rita Hayworth’s great nephew says when he walks in is: “Sorry I’m late.” Gonzalo García is not late, but it’s very like him: he is impeccably polite, accommodating, and there’s an almost gentle quality to him, a calm that’s not common but can help, especially in moments when the pressure builds. There’s a reason one of the coaches standing in the rain by the pitch where Spain’s under‑21s have just finished training says everyone here loves García. The Fulham striker shakes hands, introduces himself and ducks into the dressing room to change; then a few minutes later he’s back, apologising for a wait that wasn’t one.

Time to talk, so let’s start with Tinseltown, the family tale. García laughs. His great-aunt, born Margarita Carmen Cansino, was among the biggest stars in Hollywood, although he’s not sure he’s seen any of her films. His grandfather was a surgeon and others in the family followed. His uncles played rugby for Spain, but that wasn’t his thing. As for him, he enrolled in a degree in business management and analytics, and reckons he might have liked law, yet even that wasn’t his chosen field.

items.title: Inside women’s football’s difficult rise in Syria: ‘A joy that everyone in the country needed’
items.blurb:
A 14-year civil war ravaged the country and ground women’s football to a halt. Today, the first glimmers of hope are beginning to emerge amid difficulty

In December 2024, Syria’s under-18 women’s football team boarded a last-minute bus at midnight from Aqaba, bound for Damascus. The players had been in Jordan preparing for their final match of the WAFF women’s championship, where a win against Saudi Arabia would have kept their hopes of winning the title alive. Syria pulled out amid fears that the border would close.

Back home, a war that had been largely frozen for four years was suddenly moving at pace. Rebel forces had swept out of the northwest, taking Aleppo and were pushing south towards the capital, 350km away, threatening to topple the now-former president, Bashar al-Assad. Players from the provinces around Damascus made their way home. But those from Hasakah, in the country’s far north-east, spent the next three days stranded at Damascus airport, as airline staff fled and planes sat idle on the tarmac, until a bus was finally able to take them home.

items.title: From training clips to thirst traps: why athletes are turning to OnlyFans
items.blurb:
A professional sports career does not guarantee wealth. And a growing number of athletes are turning to alternative streams of income

“I’m sick and tired of it.” Bart Swings tossed his jacket behind him. It was August 2025, the Winter Olympics were less than six months away, and the Belgian Olympic champion’s injured knee was not getting better. The clip, profanity and all, later ran on the Belgian evening news along with the weather and the football. But the injury update didn’t come from an interview – it was broadcast on the speed skater’s OnlyFans channel.

The subscription site, best known for porn dudes, cam girls and dubiously horny couples, has quietly assembled one of the stranger rosters in professional sport. The list, about 285 athletes deep, includes Olympic speed skaters and rowers, tennis players, surfers and golfers. And, despite its racy reputation, many of the athletes on OnlyFans are not putting out adult content.

items.title: The unthinkable has come to pass: Tom Brady is a pretty good broadcaster
items.blurb:
The former NFL quarterback was widely derided when he starter his job in the Fox booth. But he has shown a human side and explains the game beautifully

I have accidentally force-fed myself Tom Brady’s commentary as my primary means of watching the NFL this season. When my favorite team, the Steelers, hired Mike McCarthy as head coach, I lodged a silent protest by declining to spend the several hundred dollars needed to get NFL Sunday Ticket. I didn’t even splurge for RedZone. That means I’ve found myself watching Fox’s NFL broadcasts on a Sunday – often an underwhelming Cowboys game – where Brady is the color commentator in the network’s No 1 booth, alongside play-by-play man Kevin Burkhardt.

This two-and-a-half-month experiment has led me to an alarming conclusion, one I’d seen others reaching gradually over the last year but never taken too seriously myself. Recently, though, the truth has become unavoidable: Tom Brady is pretty good at his job. Gone are the days of the best quarterback of all time being hopelessly outmatched on TV. What has changed is that Brady now sounds like an actual human being.

items.title: You have to laugh at LIV’s collapse but the saga reveals money is golf’s core value | Jonathan Liew
items.blurb:
Why do rich powerful men love golf? Ultimately the sport exists in a world where the politics is assumed to be settled

Farewell, then, LIV Golf. As its original figurehead Greg Norman once so delicately put it, albeit in a slightly different context: we’ve all made mistakes, you learn from those mistakes, and you move forward. Forward – in LIV’s case – to bankruptcy court and the start of liquidation proceedings some time in January 2027. And not without a certain irony, in the sense that Norman’s cherished project, established over a cacophony of human rights concerns, ended up getting dismembered and terminated on the orders of the Saudi government. Life moves on you pretty fast.

Perhaps the funniest part of LIV’s protracted demise – unless you count the television viewing figures – has been the last seven months, after Saudi Arabia abruptly pulled the plug on the seemingly abundant flow of money that had fuelled its astonishing rise. Suddenly LIV’s chief executive, Scott O’Neil, was forced to take his begging bowl up and down midtown Manhattan, panhandling for change, drawing up entirely conceptual revenue forecasts, pretending for all the world that this was an actual, real-life business proposition; a legitimate going concern with profits and a bottom line and a plan for the future.

items.title: Nothing but highlights: is Power Slap the sport we deserve?
items.blurb:
Slap fighting is the world’s newest combat sport. Built for short attention spans and super-viral moments, it’s aiming for global dominance. No flinching

In the days before Power Slap 22, in Belgrade, Serbia, in late July, the organisers of the world’s newest combat sport were taking no chances. At the Crowne Plaza hotel, where competitors were booked to stay, those facing off had been separated by floor, lest any unauthorised violence took place.

It turned out there was little need. The night before the main event, contestants mingled amiably in the lobby and bar. The atmosphere was more specialist sales conference than brewing barroom brawl. In the lobby, I joined Louis “Razor” Robinson, and Ryan “the Punisher” Kenny. “We’re all friends in slap,” Robinson said, earnestly, by way of a greeting. Robinson, a Brit from Stalybridge, Greater Manchester, is 30, stout, intense. Kenny, a Canadian, is 34, lofty, laid back.

items.title: Madagascar: Southern Africa: El Niño Status and Humanitarian Impacts (October 2026)
items.blurb:
Countries: Madagascar, Angola, Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Zambia, Zimbabwe
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached Infographic.

OVERVIEW

El Niño conditions are underway and are forecasted to strengthen through late 2026, coinciding with a strong positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD).

Key Messages
I. A high-confidence dry season is forecasted for central and southern parts of Southern Africa. Seasonal forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of below-normal rainfall, prolonged dry spells and above-normal temperatures, while above-normal rainfall and flooding risks are expected in parts of the northern areas of the region.

II. The region remains highly vulnerable following the severe 2023/24 El Niño, which affected an estimated 54.4 million people and contributed to widespread food insecurity, livelihood losses and disease outbreaks. Currently, humanitarian needs remain elevated, with 11 million acutely food insecure people across the region, while funding levels remain low.

III. Southern Africa experienced one of its largest cholera outbreaks during 2024-25, increasing public health concerns entering the 2026/27 El Niño season.

IV. Governments and partners are advancing contingency planning, preparedness and anticipatory action measures to reduce the expected impacts on food security, water resources, livelihoods, health and protection during the 2026/27 season.

V. Critical funding gaps in preparedness and anticipatory action are undermining efforts to protect vulnerable communities from the expected impacts of El Niño.

items.title: Anticipatory Action Plan (AAP) for Riverine Floods – Southwest Region Cameroon
items.blurb:
Country: Cameroon
Sources: Christian Blind Mission, Presbyterian Church, Welthungerhilfe

Please refer to the attached file.

This plan by WHH Anticipatory Humanitarian Action Facility (WAHAFA) partners Christian Blind Mission (CBM) and the Presbyterian Church in Cameroon (PCC) shows how Anticipatory Action supports flood-prone communities in Limbe, Fako Division, Cameroon, to act before severe riverine flooding occurs.

This locally developed Anticipatory Action Plan (AAP) combines rainfall forecasts and community observations to trigger early actions addressing health risks, property damage, displacement and food insecurity. Developed with communities, local authorities and organizations of persons with disabilities, the AAP includes drainage clearance, early warning communication and the distribution of water purification tablets, hygiene supplies, mosquito nets and food items.

Using a two-phase trigger mechanism based on forecasts from the National Observatory on Climate Change (ONACC) and local observations of soil saturation, the AAP enables the activation of anticipatory actions with a lead time of approximately 3-9 days and the release of pre-agreed finance from the WAHAFA Fuel funding.

items.title: oPt: One Year On, Gaza’s ‘Peace Plan’ Has Failed, Delivering More Death, Displacement, Despair – Humanitarian Scorecard
items.blurb:
Countries: occupied Palestinian territory, Guatemala, Israel
Source: Islamic Relief

One Year On, Gaza’s ‘Peace Plan’ Has Failed, Delivering More Death, Displacement, Despair – Humanitarian Scorecard

November, 19, 2026

Access the Scorecard

WASHINGTON— One year after an internationally backed ‘peace’ plan for Gaza was launched, it has received a failing score in a scorecard by five leading humanitarian organizations.

The scorecard, led by the Danish Refugee Council, Norwegian Refugee Council, Oxfam, Refugees International, and Save the Children, gave a score of 4 out of 26 to the Trump administration’s 20-point plan that was endorsed by the UN Security Council. This is down from a score of 5 in a scorecard on the same metrics at the six-month mark in April 2026.

The scorecard assesses progress against the 20-point plan’s own objectives related to civilian protection, humanitarian access, reconstruction and economic development, and freedom of movement and return.

Between the ceasefire declaration in October 2025 and mid-November 2026, at least 1,650 Palestinians were killed and 5,975 wounded, more than double the death toll at the six-month mark. Israeli forces now control up to 70% of Gaza, up from 58% at the start of the ceasefire. The UN has reported near-daily Israeli airstrikes in densely populated areas over the past year.

The ceasefire, which was endorsed by UN Security Council Resolution 2803 on 17 November 2025, stipulates an agreed-to minimum of 600 UN-coordinated aid trucks entering Gaza daily. In September, an average of 49 UN-coordinated aid trucks entered Gaza each day with only 2% carrying medical supplies.

Critical shortages of basic medicines and supplies have resulted in deaths from treatable injuries and illnesses. The scorecard, as it did in April 2026, grades humanitarian access in the ceasefire deal with a score of zero.

The Government of Israel continues to obstruct the delivery of shelter materials, medical equipment, and supplies needed to restore water and sanitation services, while nearly the entire population of 2.1 million civilians is struggling to access clean water, healthcare, and adequate food.

All six wastewater treatment plants in Gaza remain out of service and not a single hospital is fully operational.

As Gaza faces its fourth winter with little protection from cold and rain, nearly 1 million Palestinians live in sites at medium or high risk of flooding and 89% of households report rodents inside their shelters.

Already this month a rainstorm flooded more than 70,000 tents and a 9-month-old child was reported to have died of hypothermia.

The organizations urge the UN Security Council, the Board of Peace, and Member States to use their leverage to secure immediate humanitarian access and enforce the ceasefire.

Key recommendations include:

  • Lifesaving Aid and Medical Care: Press Israeli authorities to open all crossings, admit essential supplies, lift restrictions on aid operations, and restore medical evacuations and freedom of movement, including the right to return.
  • Aid Oversight: Member States, working with the Board of Peace, should replace Israeli approval and inspection processes with independent, transparent aid verification.
  • Ceasefire Enforcement and Accountability: Member States should establish UN-mandated monitoring and quarterly humanitarian reporting, and use diplomatic, legal, and economic measures to secure compliance with the ceasefire and UNSCR 2803.
  • Recovery and Reconstruction: Member States and the Board of Peace should ensure recovery protects Palestinians’ freedom of movement, prevents forced displacement, and advances commitments under the New York Declaration.

“One year into the so-called ceasefire, Palestinians are still waiting for the safety and humanitarian relief they were promised,” said Jeremy Konyndyk, President of Refugees International. “People are still being killed, Israeli forces are expanding control of Gaza, and families are facing another winter in flooded tents while desperately needed supplies sit just across the border. None of this is inevitable. Israel has clear obligations both under Trump’s peace plan and under international law to protect civilians and allow humanitarian aid into Gaza. The United States and other UN Security Council members must use their leverage to ensure those obligations are met. The commitments made a year ago mean little if they do not change the reality on the ground.”

“The suffering of Gaza’s 2.1 million people is not inevitable. The world must stop accepting it,” said Jan Egeland, CEO of Norwegian Refugee Council. “Palestinians should have the opportunity to recover, rebuild their lives and work towards a better future. But this is not possible unless Israel fulfils its obligations under international law: opening all crossings, allowing humanitarian aid to enter, and ending its unlawful occupation of Palestinian land.”

“One year ago, the world was promised that Gaza’s children would finally see safety, relief and a chance to rebuild their lives. Instead, they are colder, hungrier, more traumatized and more at risk than they were before. This was supposed to be a roadmap out of catastrophe. Instead, catastrophe has deepened. The international community cannot continue to look away. The children of Gaza do not deserve this,” said Inger Ashing, CEO of Save the Children International.

“Regretfully, the Board of Peace failed the international community and continue to ‎provide political cover for ongoing genocide and atrocities. We call on member states ‎‎— especially those with leverage over Israel – to stop issuing plans and take concrete ‎actions: impose an arms embargo, ensure unconditional humanitarian access, and ‎pursue accountability for war crimes. Protecting Palestinian lives and dignity is not ‎only for Palestinians – it is the last line of defense for what remains of our shared ‎humanity and human values,” said Mohsen Abu Ramadan, Board Member of Palestinian NGOs Network.

“The ceasefire in Gaza is failing and Palestinians are still dying, which is a direct result of policy choices made in Israel, the US, and at the UN. Instead of abiding by the ceasefire plan, the Israeli government is continuing its attacks, forcing Palestinians to try and survive without adequate food, water, shelter, or sanitation, amid open sewage and freezing rain – all while the United States does little to stop it. As we have been saying, the government of Israel must allow aid to enter, end its attacks and collective punishment on all Palestinians in Gaza, and allow the long process of rebuilding to begin,” said Abby Maxman, Oxfam America President & CEO.

“A year into the ceasefire, Palestinians in Gaza are being confined as the Yellow Line expands. Israeli forces now control nearly 70 percent of Gaza, and 1.8 million people are squeezed into displacement sites lacking clean water and sanitation. Families that have already fled up to a dozen times are forced to move again when gunfire and explosions erupt, often with no warning. This is displacement by design, and a ceasefire that allows it is a ceasefire in name only. The international community must use its leverage to halt the expansion of the Yellow Line and guarantee Palestinians’ right to return safely to their homes,” said Lilu Thapa, Danish Refugee Council Executive Director Middle East, Asia and Europe.

items.title: Around 700,000 displaced amid volatile conflict in southern Ethiopia, Islamic Relief says
items.blurb:
Countries: Ethiopia, Kenya
Source: Islamic Relief

Almost 700,000 people have been displaced amid an escalation of conflict in southern Ethiopia along the Kenya, Somalia, Ethiopia border as aid agencies prepare to respond, Islamic Relief says.

The fighting began on 22 October between Somali and Oromo communities, two ethnic groups living in Ethiopia. The epicentre of the conflict is Moyale a border town projected to be increasingly wealthy as trade grows between Kenya and Ethiopia with the two groups fighting for land.

The conflict has spread up to 300km from the town with fighting breaking out in areas across the ethnic group settlements. Approximately 329,000 people have been displaced from the Somali Region Dawa Zone and 359,798 people were displaced across Southern Oromia. Access to the locations has been challenging but aid agencies have had reports that a humanitarian response is necessary.

Hundreds of thousands of displaced people will need support before they can return to their homes. The conflict has caused the destruction and burning of homes, businesses and fuel stations, significant disruption of health, nutrition, water and sanitation services; and civilians are vulnerable to attack.

Approximately 50,000 people have crossed the Ethiopian border into Kenya seeking safety and humanitarian assistance placing additional pressure on local services and host communities.

Islamic Relief Ethiopia head of programmes, Kedir Musema Hameza said:

“This is a volatile conflict driven by two ethnic groups competing for land and wealth in the borders of Ethiopia. Unfortunately when conflict like this arises it is vulnerable civilians that end up paying a high price. We are seeing that now with this mass displacement of nearly 700,000 people fleeing the violence. This is a serious humanitarian incident which we are working to respond to.”

“Homes have been burnt and peoples lives have been hit. We need funding to respond and help these suffering communities. We have reports from local sources that fighting has stopped and UN teams are travelling to assess the condition of the displaced population and the damage.”

Islamic Relief is working to respond including with cash assistance for affected and displaced people, hygiene kits, community and psychosocial support to communities in conflict hit locations of Ethiopia.

items.title: World toilet day 2026 - Safe toilets, equal futures
items.blurb:
Countries: World, Ethiopia, Mozambique, Somalia, South Sudan, Yemen
Source: International Organization for Migration

Please refer to the attached file.

World Toilet Day 2026 focuses on the connection between sanitation and gender equality. Access to safe, private and dignified toilets is essential to protecting the health and safety of women and girls, supporting their education and livelihoods, and enabling their full participation in society.

Sanitation is foundational to gender equality. By the end of 2025, 82.2 million people were living in internal displacement within their own countries (IDMC, 2026). Many live in camps and informal settlements where sanitation facilities are shared, overcrowded or inadequate. For displaced women and girls, the lack of safe toilets can affect their daily routines, mobility and access to education and livelihood opportunities.

The sanitation crisis affects everyone, but not equally. Unsafe sanitation exposes women and girls to diseases, danger and abuse. In displacement-affected communities, communal toilets without functioning locks, adequate lighting or sex-segregated facilities can compromise privacy and expose women and girls to heightened protection risks, including gender-based violence.

Safe sanitation is a universal human right, and safe toilets mean equal futures. Everyone should have access to sanitation facilities that are safe, accessible, private, inclusive and responsive to their needs. This requires not only appropriate infrastructure, but also meaningful community participation, effective management and regular maintenance.

IOM works to ensure that migrants, displaced populations and host communities have equitable access to safe, dignified and inclusive water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, recognizing their essential role in protecting health, safety and dignity, particularly in crisis and displacement settings. In 2025, IOM reached 5.1 million people with WASH support across 61 countries and territories, including 1.26 million people with safe sanitation (IOM IQBis, 2025).

IOM designs WASH services with women and girls, including those with disabilities, so that facilities are safe, accessible and meet their menstrual health and hygiene needs. Risks of gender-based violence are identified and mitigated at every stage.

items.title: Haiti: Kenscoff violence highlights continued risk of killing, abduction and other abuses against children by gangs – new research
items.blurb:
Country: Haiti
Source: Amnesty International

Children in Haiti remain at risk of killings, abductions, sexual violence and other abuses by armed gangs, Amnesty International said in new research ahead of World Children’s Day.

Amnesty International interviewed witnesses to the Kenscoff gang raid on 23 August 2026, in which 55 people were killed and 15 more were injured, according to a municipal official. The UN said at least three boys and two girls were among those killed. A further 67 people, including 13 children, were abducted, according to municipal data.

Witnesses told Amnesty International that the attack began when dozens of gang members raided various parts of the commune of Kenscoff, south of Port-au-Prince. They attacked people in their homes, shooting them and setting houses on fire. They looted belongings and shot residents as they tried to escape. They also attacked displaced people who were taking shelter in the Ark of the New Covenant Church and shot many of them.

Children’s lives have been devastated by these horrors

Scott Edwards, Director of Amnesty International’s Crisis Response Programme

“Survivors of the Kenscoff August attack, which came just weeks after another massacre in the same commune, described how they watched as gang members killed their relatives and friends, and how they were raped, beaten and abducted,” said Scott Edwards, Director of Amnesty International’s Crisis Response Programme.

“Children’s lives have been devastated by these horrors. Survivors must have access to mental health support and necessary protection services.

“On World Children’s Day, we are again calling for the Haitian authorities and the international community to urgently increase efforts to protect Haiti’s children as escalating gang violence continues to threaten their lives. Additionally, intensified security operations must not expose children to further harm.”

World Children’s Day, celebrated annually on 20 November, marks the anniversary of the adoption of the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC), which outlines the rights of every child and what governments must do to protect them. Haiti is a state party to the CRC.

Kenscoff attacks

Organized gangs – namely Grand Ravine, Ti Bwa, 5 Segon and 400 Mawozo – started attacking the mountainous commune of Kenscoff in January 2025. All four gangs are part of the Viv Ansanm coalition.

Kenscoff borders Pétion-Ville, where many government offices, embassies and key commercial interests are situated. The 23 August attack on the population, which began around 9pm and was primarily led by a group from the 5 Segon gang, further appeared to be a retaliation for intensified security operations against the gangs.

One teenage girl told Amnesty International that she hid under her bed as gunshots rang out: “When they came inside the house, they said everybody should get out [or else] they would kill us.”

The girl was abducted and held for a little over one month alongside other abductees: “They [gang members] threatened us a lot… They came in and told us that they didn’t come all this way, risking death, for us to think that nothing would happen to us. They threatened that they would kill us.”

According to the UN, 15 women and four girls were raped. One teenage girl, who was abducted and raped, told Amnesty International: “We heard gunshots, but we didn’t have anywhere to go. We didn’t know where to go… They came in [to our house] and took everybody.”

The girl was tied up with an extension cord and beaten. She was separated from her family, and raped by two gang members on a street: “I tried to fight, but they hit me with a hammer and ripped my underwear… They tied me to a pole and told me they were going to fight with the police… The way they tied me was kind of loose. I freed myself and fled.”

One man who was among the displaced people sheltering in the church said gang members shot and killed one of his family members, a mother of two, as she tried to flee. He managed to hide alongside the two children, but one, a teenage boy, ran to a nearby burial site and was shot. The next morning, the man emerged from hiding and saw that the boy had been shot four times. The boy spent more than two weeks in hospital recovering. The man said of the boy’s condition after the attack: “He has some difficulty adapting at school… he forgets everything.”

Abduction by gangs

Amnesty International documented the abduction of at least 11 children, including three toddlers. Abductees said they were tied up and forced to walk in the dark for hours to houses that gang members had occupied.

Abductees were made to sleep on the floor. One girl said the room where she was initially held was overcrowded, so abductees had to take turns to lie down. They were given very little to eat – mostly crackers, and rice and beans – and untreated water to drink.

Abductees who escaped after security operations faced further hardship and danger as they were caught in resulting aerial attacks, including drone strikes. One girl said she ran barefoot for two days to escape, using her t-shirt to bandage her wounded feet.

The girl said she witnessed at least two boys abducted alongside her die after being injured by the drone strikes. These testimonies are a reminder to Haitian security authorities and their partners – including mercenaries, Salvadoran troops and the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force – of the importance of ensuring that members of the population are spared during security operations.

Witnesses said gang members requested money in exchange for the release of some abductees. Some family members said they simply could not afford to make the ransom payments. At least one family paid close to USD 700 to ensure the release of an adolescent girl, but the gang members didn’t let her go.

On 28 August, UNICEF reported that six children and seven women who were abducted had been released. Others remained in captivity for varying periods, with the whereabouts of some still unknown.

The repeated attacks on Kenscoff have caused multiple waves of displacement. The August attack displaced more than 4,200 people. Interviewees described difficult living conditions in displacement and said many displaced children were struggling to return to school. Insecurity has also disrupted agricultural production in the farming commune.

Community members and Haitian and international human rights monitors criticized the apparent inadequate response of security forces to the attacks.

Need for accountability

Authorities are investigating the Kenscoff violence. They must be transparent about these investigations, and make clear the fate of residents who were caught up in the subsequent security operations.

Previous investigations into various massacres by gangs in recent years have not yet amounted to credible trials. Authorities must ensure that impunity is tackled through independent and impartial investigations that hold to account those suspected of criminal responsibility, including politicians supporting gangs.

“Amnesty International continues to call on the Haitian government and international partners to develop and implement a comprehensive child protection plan, ensuring access to education, healthcare and justice for survivors. Protecting children must be an essential part of any response to Haiti’s security crisis,” said Ana Piquer, Americas Director at Amnesty International.

In the months ahead, Amnesty International will release more outputs based on research conducted between September and November 2026, which included a visit to Haiti and more than 60 interviews. The research is part of the organization’s work on the impact of the crisis on children. Since the assassination of President Jovenel Moïse in July 2021, violence by armed gangs has escalated significantly in Haiti and has amounted to an assault on childhood.
