items.title: Afghanistan: Afghan women call for greater opportunities at Global Open Day with SRSG Fatima | United Nations Peace Operations
items.blurb:
Country: Afghanistan
Source: UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan

KABUL- Afghan women leaders, journalists, entrepreneurs and civil society representatives met with the Special Representative of the Secretary-General and Head of UNAMA, Rabab Fatima, during a United Nations-supported Global Open Day event in Kabul, calling for greater opportunities and meaningful participation for women in Afghan society.

The event brought together around 50 women's rights advocates, media representatives, business leaders, and community members to discuss the challenges facing Afghan women and girls and exchange ideas on how to address them.

In her remarks, Fatima commended the contributions of Afghan women. "Across the country, I have seen the determination, contribution and leadership of women," she said, emphasising that women do not want to be passive recipients of support but active participants in shaping the decisions and policies that affect their lives.

Participants stressed the importance of ensuring women's meaningful participation in public life, including access to education, employment and other fundamental rights. Their calls come amid continued restrictions on women and girls. As of 2026, an estimated 2.4 million girls remain excluded from secondary education, reversing two decades of progress in expanding access to learning opportunities.

"What will happen to Afghanistan in 20 years without educated women?" asked one participant.

Launched by the United Nations Security Council in 2010, Global Open Day events are held worldwide to promote dialogue between United Nations representatives and women's organizations, raise awareness of women's contributions to peace and security, and support their participation in conflict prevention and resolution.

items.title: Nepal: Au milieu des souffrances causées par les inondations, une clinique d’urgence de la Croix-Rouge contribue à faire naître de nouvelles vies au Népal. | IFRC
items.blurb:
Country: Nepal
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

Par Fleur Verwer, IFRC coordinator à l'IFRC pour l’opération d’urgence liée aux inondations au Népal.

---

La clinique d’urgence de la Société de la Croix-Rouge népalaise (CRN) venait tout juste d’ouvrir ses portes pour la journée lorsqu’une jeune femme enceinte et son compagnon s’y sont présentés. Ses vêtements étaient trempés, elle souffrait énormément et ne savait pas quoi faire.

Se rendre à l’hôpital était impossible : les eaux de crue avaient emporté le pont qui y menait, et elle ne pouvait pas traverser la rivière.

Ayant entendu parler de la clinique d’urgence de la Croix-Rouge, elle avait décidé de s’y rendre pour chercher de l’aide.

Le Dr Gyanendra Jora était de garde lorsque la jeune femme est arrivée.

« Elle n’avait que 18 ans et ne savait manifestement pas quoi faire. Elle nous a expliqué que sa poche des eaux s’était rompue brusquement la veille », se souvient-il.

Pour le Dr Jora, il était immédiatement évident qu’il fallait agir sans perdre de temps. Après un examen rapide de la mère et du bébé, il a organisé son transfert en urgence vers un centre d’accouchement, où elle pourrait bénéficier d'un suivi médical et accoucher en toute sécurité.

Le Dr Gyanendra Jora devant la clinique médicale d’urgence de la Croix-Rouge népalaise à Bidur, où il a travaillé pendant plusieurs semaines après les inondations.

Photo: IFRC

Moins d’une demi-heure après son arrivée, la jeune femme était déjà en route. Le Dr Jora, accompagné d’une infirmière de la Société de la Croix-Rouge népalaise (CRN) et d’un volontaire, l’a escortée à bord d’une ambulance de la CRN jusqu’à un centre de santé urbain situé à environ 25 kilomètres. Son travail était déjà bien avancé et chaque minute comptait. Une trentaine de minutes plus tard, l’équipe l’a confiée au personnel du centre d’accouchement, s’est assurée qu’elle était entre de bonnes mains, puis est retournée à la clinique.

Trois heures et demie plus tard, une petite fille en bonne santé venait au monde.

Lorsque la nouvelle de la naissance est parvenue à la clinique, un immense soulagement a envahi l’équipe qui avait pris cette première décision déterminante.

Plus tard, une équipe de l'IFRC et de la CRN, comprenant Sachiko Kawase, déléguée Santé de l’IFRC, s’est rendue auprès de la mère et de son nouveau-né pour prendre de leurs nouvelles. Elle a constaté que le bébé était en bonne santé et se portait bien.

Pour accompagner la famille dans les jours à venir, l’équipe a remis à la mère un kit de dignité, comprenant notamment un foulard pour le bébé, ainsi qu’un kit d’hygiène. Cette visite constituait la dernière étape d’une chaîne de soins : du premier examen médical au transport en ambulance, jusqu’à cette visite de suivi, la Croix-Rouge avait accompagné la famille à chaque étape.

Au milieu du deuil, de la douleur et des pertes causés par les inondations, cette nouvelle vie a fait naître une lueur d’espoir.

Un membre de la Croix-Rouge népalaise examine une femme à la clinique, qui a pris en charge plus de 1 500 personnes en 24 jours.

Photo: IFRC

Un soutien vital après les inondations

L’histoire de cette jeune mère n’est qu’une parmi tant d’autres qui se sont déroulées à la clinique d’urgence de la Croix-Rouge à Bidur.

Après les inondations dévastatrices du 26 août, la ville s’est retrouvée largement coupée des services de santé. Le pont qui reliait l’hôpital public à l’autre partie de la ville a été emporté par la violence des eaux. Les personnes qui dépendaient de cet hôpital pour obtenir des médicaments, bénéficier de soins gratuits ou recevoir une assistance médicale d’urgence se sont soudainement retrouvées sans solution.

Pour maintenir l’accès aux soins de santé essentiels, la Croix-Rouge népalaise (CRN) a mis en place cette clinique d’urgence, devenue indispensable.

La clinique n’était pas nouvelle, mais son rôle était plus crucial que jamais. Elle avait été déployée pour la première fois après le séisme de 2015 au Népal. Une fois encore, elle a constitué un maillon essentiel de la réponse, faisant toute la différence entre avoir accès aux soins de santé de base et en être totalement privé.

Au cours des 24 jours de fonctionnement de la clinique, les médecins ont pris en charge plus de 1 500 personnes présentant des problèmes de santé très variés : des affections bénignes aux maladies chroniques, comme l’hypertension artérielle et la bronchopneumopathie chronique obstructive, en passant par des cas nécessitant une orientation urgente vers un hôpital.

Des membres de la Croix-Rouge népalaise apportent leur aide à deux personnes touchées par les inondations au niveau de la pharmacie de la clinique.

Photo: IFRC

Soutenir la communauté

Âgée de 17 ans, Isha, volontaire de la Croix-Rouge, était présente dès le premier jour d’ouverture de la clinique après les inondations.

« J’habite juste derrière la clinique. Heureusement, ma maison n’a pas été touchée par les inondations et ma famille est en sécurité. Lorsque j’ai appris que la clinique d’urgence était en cours d’installation, j’ai immédiatement voulu apporter mon aide. J’ai assisté le pharmacien et contribué à alléger sa charge de travail », raconte Isha.

Les volontaires comme Isha n’étaient pas les seuls à se dévouer pleinement. Le Dr Jora, qui a travaillé à la clinique pendant plusieurs semaines, ne s’est pas contenté de soigner les patients : il leur a également prêté une oreille attentive et a été profondément touché par les témoignages qu’ils lui ont confiés.

« Je savais que j’étais là pour fournir des soins médicaux, mais les histoires que les gens me racontaient m’ont profondément marqué. Tant de personnes portaient en elles une immense souffrance. Pas seulement physique, mais aussi émotionnelle », confie le Dr Jora.

Il se souvient notamment d’un homme qui avait subi trois crises convulsives successives, chacune durant plusieurs minutes.

« Il vivait seul et était resté inconscient pendant des heures. Ce n’est que plusieurs jours plus tard qu’il s’est présenté à la clinique. Quand j’ai réalisé qu’il avait dû affronter seul cette situation, sans aucune aide pendant une expérience aussi terrifiante, cela m’a profondément bouleversé. Et ce n’était qu’une histoire parmi tant d’autres. Il y en avait tellement.

« C’est pourquoi j’étais reconnaissant de pouvoir être auprès de ces personnes au moment où elles en avaient le plus besoin », ajoute-t-il.

Isha, 17 ans, qui habite juste derrière la clinique, s’est portée volontaire pour assister le pharmacien dès le jour de l’ouverture de la clinique.

Photo: IFRC

Le chemin vers le rétablissement

La clinique d’urgence de la Croix-Rouge ne représentait qu’une partie de l’intervention menée par la Croix-Rouge. En collaboration avec les autorités nationales et locales, et avec le soutien de la Fédération internationale des Sociétés de la Croix-Rouge et du Croissant-Rouge (IFRC), la Croix-Rouge népalaise (CRN) a notamment eu recours à des hélicoptères pour acheminer des articles de secours vers les communautés isolées en raison des infrastructures endommagées.

Là où les ponts avaient été emportés par les eaux, les volontaires de la CRN ont aidé les populations à traverser les rivières à l’aide de tuin, de simples nacelles se déplaçant le long d’un câble tendu et permettant de transporter des personnes ainsi que des biens de première nécessité vers l’autre rive, notamment pour se rendre à l’hôpital de district de Nuwakot.

La CRN a également rétabli l’accès à l’eau potable pour plus de 13 900 personnes et fourni des premiers secours psychologiques ainsi qu’un soutien psychosocial à plus de 1 700 autres personnes. À Bidur, elle a été la première organisation à commencer à fournir une assistance financière aux familles dans le besoin.

Derrière cette intervention se trouvait un financement mobilisé presque immédiatement : le jour même des inondations, l’IFRC a débloqué près d’un million de francs suisses (CHF) de son Fonds d’urgence pour les réponses aux catastrophes (DREF). Le lendemain, un appel d’urgence de 25 millions de francs suisses, prévu pour une durée de 24 mois, a été lancé.

Cette durée témoigne de l’ampleur des besoins qui restent à satisfaire. Les équipes poursuivent leurs efforts pour renforcer les interventions dans les domaines de l’hébergement, de l’accès à l’eau potable et à l’assainissement, des services de santé, du soutien psychosocial et de l’assistance financière. À terme, l’objectif est d’aider les familles à quitter les tentes et les sites d’évacuation pour rejoindre des logements plus sûrs et durables, tout en leur permettant de retrouver leurs moyens de subsistance.

L’histoire de cette mère et de son bébé illustre ce qu’une assistance apportée en temps opportun peut accomplir. Pour permettre à davantage de familles de bénéficier d'un soutien similaire, nous vous invitons à contribuer à l’appel d’urgence de l’IFRC pour les inondations au Népal.

items.title: World: ICRC: Landmines, booby-traps and other devices continue to inflict grave suffering on civilians
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: International Committee of the Red Cross

Statement on the Occasion of the 28th Annual Conference of the High Contracting Parties to Amended Protocol II on Prohibitions or Restrictions on the Use of Mines, Booby-Traps and Other Devices, 13 November 2026

In far too many places around the world, everyday activities like driving to the market, walking to school, playing outdoors, cultivating land or herding animals, and even handling ordinary devices entail deadly risks.

Landmines, booby-traps and other devices continue to inflict grave suffering on civilians. They impede access to health-care facilities and other essential services, and hamper humanitarian operations. Even once the fighting has ended, these weapons leave behind long-term explosive hazards that impede the safe return of displaced populations and hinder reconstruction and development.

Year after year, mines, booby-traps and other explosive devices claim thousands of lives. According to the Landmine Monitor 2025, the overwhelming majority of victims are civilians, many of them children – the very people who must never be attacked and must be protected from the dangers of military operations. Last year alone, ICRC teams in 28 countries provided physical rehabilitation services for more than 25,000 people suffering with often life-altering injuries because of mines, cluster munitions and other explosive remnants of war. Many of those we treat are grappling with debilitating physical injuries that also have psychological and financial impacts.

The ICRC is particularly concerned about the dramatic increase in the use of anti-personnel landmines – both manufactured and improvised – including on the territories of High Contracting Parties.

Anti-personnel mines have indiscriminate effects. The ICRC and the wider International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement, along with states party to the Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention, condemn the use of anti-personnel mines by any actor, and the ICRC urges all those who continue to use anti-personnel mines to cease such use immediately. We recall in this connection that High Contracting Parties bound by both the Protocol and the Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention are prohibited from using anti-personnel mines in all circumstances. We urge High Contracting Parties to give effect to relevant prohibitions and restrictions in their domestic legislation and military instructions, and to reflect these measures in their National Annual Reports submitted under the Protocol.

In addition, we call on all those who use anti-vehicle mines to step up their efforts significantly to protect civilians against their indiscriminate effects. The ICRC has long called for the rules of international law applicable to such mines to be strengthened to enhance the protection of civilians. An anti-vehicle mine (AV mine) does not distinguish between a military, civilian or humanitarian vehicle. Consequently, AV mines can considerably hinder the delivery of humanitarian assistance to vulnerable populations. They can also hamper the return of displaced civilians, the cultivation of valuable farmland and reconstruction efforts at the end of active hostilities. Further steps are needed to effectively address the harm caused to civilians by anti-vehicle mines.

Such steps could include, for example, the High Contracting Parties that endorsed the 2006 Declaration on Anti-vehicle Mines using the opportunity of this Review Conference and subsequent meetings of High Contracting Parties to report on their implementation of the Declaration’s commitments. This could also include confirmation that these commitments are now part of military doctrine and policy.

High Contracting Parties must strictly comply with the requirements of Amended Protocol II and its Annex. Recording, retaining and sharing information concerning minefields, mined areas, mines, booby-traps and other devices, as required by Article 9, is key to the implementation of life-saving measures. Another notable obligation is the removal of mines without delay after the cessation of active hostilities, in line with Article 10. States party to both Protocols II and V can develop a joint system to implement the two Protocols and make the process less resource intensive. Helpful guidance is available in the Technical Annex to Protocol V and in the ICRC’s briefing note on preventing and eradicating the deadly legacy of explosive remnants of war.

Madam President,

Today, the ICRC partners with 20 National Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, with more than 2,100 staff and volunteers, working alongside communities to help reduce their exposure to the risks posed by mines, cluster munitions and other explosive remnants of war. This work includes technical support in clearance operations, raising awareness of and promoting safer behaviour, physical rehabilitation services, and support for the social and economic inclusion of survivors.

For the protection of civilians, it remains critically important that Amended Protocol II is universally adhered to. We encourage all High Contracting Parties to redouble their efforts to promote its universalization and we call on states that have not already joined the Protocol to do so without further delay.

items.title: Quarter of a Million Landmines Removed from Zimbabwe - The HALO Trust has destroyed four mines per person in north-east Zimbabwe
items.blurb:
Countries: Zimbabwe, Afghanistan, Angola, Colombia, Sri Lanka, Syrian Arab Republic, Ukraine, Yemen
Source: HALO Trust

Harare, Zimbabwe, 19 Nov. The world’s largest landmine clearance charity, the HALO Trust, has reached a significant milestone in Zimbabwe, destroying 250,000 landmines since 2013.

Dense belts of landmines, including the highly sensitive R2M2 models, were laid along Zimbabwe’s borders with Mozambique and Zambia during the Liberation War in the 1970s. They’ve killed or injured more than 1,500 people and 120,000 cattle since independence in 1980.

For 13-years, HALO’s Zimbabwean teams have cleared these minefields in Rushinga and Mount Darwin, saving lives and limbs while restoring farmland, reconnecting communities and laying the foundations for investment and economic growth.

“The destruction of 250,000 landmines is an extraordinary achievement, built on the dedication and courage of Zimbabwean men and women working in some of the country’s most dangerous areas” said Oliver Gerard-Pearse, HALO Trust Zimbabwe Programme Manager.

In Rushinga, where losing a single cow to a landmine can cost a family the equivalent of six months’ school fees, clearance has directly benefited more than 14,000 residents, allowing families to reclaim farmland, graze livestock, grow cash crops and safely access clean water, schools, clinics and markets.

***“We would walk in fear”***saysresidentMunesa Takawira “Now, we are free to walk as we please, and the cows and other domestic animals that used to be hit by landmines can freely move around. We can send children to fetch firewood without fear that they will get injured.”

In Mount Darwin, where HALO became the first operator to hand over an entire district as landmine-free in 2021, deaths and injuries from explosives fell to zero, incomes rose by 90% for nearly a third of local farmers, and land-owning families in six communities increased by more than 80%.

As the largest demining organisation in the country, HALO also provides vital local employment in areas where jobs are scarce. The organisation trains female deminers who are often the main breadwinners for their families and support an average of eight relatives through their clearance work.

Drones, state of the art detectors and mini excavators are helping HALO clear faster and more safely. But technology alone cannot fully counter the impact of sweeping global aid cuts, which threaten Zimbabwe’s aim to achieve mine-free status by 2030.

Just 4% of land remains contaminated says Gerard Pearse who estimates that it would take $6.5 million in donations to free the country from mines by the end of the decade.

“We have seen how safe land can boost investment and development in other countries where HALO works. In neighbouring Mozambique, GDP rose significantly when it was declared mine-free in 2015” he says.

“In Zimbabwe we are now so close to lasting safety for generations to come. We cannot afford to lose momentum at this final stage of a decades-long effort.”

Please find footage of our demining operations here and images here (credit: The HALO Trust)

For more information or to arrange interviews or site visits, please contact media@halotrust.org

Notes to editors

  • Zimbabwe ranked second globally in anti-personnel landmine destruction after Cambodia, according to the Clearing the Mines 2025 report.
  • HALO has trained over 17,000 adults and 73,000 children how to stay safe from explosives since 2015, working closely with Happy Readers, a local charity that provides children with educational books on the risks of mines.
  • HALO also works with Cassim's Prosthetics to support amputees.
  • The HALO Trust is the world's largest humanitarian landmine clearance organisation, working in in 30+ countries including Ukraine, Afghanistan, Yemen, Syria, Colombia, Angola and Sri Lanka.
  • We deploy groundbreaking technology in conflict and post-conflict settings to help people rebuild their homes, restore their livelihoods and keep their children safe.
  • HALO also runs programmes in weapons and ammunition management and safety training. During emergencies, we also provide humanitarian aid and logistical support.
  • HALO was founded in 1988 in Afghanistan.
  • We employ over 8,000 staff worldwide and recruit 95% of them locally.

items.title: Cameroon: North-West and South-West Situation Report No.87, July to September 2026
items.blurb:
Country: Cameroon
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached file.

HIGHLIGHTS

  • More than 1,600 protection incidents recorded in the North-West and South-West regions.
  • Nearly 900 people displaced in the North-West and South-West regions due to violence and insecurity.
  • More than 4,000 people affected by floods and landslides, with about 500 displaced and five deaths reported.
  • Four improvised explosive devices incidents recorded in the North-West region.
  • A total of 736 children with severe acute malnutrition received life-saving treatment in partner-supported treatment centres.

SITUATION OVERVIEW / HUMANITARIAN ACCESS

During the reporting period July-September 2026, the humanitarian situation in Cameroon’s North-West and South-West (NWSW) regions remained fragile and deteriorated further amid continued clashes between State security forces (SSF) and non-State armed groups (NSAGs). Persistent insecurity, including kidnapping for ransom, arbitrary arrests, the proliferation of illegal checkpoints, extortion, and roadblocks, continued to restrict population movements, hinder access to basic services and livelihoods, and heighten protection risks for affected communities.

The situation remained volatile, with at least 11 improvised explosive devices (IED) incidents recorded during the reporting period, including 10 in the North-West and one in the South-West. While these attacks primarily targeted SSFs and their convoys, civilians remained at significant risk of injury or death from accidental explosions.

Attacks and threats against education intensified ahead of the 2026/2027 school year. NSAGs enforced school-related restrictions, imposed school levies in some areas, and increased intimidation of education personnel, including the abduction of five teachers in Wum (Menchum division, North-West). In September, armed actors also attacked a secondary school in the North-West, disrupting learning activities.

Humanitarian needs remained severe across the two regions, exacerbated by successive lockdowns imposed by NSAGs between 1 and 21 September. The measures restricted movement, disrupted education, livelihoods, and economic activities and limited access to essential services. Lockdown enforcement through threats and sporadic attacks resulted in civilian casualties in both regions and further affected already vulnerable communities.

Continued clashes between parties to the crisis triggered new population displacement and humanitarian needs across the North-West and South-West. In Momo division, an estimated 875 people (175 households) were displaced from Diku to Tikom during the reporting period with many families seeking refuge in nearby bushes. Heavy rainfall that caused flooding and landslides on 5 August affected over 4,157 people, displaced more than 500, caused five reported deaths, including a pregnant woman, and destroyed or damaged 16 houses infrastructure, livestock, and community water systems in Limbe (Fako division), Kumba (Meme division) in the South-West, and in Tinifoimbi Village (Boyo division) in the North-West. While many affected households have returned, those whose shelters were destroyed or damaged remain displaced and in need of assistance. Priority needs include shelter, food assistance, health, WASH, protection, education and livelihood support. In coordination with OCHA and area-based coordination co-chairs, humanitarian partners delivered multipurpose cash assistance, shelter support, psychosocial services, and gender-based violence prevention interventions across affected communities, in addition to the assistance delivered by authorities.

Humanitarian access remained constrained due to insecurity, prolonged lockdown and the presence of illegal checkpoints along key road corridors, including the Bamenda-Widikum axis in Momo division and the Bamenda-Ndop road. These restrictions significantly hindered population movements and limited the transportation of agricultural produce. The operational environment remained highly challenging and required continuous access negotiations amid a fragile, volatile, and rapidly evolving context.

items.title: World: Governments Pressed to Deliver on 250+ New Pledges at the End Violence Against Children Summit
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: Save the Children

MANILA, 18 November 2026 - Governments announced more than 250 new commitments to prevent violence against children at a key global summit on child protection in Manila, with Save the Children urging leaders to turn those promises into funded action.

At the second Global Ministerial Conference to End Violence Against Children (EVAC), representatives from over 80 of the 130 countries present [1] made pledges across a range of areas, from combatting the recruitment and use of children in armed conflict and tech facilitated violence, to expanding child protection services to helping children recover from abuse.

Almost 40% of the countries making pledges did so for the first time, underscoring growing global momentum to make children safer, said Save the Children.

The new pledges come at a critical time for children, as conflict, climate shocks, poverty and inequality continue to expose millions of children to violence in their homes, schools, online and in their communities.

Violence against children encompasses any form of physical, emotional, digital or online abuse, sexual abuse, neglect, exploitation, or harmful traditional practices directed at children.

Every year, an estimated 1.6 billion children experience violence globally, including 90 million who experience sexual violence.[2], which can have lifelong consequences for children's health, learning, development, and wellbeing.

While progress has been made in recent years, far too many children still face violence every day, with devastating and often lifelong consequences for their health, wellbeing and future opportunities.

Save the Children urged leaders to turn promises into funded action.

Rebecca Smith, Global Head of Child Protection, Save the Children, said:

“We know how to prevent violence against children, now we need real commitment to make their safety a reality. These new pledges are a very welcome and important step forward, but they must now be backed by sustained investment, strong accountability and meaningful action that reaches children, wherever they live in the world, because millions of children continue to experience abuse, exploitation and harm every single day and their safety cannot be an afterthought. Children’s experiences and their voices must be at the heart of all violence prevention and survivor support initiatives.”

In 2025, Save the Children’s programmes reached 5.5 million children and caregivers globally through violence prevention and response interventions.

Financial stress on families can increase the risk of violence against children. Through our Money Matters Toolkit Save the Children helps caseworkers to engage families in conversations about budgeting and financial decision-making to help families make informed decisions and be more resilient.

Save the Children’s Safe Families initiative works with children of all ages, caregivers and communities to support families to better communicate and solve problems together, encourage adults to better understand child development and see children as rights holders with their own views and perspectives with separate sessions just for children.

ENDS

Notes to editors:

[1] https://www.who.int/news/item/17-11-2026-governments-make-over-230-new-pledges-to-prevent-violence-against-children

[2] https://data.unicef.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/UNICEF-Data-brief-on-VAC-at-home_Nov-2025.pdf

*Enhancing the climate-adaptive capacity of smallholder farming communities
in the Poro Region, focusing on vulnerable women and youth*

Context

Climate shocks are undermining food systems in
northern regions of Côte d’Ivoire, such as Poro. Since
the 1980s, this region has experienced erratic rainfall
patterns, resulting in repeated drought episodes and a
gradual decline in average annual precipitation.
These challenges are becoming more severe as
temperatures continue to rise and weather patterns
become less predictable. Combined with recurrent
droughts and land degradation, they are significantly
reducing agricultural productivity in a region where
livelihoods depend heavily on rain-fed agriculture.
Women farmers, who play a central role in local food
systems, continue to face systemic barriers to
accessing land, water, financial services, and climate
information. These challenges limit their ability to adapt
to climate shocks, strengthen their productivity, and
build resilient livelihoods.
Climate projections indicate that the share of arable
land affected by drought could increase from 7% in
2000 to 23% by 2080, leading to yield declines of up
to 9% for maize and 10% for millet and sorghum.
This would further exacerbate food insecurity and
livelihood vulnerabilities.
Climate shocks are therefore not a future risk;
they are a current threat to food security,
livelihoods, and economic empowerment of
women and youth.

items.title: Statement: USCRI Urges European Countries to Stop Plans to Send People Who Sought Asylum to Rwanda
items.blurb:
Countries: Rwanda, Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece, Netherlands, World
Source: US Committee for Refugees and Immigrants

On November 16, 2026, five European countries announced plans to send people who sought asylum in Europe and cannot be returned to their home country to Rwanda. The “Group of Five”—which includes Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Greece, and Denmark—states that it will send people whose asylum claims have been adjudicated and denied to a return hub overseas because they have no right to stay in Europe. The enforcement of returns should not come at the cost of eroding human rights for migrants, refugees, and asylum seekers. USCRI strongly urges the “Group of Five” to retract their deal with Rwanda and stop pursuing return hubs.

Return hubs expose vulnerable groups to the danger of refoulement, or the forcible return of a person to a country where they face a risk of persecution, torture, or serious harm. The principle of non-refoulement is a core human rights guarantee that is enshrined in several key international treaties, including the 1951 Refugee Convention.

“The Group of Five is attempting to skirt this international legal and moral obligation by sending people to a country where they have no ties and will feel pressured to either face the danger of an unfamiliar legal process in Rwanda or face the danger of returning to the place where they fled,” said Eskinder Negash, President and CEO of the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants (USCRI).

This announcement follows a meeting in September between the Group of Five, where they announced intentions to pursue a deal with a non-European country to host migrant return hubs. Despite legal controversy surrounding return hubs, the European Parliament adopted regulation in June 2026 allowing countries to pursue deals to establish them.

“The idea of sending anyone who fled their country to seek safety to an offshore site should be against our moral principles as an international community,” Negash continued. “Global coordination should be in pursuit of protecting people who face danger, rather than exposing them to more risks.”

Deals with Rwanda on migration have been widely criticized. In July 2024, a deal between the United Kingdom and Rwanda to send asylum seekers for processing was scrapped after heavy scrutiny from human rights advocates and international human rights organizations. Rwanda has reportedly received $7.5 million from the United States to accept third country removals, a practice that is currently subject to legal challenge.

The Group of Five stated that it is working with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and the International Organization for Migration. Both organizations have stated that human rights must be guaranteed and that they will engage with the countries as they move forward.

USCRI is closely tracking these developments. The danger of globally institutionalizing third country returns is at risk. Follow these developments through The Legal Landscape or USCRI’s Third Country Deportations Tracker.

items.title: DR Congo: Ebola response cannot succeed without broader humanitarian effort | NRC
items.blurb:
Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Source: Norwegian Refugee Council

A more comprehensive and inclusive approach is essential if the spread of Ebola is to be halted, warns the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC)

Press release

DR Congo Published 19. Nov 2026

Six months after Ebola was declared in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo), the outbreak remains out of control and continues to devastate communities.

Insecurity remains a major concern in affected areas, where regular violent attacks continue to cause displacement, hindering access to healthcare and disrupting contact tracing and the monitoring of Ebola patients. Violent conflict allows the virus to spread unchecked, with devastating implications for the population. Experience on the ground demonstrates that containing the virus requires more than just a health response. It also requires a broader humanitarian approach that puts community protection and recovery at the heart of its priorities.

Against this backdrop, maintaining access to essential services and strengthening infection prevention and control (IPC) are critical. In more than 100 schools, 25 health centres, and 10 communities, the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) supports the installation of triage systems and handwashing facilities, the provision of hygiene supplies, and the adoption of good IPC practices. These interventions help create safer environments for children, teachers, patients and health workers, while strengthening institutional capacities to prevent and mitigate the risk of Ebola transmission.

At the community level, risk awareness and communication activities bring key messages closer to the population. Working directly with local communities is central to addressing concerns and misconceptions, encouraging protective behaviours, strengthening trust and allowing for the rapid uptake of recommended prevention measures.

“I am living proof that early action saves lives,” explained one Ebola survivor in Ituri during an interview with NRC staff.

“As soon as I recognised the symptoms, I sought medical assistance. This decision saved my life and helped protect my family, my colleagues and the wider community. We really need to make sure people understand how important it is to act early. Without community awareness, we cannot fight this virus effectively,” he added.

The impact of the outbreak also extends beyond the immediate risk of infection. The high levels of disruption and fear triggered by the outbreak can affect children's emotional well-being and ability to learn. Through its Better Learning Programme (BLP), NRC works with schools to help children manage stress and anxiety, maintain their concentration and continue engaging in learning despite the challenges they face.

“Responding effectively to Ebola goes beyond preventing the transmission of the virus. It is also about protecting children, safeguarding the future of entire populations, and supporting those who survive Ebola to safely reintegrate into their communities,” said Silvia Beccacece, NRC emergency response team leader in Ituri.

“Every day, our teams work alongside communities, engaging with people, listening to their concerns and mobilising them to play an active role in the response. Six months into this outbreak, sustaining these efforts is a shared responsibility, and our commitment must remain strong for as long as people need support,” she added.

As the outbreak evolves, it is essential that the response becomes more effective and more embedded in communities. Authorities, humanitarian organisations and donors all have a role to play in ensuring that community-based prevention and protection activities can continue. This requires sustained political attention, meaningful support for local engagement, and predictable funding. Maintaining these efforts is essential not only to contain the outbreak, but also to protect the lives, rights and dignity of the people and communities affected.

Notes to Editors:

  • The latest figures on confirmed cases and deaths are available here: DRC Ebola Bundibugyo - Epidemic Intelligence Dashboard
  • Among the 68 health zones affected by the outbreak, NRC operates in 19, contributing to infection prevention and control and protection efforts. NRC's interventions combine support to health facilities, schools, and communities, to strengthen hygiene, reduce exposure to the virus and promote safer practices.
  • The Africa CDC has repeated its view that the current outbreak remains out of control (Reuters)

Source: UN Women

Please refer to the attached file.

The Government of Uganda, through the Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development (MoGLSD), conducted a Rapid Gender Analysis (RGA) to strengthen gender-responsive, inclusive and protection-sensitive Ebola preparedness and response efforts. The assessment examined how Ebola outbreaks and related interventions affect women, men, girls, boys, persons with disabilities, older persons, refugees and other at-risk groups differently, identifying barriers, vulnerabilities, capacities and priority needs.

The assessment covered nine districts and Kampala, including refugee settlements, and examined key areas such as coordination and participation, disease surveillance and referral, risk communication and community engagement, case management, psychosocial wellbeing, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), infection prevention and control, continuity of essential health services, protection, accountability and livelihoods.

The assessment was led by MoGLSD, with technical, coordination and operational support from UNFPA, UNHCR, UN Women, War Child and Oxfam, and collaboration with the Ministry of Health, district authorities, refugee leadership, health workers, community leaders and community members.

The findings and recommendations provide evidence to guide government institutions and humanitarian and development partners in strengthening Ebola preparedness and response planning, informing resource allocation, addressing gender and inclusion gaps, and promoting meaningful community participation, protection and accountability.

items.title: Amid pain caused by the floods, a Red Cross emergency clinic helps bring new life in Nepal | IFRC
items.blurb:
Country: Nepal
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

By Fleur Verwer, IFRC Communications Coordinator for the Nepal Floods Emergency

---

The Nepal Red Cross Society (NRCS) emergency clinic had only just opened for the day when a pregnant young woman and her partner walked in. Her clothes were soaked, she was in severe pain, and she did not know what to do.

Reaching the hospital was not an option: floodwaters had swept away the bridge leading to it, and she could not cross the river.

Having heard about the Red Cross emergency clinic, she decided to go there in search of help.

Dr. Gyanendra Jora was on duty when the woman arrived.

“She was only 18 years old and clearly did not know what to do. She told us that her water had suddenly broken the day before,” he recalled.

For Dr. Jora, it was immediately clear that there was no time to lose. After a quick examination of the mother and baby, he arranged her urgent referral to a birthing centre, where she could be monitored and deliver safely.

Dr. Gyanendra Jora outside the Nepal Red Cross Society emergency field clinic in Bidur, where he worked for weeks after the floods.

Photo: IFRC

Less than half an hour after she arrived, she was on her way. Dr. Jora, together with a nurse from NRCS and a volunteer, accompanied her in a NRCS ambulance on the journey to an urban health centre approximately 25 kilometres away. She was already far along in her labor, so the timing mattered. Around 30 minutes later, the team handed her over to the birthing centre staff, made sure she was in safe hands, and only then returned to the clinic.

Three and a half hours later, a healthy baby girl was born.

When news of the birth reached the clinic, a wave of relief swept through the team that had made the first, decisive call.

Later, a team from the IFRC and NRCS, including IFRC Health Delegate Sachiko Kawase, visited the mother and her newborn daughter to see how they were doing. They found the baby healthy and thriving. To support the family in the days ahead, the team gave the mother a dignity kit, including a scarf for the baby, and a hygiene kit. It was the latest step in a chain of care: from the first examination and the ambulance ride to this follow-up visit, the Red Cross had accompanied the family at every stage.

Amid the grief, pain, and loss caused by the floods, a new life brought a spark of hope.

A member of the Nepal Red Cross Society examines a woman at the clinic, which treated more than 1,500 people in 24 days.

Photo: IFRC

A vital lifeline after the floods

The young mother’s story was just one of many that unfolded at the Red Cross emergency clinic in Bidur.

After the devastating floods on 26 August, the town was largely cut off from healthcare services. The bridge that connected the public hospital to the other side of town was washed away by the sheer force of the water. People who relied on the hospital for medication, free healthcare, or urgent medical assistance suddenly had nowhere to turn.

To keep essential healthcare within reach, the NRCS set up the desperately needed emergency clinic.

The clinic itself was not new, but it was just as vital as ever. It had first been deployed after the 2015 earthquake in Nepal. Once again, it provided a critical lifeline, making the difference between having access to basic healthcare and having none at all.

In the 24 days the clinic was open, doctors treated more than 1,500 people with a wide range of conditions, from minor health problems and chronic illnesses such as high blood pressure and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease to conditions requiring urgent referral to a hospital.

No two days were the same.

Yet every day, doctors, nurses, a pharmacist, and psychosocial support volunteers were ready to serve their community. For twenty-four consecutive days without a break, they served with a friendly smile and a dedication to helping others.

Nepal Red Cross Society members help two people affected by the floods at the clinic’s pharmacy.

Photo: IFRC

Supporting the community

Seventeen-year-old volunteer Isha was there from the day the clinic first opened after the floods.

“I live just behind the clinic. Luckily, my home was not affected by the flood, and my family is safe. When I heard the emergency clinic was being set up, I wanted to help immediately. I assisted the pharmacist and took some of the workload off his shoulders,” Ischa said.

Volunteers like Isha were not the only ones giving their all. Dr. Jora, who worked at the clinic for weeks, did more than treat patients: he also offered a listening ear, and he was deeply affected by the stories they shared.

“I knew I was there to provide medical care, but the stories people shared stayed with me. So many people were carrying so much pain. Not only physically, but emotionally as well,” Dr. Jora said.

He recalled one man who had suffered three seizures in quick succession, each lasting several minutes.

“He lived alone and was unconscious for hours. It was only days later that he came to the clinic. When I thought about the fact that he had to face that situation alone, without any help during such a frightening experience, it really affected me. And that was only one story. There were so many more.

“That is why I was grateful to be there for these people when they needed it most,” he added.

Isha, 17, who lives just behind the clinic, volunteered to help the pharmacist from the day the clinic opened.

Photo: IFRC

The path to recovery

The Red Cross emergency clinic was only one part of the Red Cross response. Working with national and local authorities and supported by the IFRC, the NRCS had used helicopters to deliver relief supplies to communities cut off by damaged infrastructure.

Where bridges had been washed away, NRCS volunteers helped people cross the river on a tuin, a simple trolley running along a rope line that carried people and everyday items to the other side, including on the way to the district hospital in Nuwakot. The NRCS had also restored access to safe water for more than 13,900 people and provided psychological first aid and psychosocial support to over 1,700 others. In Bidur, it was the first agency to begin providing cash assistance to families in need.

Behind this work was funding that was mobilized almost immediately: the IFRC released nearly CHF 1 million from its Disaster Response Emergency Fund the same day the floods struck, and a CHF 25 million Emergency Appeal, set to run for 24 months, followed the next day.

The long timeframe reflects how much remains to be done. Teams are still working to scale up shelter, clean water and sanitation, health services, psychosocial support, and cash assistance. Over time, the aim is to help families leave tents and evacuation camps for safer, lasting homes and to restore their livelihoods.

The story of one mother and her baby shows what timely help can do. To reach more families like hers, please consider supporting the IFRC Nepal Floods Emergency Appeal.

Source: UN Children's Fund

Highlights

  • Somalia's humanitarian needs remained high during the quarter, driven by drought, conflict, displacement, disease outbreaks and declining humanitarian assistance. An estimated 5.1 million people faced acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3+), while 1.92 million children were projected to suffer acute malnutrition between July 2026 and June 2027. About 75,000 displacement movements and over 1,400 conflict events were recorded.
  • UNICEF sustained lifesaving assistance across priority sectors, reaching 98,241 children with SAM treatment, 244,022 caregivers with IYCF counselling, 145,671 people with primary health care, and 286,006 people with safe water. Education support benefited 71,644 children, while 48,991 people accessed child protection services. Monthly cash transfers supported 13,493 vulnerable women, strengthening household resilience.
  • The 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal was 27 per cent funded (US$32 million) against US$121 million required, leaving a US$89 million gap. Underfunding continued to constrain service coverage, operational capacity and emergency preparedness for anticipated El Nino impacts.

items.title: World: Resumen ejecutivo: Informe Alto a la guerra contra la niñez – Hacer posible un futuro mejor
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: Save the Children

Please refer to the attached file.

INFORME ALTO A LA GUERRA CONTRA LA NIÑEZ - HACER POSIBLE UN FUTURO MEJOR

En la actualidad, uno de cada cuatro niños y niñas del mundo vive en zonas de conflicto, una cifra récord desde que se empezó a tener registro de esto en 1990. Una de las preocupaciones políticas y humanitarias más acuciantes de nuestros días es el sufrimiento de la infancia afectada por conflictos armados. Sin embargo, sigue siendo una de las cuestiones más desatendidas.

Los niños y las niñas sufren de manera desproporcionada durante los conflictos. Sus cuerpos pequeños, aún en crecimiento, son extremadamente vulnerables al impacto de los explosivos. Sus mentes, que aún están forjando su propia identidad, construyendo su sentido de seguridad y comprendiendo el mundo, viven el trauma de un modo diferente, que puede dejar huellas a largo plazo y afectar su desarrollo. Estos impactos pueden poner en riesgo toda su niñez y tener consecuencias que perduren más allá del fin de las hostilidades, atravesando, a veces, múltiples generaciones.

Durante los conflictos, aumenta el riesgo de vivir en la pobreza, las redes de apoyo se debilitan, y puede que los niños y las niñas sean separados de sus familias. Suelen interrumpirse los servicios básicos y cerrarse las escuelas, los niños y las niñas interrumpen su escolaridad y no logran las metas educativas, con el consiguiente impacto en su futuro. Alimentarse bien y acceder a servicios de salud esenciales puede convertirse en algo muy difícil, con un impacto devastador en la salud mental de la infancia y de quienes están a cargo de su cuidado.

El último informe de nuestra serie Alto a la guerra contra la niñez mide el nivel de exposición de los niños y las niñas a los conflictos y el daño que esto les genera. Se basa en el análisis de las violaciones graves contra la infancia documentadas por el mecanismo de vigilancia y presentación de informes de la ONU entre 2005 y 2025, que forma parte de los informes presentados anualmente por del Secretario General sobre los niños y los conflictos armados. Hemos complementado esta información con cifras actualizadas del Instituto de Investigación para la Paz de Oslo (PRIO, por sus siglas en inglés) sobre los niños y las niñas que viven en zonas de conflicto, entendidas como áreas situadas en un radio de 50 km de algún incidente relacionado con un conflicto en un año dado.

Veinte años después de establecido el mecanismo de la ONU, las cifras de violaciones graves contra niños y niñas en el contexto de conflictos armados siguen siendo extremadamente altas. Los sistemas de protección se encuentran al límite de su capacidad. El financiamiento humanitario está disminuyendo y algunos países están dejando atrás los compromisos asumidos en los tratados y los mecanismos de rendición de cuentas, en un momento en que son tan necesarios. No se presta la debida atención a las experiencias de los niños y las niñas, y las investigaciones que llegan a realizarse sobre las violaciones perpetradas suelen carecer de los recursos y el personal especializado necesarios.

El Derecho Internacional Humanitario confiere a los niños y las niñas un respeto y protección especiales. Sin embargo, la forma de hacer cumplir la ley y las herramientas utilizadas para proteger a la población civil están concebidas en torno a las personas adultas, y no tienen en cuenta las vulnerabilidades particulares de la infancia. Las nuevas formas de la guerra y las tecnologías emergentes generan mayores riesgos, que los sistemas de protección actuales aún no abordan de manera adecuada.

Para cerrar estas brechas, es preciso implementar sostenidamente medidas de prevención, respuesta y recuperación. Los ejemplos que se presentan en este informe, que surgen de las experiencias del personal de Save the Children en todo el mundo, muestran que es posible reforzar la protección cuando existen responsabilidades claras, se promueve la participación significativa de la infancia, y se dispone de personal capacitado, servicios que funcionan, un firme compromiso político, acceso a la ayuda humanitaria y financiamiento predecible.

items.title: World: Résumé du rapport : Stop à la guerre contre les enfants - Changer la donne
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: Save the Children

Please refer to the attached file.

DU RAPPORT : STOP À LA GUERRE CONTRE LES ENFANTS – CHANGER LA DONNE

Près d’un quart des enfants à travers le monde vivent aujourd’hui dans des zones de conflit. Jamais encore un tel niveau n’avait été atteint depuis le début de cette comptabilisation en 1990. Les souffrances des enfants touchés par des conflits armés constituent actuellement l’une des préoccupations politiques et humanitaires les plus pressantes. C’est pourtant l’une des plus négligées.

Les enfants souffrent de manière disproportionnée durant les conflits. Leurs petits corps, en plein développement, sont particulièrement vulnérables aux conséquences des armes explosives. Leurs esprits, qui forgent encore leur image d’eux-mêmes, leur sentiment de sécurité et leur compréhension du monde, vivent différemment les traumatismes, avec des effets potentiellement durables sur leur développement. Ces conséquences peuvent mettre en péril toute leur enfance, avec des répercussions qui persistent bien après la fin des hostilités, parfois pendant plusieurs générations.

Le risque de pauvreté augmente, les réseaux de soutien sont affaiblis et les enfants peuvent être séparés de leurs familles. Les services vitaux sont souvent perturbés et les écoles fermées ; les enfants ratent ainsi des étapes clés de l’éducation, ce qui impacte leur avenir. Il peut aussi devenir incroyablement difficile de bien manger et d’accéder aux soins de santé vitaux. Tout cela peut avoir un impact dévastateur sur la santé mentale des enfants et celle des personnes qui s’en occupent.

Le tout dernier rapport de notre série Stop à la guerre contre les enfants montre à quel point les enfants sont exposés aux conflits et les préjudices qu’ils subissent. Il s’appuie sur l’analyse des violations graves commises contre des enfants documentées dans le cadre du Mécanisme de surveillance et de communication de l’information des Nations Unies entre 2005 et 2025, présentée dans les rapports annuels du Secrétaire général sur les enfants et les conflits armés. Nous avons rapproché celle-ci des estimations actualisées de l’Institut de recherche sur la paix d’Oslo (PRIO) portant sur le nombre d’enfants vivant dans des zones de conflit ; ce terme étant défini comme les zones situées dans un rayon de 50 kilomètres autour d’un conflit sur une année donnée.

Vingt ans après la création de ce mécanisme, le nombre de violations graves commises contre des enfants en situation de conflit reste exceptionnellement élevé. Les systèmes de protection sont sous tension. Les financements humanitaires sont en baisse et certains États se retirent des engagements pris dans le cadre de traités et des mécanismes de redevabilité, à l’heure où ils sont plus indispensables que jamais. Les expériences vécues par les enfants ne suscitent pas un grand intérêt et lorsque des enquêtes sont effectivement menées sur des violations, l’expertise spécialisée et les ressources requises font souvent défaut.

Le droit international humanitaire confère aux enfants un droit particulier au respect et à la protection. Or, les modalités d’application des lois et les outils utilisés pour protéger les civils restent largement conçus pour les adultes et ignorent souvent les vulnérabilités distinctes des enfants. L’évolution des guerres et les technologies émergentes créent des risques supplémentaires auxquels les mesures de protection existantes ne répondent pas correctement.

Des actions durables de prévention, de réponse et de rétablissement sont nécessaires pour combler ces lacunes. Les exemples présentés tout au long de ce rapport, qui s’appuient sur les constatations faites par le personnel de Save the Children à travers le monde, montrent que des responsabilités clairement définies, un personnel formé, des services qui fonctionnent, une participation significative des enfants, un engagement politique durable, un accès humanitaire et des financements prévisibles peuvent renforcer la protection.

items.title: World: Children affected by armed conflict, 1990–2025
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: Peace Research Institute Oslo

Please refer to the attached file.

More children than ever live in conflict zones

Posted Thursday, 19 Nov 2026 by Gudrun Østby & Siri Aas Rustad

More children now live near armed conflict than the combined populations of the United States, Canada and Mexico.

Armed violence escalated sharply across the globe in 2025. Data from the Uppsala Conflict Data Program (UCDP) shows that conflict-related fatalities rose to 244,600, up from approximately 187,000 in 2024. This made 2025 one of the deadliest years since the end of the Cold War. Much of the increase was driven by a dramatic rise in violence targeting civilians, particularly in Sudan.

While armed conflict affects entire populations, children are among those who suffer the most severe and lasting consequences.

Children face grave violations, including killing and maiming, recruitment by armed groups, sexual violence, abduction, attacks on schools and hospitals, and denial of humanitarian access. But the consequences of war extend far beyond direct violence. Children living in conflict-affected areas are more likely to drop out of school, lack access to clean water, and face heightened risks of death from illness, malnutrition, or lack of vaccines and medical care.

Today, Save the Children launches its new report, Stop the War on Children 2026. The report is based on PRIO’s tenth annual mapping of children in armed conflict covering the period 1990–2025.

Our latest estimates show that 589 million children, more than one in five of the world's children, were living in conflict zones in 2025. This represents a 7% increase from 2024, when an estimated 550 million children were affected. It marks a new all-time high both in absolute numbers and as a share of the global child population.

While the figures have fluctuated from year to year, the long-term trend is clear. The proportion of children living in conflict zones has more than doubled since the mid-1990s, rising from around 10% to 23.4% in 2025.

How we estimate the number of conflict-affected children

Most conflicts occur within limited, localized areas of countries. To estimate the number of children living in conflict zones, it is essential to isolate these areas. The UCDP Georeferenced Events Dataset (UCDP GED) provides precise data on the location of each separate conflict event or incidence of organized violence, including geographical coordinates. Using this data, we map circles with a 50 km radius around each conflict event and estimate the number of children residing within these areas based on population data from CIESIN and the United Nations. We define children affected by conflict as those living within 50 km of one or more conflict events. This 50 km radius is considered a reasonable distance within which conflict can significantly disrupt children's daily lives.

Key findings from the latest update

  • An estimated 1.5 billion children lived in a conflict-affected country in 2025. Of these, 589 million, more than one in five children worldwide, lived in a conflict zone.
  • 355 million children lived in high-intensity conflict zones (with 1,000 or more battle-related deaths) in 2025. This represents an increase of more than 11% from 319 million in 2024.
  • Africa had the largest number of children living in conflict zones, with 260 million. The Middle East had the highest share relative to its child population, at 40.2%.

What can be done to protect children in conflict zones?

Now, more than ever, the need to protect millions of children in conflict zones is urgent. While the devastating impacts of war in Ukraine and the Middle East continue to demand sustained international attention, the growing concentration of conflict-affected children in Africa underscores the need for greater focus on the continent. Africa is now home to 44% of the world's conflict-affected children, and humanitarian needs continue to rise rapidly.

Addressing the growing impact of armed conflict on children worldwide will require sustained commitment from governments, donors, humanitarian organizations, and local communities. Priorities include:

  • Invest in research and data collection to better understand how armed conflict affects children.
  • Ensure adequately resourced and high-quality peacekeeping operations in conflict-affected areas.
  • Partner with local peacebuilders and place children's needs at the centre of peace processes from the outset.
  • Establish and protect safe spaces where children can learn, play, and access essential services.
  • Strengthen accountability mechanisms, including credible sanctions against armed groups responsible for grave violations against children.
  • Increase support to conflict-affected countries to rebuild essential infrastructure, particularly education and health systems, at a time when aid budgets are under growing pressure.

For more information, read Save the Children’s full 2026 report, Stop the War on Children 2026. Available at: https://resourcecentre.savethechildren.net/document/stop-the-war-on-children-changing-the-odds-2026

For a policy brief describing our update of the annual mapping of children affected by armed conflict, read our PRIO Conflict Trends Policy Brief 0X/2026: ‘Children Affected by Armed Conflict, 1990–2025’

items.title: World: Estado de la Población Mundial 2026: Generaciones venideras - Empoderar a la juventud para que trace su propio futuro
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: United Nations Population Fund

Please refer to the attached file.

PRÓLOGO

Desde que se aprobó la Carta de las Naciones Unidas en 1945, el mundo se comprometió a "preservar a las generaciones venideras del flagelo de la guerra". Ha llegado el momento de que esta promesa vaya aún más lejos: las generaciones venideras también han de tener la oportunidad, la libertad y el poder de moldear el mundo que heredarán.

Este informe nos da motivos tanto para actuar con urgencia como para mantener la esperanza. Las personas jóvenes de hoy en día están mejor formadas y conectadas que cualquier otra generación anterior: innovan, emprenden, lideran movimientos comunitarios y actúan como agentes de cambio. Sin embargo, hay un porcentaje desproporcionado de jóvenes que, a pesar de su enorme potencial, se enfrenta a un horizonte de oportunidades cada vez más reducido.

El costo de la vida está aumentando; cada vez es más difícil encontrar un trabajo seguro y una vivienda asequible; los conflictos, el cambio climático y la desigualdad están transformando las vidas y las expectativas; los avances en materia de salud sexual y reproductiva no pueden darse por sentados; y son demasiadas las personas jóvenes que se ven excluidas de los espacios donde se toman las decisiones sobre su futuro.

Estas condiciones tienen repercusiones que van mucho más allá de las políticas de juventud, ya que influyen en algunas de las decisiones más trascendentales de la vida de las personas, por ejemplo, si pueden o no independizarse, encontrar un trabajo digno, formar una relación, tener hijos si lo desean y cuando lo deseen, y construir la vida que imaginan para sí mismas. El futuro demográfico dependerá, en última instancia, de millones de decisiones individuales de este tipo, así como de que las personas cuenten con los medios y las oportunidades necesarios para tomarlas libremente.

Apoyándose en las opiniones de más de 100.000 jóvenes, este informe pone de relieve que las generaciones actuales son perfectamente conscientes de las dificultades a las que se enfrentan, pero no tienen la menor intención de tirar la toalla. La juventud considera que los sistemas actuales pueden cambiar. Quiere sociedades más inclusivas y que rindan cuentas; economías que generen oportunidades reales; comunidades libres de violencia basada en género y discriminación; e instituciones en las que la participación permita influir realmente en las decisiones.
Lo más importante es que no están pidiendo a otras personas que construyan ese futuro por ellas; ya lo están construyendo por sí mismas.

He sido testigo de lo que personas jóvenes de todo el planeta son capaces de lograr cuando disponen del espacio, los recursos y el poder necesarios para llevar a la práctica sus ideas, y, a lo largo de estas páginas, podrán conocer la historia de algunas de ellas.

La juventud nos ha dejado claro, una y otra vez, qué es lo que le importa; la pregunta es cómo responderemos a lo que nos ha transmitido.

Nuestra responsabilidad es garantizar que sus aspiraciones se conviertan en opciones reales.
Esto implica invertir en salud, educación y oportunidades económicas para las personas jóvenes; implica proteger su capacidad de tomar decisiones sobre sus propios cuerpos y vidas; e implica hacer algo más que invitarlas a participar en el diálogo: debemos compartir con ellas la responsabilidad de la toma de decisiones.

El futuro no es algo dado, sino aquello que las generaciones construyen juntas.

Este informe lanza una invitación —y un desafío— para que empecemos a construirlo desde ya.

Diene Keita
Directora Ejecutiva
Fondo de Población de las Naciones Unidas

items.title: World: Ending violence against children: From commitment to reality
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: UN Children's Fund

Please refer to the attached file.

Violence against children remains one of the most widespread violations of children’s rights worldwide. Despite global commitments to end all forms of violence against children, millions of children continue to experience violence across regions and income levels, revealing the persistent gap between commitment and reality.

This brief presents the latest available global estimates on violent discipline by caregivers in the home and sexual violence in childhood, drawing on evidence from both development and humanitarian contexts. The brief illustrates why accelerating progress towards SDG Target 16.2 remains an urgent priority and highlights the essential role of both universal and targeted prevention efforts and a strong, accessible social service workforce equipped with a package of evidence-based family support and child protection services.

Accelerating progress will require renewed political commitment, sustained investment, stronger child protection systems capable of delivering evidence-based services at scale in cooperation with allied services such as health, education, and justice, and the large-scale implementation of proven universal and targeted prevention interventions.

items.title: World: A record high of nearly one in four children now live in conflict zones - Save the Children report
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: Save the Children

· Nearly one in four children worldwide live in conflict zones, new report finds

· Africa now accounts for 44% of children living near conflict worldwide, with an unprecedented two in five African children impacted

· Verified incidents of denial of humanitarian access against children have increased almost 16-fold in a decade to almost one an hour

AMMAN, 19 November 2026 – Almost one in four children worldwide are now living in conflict zones, the highest number since records began in 1990, according to a new Save the Children report.

The figure represents an increase of more than 50% in a decade, jumping from 378 million in 2015 to 589 million in 2025, according to the report Stop the War on Children: Changing the Odds, which draws on data from the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO).

The report found that the share of the world’s children living in conflict zones more than doubled from about 10% in the mid-1990s to 23.4% in 2025.

Africa is home to the highest number of children living in conflict zones, accounting for about 260 million, or 44% of the global total. This is nearly a 20% increase from the 218 million children in Africa who lived in conflict zones in 2024.

Across Africa, the proportion of children living in conflict zones more than tripled from about one in eight children in 2010 to about two in five in 2025, the highest level ever recorded for the continent. This puts Africa on par with the Middle East, where both regions now have two in five children living in conflict zones.

Elsewhere, about one in four children (24.2%) in the Americas lived in conflict zones in 2025, one in seven (14.3%) in Asia, and nearly one in nine (10.6%) in Europe.

The report also examined United Nations verified grave violations against children in armed conflict between 2005 and 2025, including killing and maiming, recruitment by armed forces or groups, sexual violence, abduction, attacks on schools and hospitals, and denial of humanitarian access. These numbers represent the tip of the iceberg for grave violations against children, as most attacks on children go unverified, said Save the Children.

Killing and maiming accounted for the largest share of violations against children over the past two decades, with 171,712 cases verified since 2005. More than 70% of the cases were committed against children in five countries: the occupied Palestinian territory, Afghanistan, Somalia, Syria and Yemen.

The report also found that the fastest-growing grave violation against children is the denial of humanitarian aid, with verified incidents skyrocketing from 509 in 2015 to 8,322 in 2025, more than a 16-fold increase in a decade. This amounts to almost one verified incident of denial of humanitarian aid every hour, on average, in 2025. More than 70% of all verified aid denial last year took place against Palestinian children.

Denial of humanitarian access rose from just over 2% of all verified grave violations in 2015 to more than 21% in 2025, making it the second most frequently verified violation after killing and maiming.

Rape and other forms of sexual violence against children are widely underreported. Even so, the report found that 28,909 cases have been verified since reporting began. The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) accounts for 12,698, or almost 44% of the total, followed by Somalia with 4,534 and Chad with 2,979. Together, the three countries account for around 70% of all verified cases.

In eastern DRC, 17-year-old Ana* experienced the devastating consequences of conflict after violence forced her family from their home. After months of displacement, they returned, only for armed men to break into their house, shoot Ana’s brother dead and rape her while other family members were assaulted.

“We had fled the war, but it came knocking at our door again. [When the attackers came to our home] I screamed; I begged for mercy… but no one listened. My brother was killed before my eyes. I was raped,” Ana said. “[Afterwards] the hardest part wasn’t the pain. It was people’s mockery. They pointed fingers at me, as if I were to blame for what had been done to me.”

The next morning, neighbours helped Ana reach a local health centre supported by Save the Children, where she received emergency medical care, including treatment to prevent pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections, as well as ongoing psychosocial support.

Gudrun Østby, Research Professor at PRIO, said: “We estimate that 589 million children were living close to armed conflict last year. These record-high figures are a stark reminder that conflict is devastating the daily lives, education, health and future prospects of hundreds of millions of children. Unless greater efforts are made to protect children in conflict settings, the consequences of today's wars will be felt for decades to come.”

Inger Ashing, CEO of Save the Children International, said:

“Almost one in four children around the world now lives in a conflict zone. What could be more important than their protection? The scale of this crisis is rapidly growing, and the systems meant to protect children are being pushed to breaking point.

“We're seeing aid weaponised, attacked and deliberately disrupted. Humanitarian organisations are denied access, funding is being slashed, and needs are outpacing our ability to reach every child in crisis. Meanwhile, parties to conflict continue to disregard the rules of war, while new military technologies are changing how wars are fought, increasing the risk further for children in conflict settings.

“Children’s rights and needs must be at the centre of decisions about war, peace and security. More than 20 years of monitoring violations have made the horrors children face visible and created opportunities to prevent further harm. This work must be protected, supported and translated into action.

"Parties to conflict must uphold the rules of war, and those responsible for violations must be held to account. But ensuring the protection of children isn’t only the responsibility of those fighting. States, donors and companies with leverage over perpetrators must use it, through diplomatic and political pressure. To truly change the odds for children living in conflict zones, we must put their protection first and work towards the peace they deserve.”

Save the Children is calling on parties to the conflict to uphold international humanitarian law, accounting for children’ distinct vulnerabilities, and to facilitate safe and unimpeded humanitarian relief to civilians. It is also urging governments to strengthen accountability for violations against children, implement international treaties and declarations that protect children and education in war zones, address the root causes of conflict and ensure children’s voices are heard in decisions affecting their futures.

In 2025, Save the Children worked in 107 countries, reaching more than 58.2 million people, including 37.8 million children. The child rights organisation also responded to 113 humanitarian crises in 63 countries, supporting over 24 million people, including 13.6 million children.

ENDS

Notes to Editor:

Read the full report here: https://resourcecentre.savethechildren.net/document/stop-the-war-on-children-changing-the-odds-2026

· The updated analysis on the number and share of children living in conflict zones is conducted by the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO). The core dataset used to map conflict patterns in this report is the Uppsala Conflict Data Program’s Georeferenced Event Data Set (UCDP GED) until 2025. To estimate the number of children living in conflict areas, and populations more generally, PRIO integrated the UCDP conflict data with population data from CIESIN’s Gridded Population of the World (GPW) and from the UN World Population Prospects. PRIO uses UCDP’s definition of armed conflict: ‘armed force used by an organized actor against another organized actor, or against civilians, resulting in at least 25 battle-related deaths in one calendar year’. A ‘conflict zone’ is defined as an area within 50km of where one or more conflict incidents take place in a given year, within the borders of a country.

· The UN Security Council has identified six grave violations against children in situations of armed conflict: killing and maiming of children; recruitment or use of children by armed forces and groups; sexual violence against children; abduction of children; attacks against schools and hospitals; and denial of humanitarian access for children. These grave violations were defined on the basis of their egregious nature and their severe impact on children’s wellbeing.

· Stop the War on Children

items.blurb:

Source: Famine Early Warning System Network
