Africa Weather Hazards

Erratic rainfall has led to dryness in eastern Horn of Africa; high flood risks remain in many areas of Eastern Africa and Southern Africa.

1) Inundation persists in the Sudd Wetlands of South Sudan.

2) A large part of western Eastern Africa faces dryness due to persisting, below-average rainfall over the past 90 days. Southern and southeastern South Sudan and northern Uganda have already experienced deteriorated vegetation conditions, which have resulted in droughts in the region.

3) Flooding is likely to continue in Gemena of northwestern DRC, parts of Gabon, Congo, western DRC, along the Juba River in southern Somalia, the KwaZulu-Natal of eastern South Africa, and Eswatini as additional rainfall is forecast in each region during the next week.

4) High flooding risks also exist in southern Ethiopia, southern Kenya, northern and western Tanzania, westcentral Angola, north-central Mozambique, and central Madagascar due to the forecast, additional rainfall during the next week.

5) Southeastern Ethiopia and central Somalia face dryness due to poor rainfall over the past four weeks.

6) Hot conditions are predicted over parts of far western West Africa, Eastern Africa, and a wide area in central and eastern Southern Africa.

items.title: Belize: Los países del MIRPS reafirman su compromiso con el fortalecimiento de los sistemas de protección, la promoción de soluciones duraderas y la generación de oportunidades de inclusión para personas con necesidades de protección
items.blurb:
Countries: Belize, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Panama
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

SAN SALVADOR – Los siete países que integran el Marco Integral Regional para la Protección y Soluciones (MIRPS) –Belice, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, México y Panamá– concluyeron hoy la IX Reunión Anual del MIRPS con la adopción de la Declaración de San Salvador II, mediante la cual renovaron sus compromisos para fortalecer los sistemas nacionales de protección, ampliar las oportunidades de inclusión socioeconómica y avanzar en soluciones duraderas para personas con necesidades de protección y las comunidades que las acogen.

Durante el encuentro, celebrado bajo el liderazgo del Gobierno de El Salvador en su calidad de Presidencia Pro-Témpore 2026, autoridades de los países MIRPS, representantes de la Plataforma de Apoyo y socios estratégicos realizaron un balance de los avances alcanzados durante 2026 y examinaron las oportunidades y las prioridades que orientarán la cooperación regional en 2027. El diálogo destacó los resultados y buenas prácticas en materia de asilo, protección a nivel territorial, gobernabilidad local y medios de vida.

La Reunión Anual culminó con la adopción de la Declaración de San Salvador II, en la que los Estados acordaron promover procedimientos de asilo más accesibles, eficientes y de calidad, ampliar el acceso a empleo, educación y medios de vida, e incorporar enfoques de protección en las políticas de gestión del riesgo de desastres y adaptación al cambio climático.

Los países también destacaron la importancia de profundizar la cooperación con otros mecanismos regionales y fortalecer las alianzas con gobiernos locales, sociedad civil, organizaciones lideradas por personas refugiadas, academia, sector privado y actores del desarrollo, con el propósito de ampliar el alcance y la sostenibilidad de las respuestas. Asimismo, reconocieron el valor del MIRPS como una plataforma regional que permite promover respuestas coordinadas en beneficio de las personas con necesidades de protección y las comunidades de acogida.

La Organización de los Estados Americanos (OEA), que integra junto con ACNUR la Secretaría Técnica del MIRPS, destacó los avances del Fondo MIRPS, cuyos proyectos han beneficiado a más de 33.000 personas en la región, y agradeció las contribuciones de España, la República de Corea y Portugal. “El desplazamiento sigue afectando a personas y familias en todo nuestro hemisferio. Atender sus necesidades va más allá de brindar protección inmediata y requiere instituciones sólidas, políticas inclusivas y una cooperación regional que abra caminos hacia la estabilidad y las oportunidades. Estos principios guían la Agenda de Paz y Prosperidad para las Américas de la OEA. En nuestro trabajo con las personas desplazadas, esto significa acceso a la protección, la documentación, la educación y el empleo, así como oportunidades para desarrollar su autonomía y vivir con dignidad”, afirmó Albert R. Ramdin, Secretario General de la OEA, al destacar el compromiso de la Organización con la protección y la inclusión de las personas con necesidades de protección.

En el marco del 75.º aniversario de la Convención sobre el Estatuto de los Refugiados de 1951, ACNUR destacó la importancia de mantener el compromiso regional con la protección internacional. “La adopción de la Declaración de San Salvador II demuestra que los países de la región siguen apostando por la cooperación, la solidaridad y la responsabilidad compartida para responder al desplazamiento. A través del MIRPS, los Estados continúan transformando sus compromisos en acciones concretas para las personas refugiadas, desplazadas y las comunidades que las acogen", afirmó Isabel Márquez, Directora Regional de ACNUR para las Américas.

Los miembros de la Plataforma de Apoyo al MIRPS reafirmaron su compromiso de continuar acompañando los esfuerzos de los países mediante la cooperación técnica, la movilización de recursos y el fortalecimiento de alianzas estratégicas para apoyar la implementación de las prioridades nacionales y regionales, ampliar las oportunidades de protección y soluciones duraderas, y contribuir a la sostenibilidad de los esfuerzos impulsados por los Estados que integran este Mecanismo.

Al cierre de la IX Reunión Anual, El Salvador traspasó la Presidencia Pro-Témpore del MIRPS a Guatemala, que liderará el mecanismo durante 2027, en un año particularmente significativo en el que el MIRPS conmemorará su décimo aniversario.

A una década de la adopción de la Declaración de San Pedro Sula, este Mecanismo continúa consolidándose como una plataforma regional de cooperación, innovación y responsabilidad compartida que permite a los Estados avanzar conjuntamente en la protección, la inclusión y las soluciones para las personas refugiadas, desplazadas y otras personas con necesidades de protección internacional.

El Marco Integral Regional para la Protección y Soluciones (MIRPS) está integrado por Belice, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, México y Panamá. Es un mecanismo regional para la aplicación del Pacto Mundial sobre los Refugiados que promueve la cooperación y la responsabilidad compartida en materia de prevención, protección y soluciones duraderas frente al desplazamiento. La Plataforma de Apoyo al MIRPS, creada en 2019, contribuye a movilizar recursos y cooperación internacional. ACNUR y la OEA, a través de su Departamento de Acceso a Derechos (DAR), integran la Secretaría Técnica del MIRPS y su Plataforma de Apoyo.

items.title: Bangladesh: Estudios de ACNUR y la Universidad de Oxford advierten que el recorte de fondos aumenta el riesgo de que los refugiados sean víctimas de trata y explotación infantil
items.blurb:
Countries: Bangladesh, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Myanmar, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan
Sources: UN High Commissioner for Refugees, University of Oxford

GINEBRA/OXFORD – Los recortes cada vez más profundos en la financiación están aumentando el riesgo de que las personas refugiadas – especialmente las niñas y los niños – sean víctimas de trata, explotación o abuso, a medida que se van debilitando los sistemas de protección que garantizan su seguridad, de acuerdo con dos nuevos estudios presentados hoy por ACNUR, la Agencia de la ONU para los Refugiados, y el Nuffield College de la Universidad de Oxford.

Los informes se centran en dos importantes países que acogen refugiados, Bangladés y Etiopía, cada uno de los cuales acoge a más de un millón de personas refugiadas y solicitantes de asilo. En ambos casos, los estudios han encontrado pruebas de que, cuando se recortan simultáneamente los servicios de protección y la asistencia esencial – como el alojamiento y la educación –, se debilitan las salvaguardias fundamentales y la población refugiada, que ya se encuentra en situación de vulnerabilidad, se enfrenta a riesgos cada vez mayores de explotación, trabajo peligroso y trata.

“Estos estudios destacan una realidad crítica y a menudo pasada por alto: los servicios de protección, como la asistencia jurídica, los espacios seguros, el apoyo psicosocial, la prevención de la violencia de género y la protección de las niñas y los niños, se encuentran entre las salvaguardias más sólidas contra la trata y la explotación”, afirmó Elizabeth Tan, Directora de Protección Internacional y Soluciones de ACNUR. “Cuando se recortan, las vulnerabilidades se agravan y a los traficantes les resulta más fácil aprovecharse de personas que ya se encuentran en situación de riesgo. Invertir en protección ahora previene la explotación futura”.

En Bangladés, los casos de trata detectados en el mayor asentamiento de refugiados del mundo, cerca de Cox’s Bazar, aumentaron un 28 por ciento entre 2024 y 2025. Las niñas y los niños representaron el 17 por ciento de las víctimas detectadas en 2025, frente al 14 por ciento en 2024. Entre enero y septiembre de 2026, se identificaron 411 víctimas de la trata, de las cuales casi el 23 por ciento eran niñas y niños, lo que subraya los crecientes riesgos en materia de protección a los que se enfrentan las personas refugiadas rohingyas.

Estos riesgos se agravan a medida que los recursos humanitarios se reducen mientras que las necesidades aumentan. Entre 2024 y 2025, la población refugiada rohingya en Bangladés aumentó en torno al 17 por ciento, lo que supone más de 170.000 refugiados, mientras que el presupuesto operativo de ACNUR se redujo en más del 8 por ciento en 2025 y se enfrentó a un déficit de financiación del 59 por ciento en comparación con las necesidades totales. Alrededor del 88 por ciento de los hogares rohingyas informaron de un deterioro del estado de sus alojamientos, y a casi ninguno de los refugiados recién llegados se le pudo asignar un alojamiento propio. La disponibilidad de agua potable descendió de 33 litros por persona y día en 2024 a 23 litros en 2025, situación agravada en parte por la prolongada sequía en la zona, con un promedio de 21 personas compartiendo cada letrina.

Debido a las restricciones de la libertad de movimiento y de empleo, las personas refugiadas rohingyas – la gran mayoría de las cuales son además apátridas – siguen dependiendo en gran medida de la asistencia humanitaria, y el 35 por ciento de los hogares dependía por completo de la ayuda en 2025. A medida que la asistencia y los servicios esenciales se ven sometidos a una gran presión y los recortes de financiación afectan a todos los actores humanitarios sobre el terreno, las personas refugiadas se ven expuestas a mayores riesgos de trata, trabajo forzado, matrimonio forzado, trabajo infantil y peligrosos viajes marítimos en busca de protección y dignidad.

En Etiopía, los recortes presupuestarios han reducido significativamente los servicios de protección para las niñas y los niños refugiados, que representan el 52 por ciento de la población refugiada del país – procedentes principalmente de Sudán del Sur, Somalia, Eritrea y Sudán –, entre los que se incluyen al menos 31.000 menores no acompañados y separados de sus familias. En 2025, la operación de ACNUR en Etiopía contó con menos de un tercio de la financiación prevista, mientras que solo se cubrió el 18 por ciento de las necesidades previstas en materia de protección infantil durante el año.

Los recortes presupuestarios están debilitando la red de agentes de protección, las estructuras comunitarias y las vías de derivación que contribuyen a que los niños refugiados sigan siendo visibles y estén a salvo. Seis socios de protección de ACNUR en Etiopía se vieron obligados a reducir su plantilla en casi la mitad. Entre 2024 y 2025, el apoyo de ACNUR a la localización de familiares y a la reunificación familiar de los niños en Etiopía separados de sus padres y cuidadores se redujo en más de la mitad, pasando de 4.071 a 1.887 niños atendidos. Tanto la atención alternativa para menores no acompañados como los programas de fortalecimiento familiar se redujeron en aproximadamente la mitad, y el número de niñas y niños refugiados sujetos a procedimientos de ‘interés superior’ – destinados a garantizar que las decisiones que les afectan den prioridad a su seguridad, bienestar y derechos – se redujo en un tercio. La falta de financiación también afectó a 57 escuelas primarias que atienden a alrededor de 110.000 niñas y niños refugiados, mientras que el apoyo psicosocial se redujo en un 29 por ciento.

En este sombrío contexto de financiación, observaciones recientes sobre el terreno apuntan a un preocupante aumento del trabajo infantil entre los refugiados, incluido el trabajo en la agricultura y el desplazamiento hacia zonas mineras informales. Junto con la reducción de los servicios, estas tendencias dejan a niñas y niños refugiados – ya de por sí vulnerables, especialmente a aquellos que huyeron solos, se vieron separados de sus familias o a las niñas refugiadas – más expuestos a la explotación, la violencia sexual, el matrimonio infantil y la trata con fines de trabajo forzado y explotación sexual, al tiempo que reducen las oportunidades de identificar y responder a los riesgos.

“Estos casos de estudio ilustran lo que se puede lograr cuando se establece un vínculo eficaz entre los ámbitos de la investigación, las políticas y la práctica. El Nuffield College se enorgullece de haber colaborado con ACNUR para crear algo que ninguna de las dos partes habría podido lograr por sí sola”, afirmó el profesor Andrew Thompson, del Nuffield College de la Universidad de Oxford. “Los resultados dan mucho que pensar y constituyen una severa advertencia a la comunidad internacional sobre lo que podría suceder si los servicios esenciales de prevención y protección para las personas refugiadas siguen sin contar con los recursos suficientes”.

Aunque ACNUR y sus socios siguen estableciendo prioridades, adaptándose e innovando bajo graves restricciones financieras, ambos estudios concluyen que una financiación sostenida, flexible y predecible sigue siendo esencial para garantizar la protección de los refugiados. Sin embargo, la situación sigue siendo grave en 2026: los programas globales de ACNUR para la protección de la niñez solo cuentan con un 25 por ciento de financiación, y las iniciativas para prevenir y responder a la violencia de género, con apenas un 24 por ciento hasta julio de 2026.

Los estudios refuerzan el llamado a la acción urgente y destacan que la inversión en la protección de las personas refugiadas y de la niñez, así como en el fortalecimiento de los sistemas nacionales, no solo es un imperativo humanitario y de protección, sino también una inversión rentable en prevención, resiliencia y soluciones.

Para más información sobre este tema, favor de contactar:

  • ACNUR: En Ginebra, Carlotta Wolf, wolf@unhcr.org, +41 79 546 6707
  • Universidad de Oxford: En Oxford, Professor Andrew Thompson, andrew.thompson@history.ox.ac.uk

items.title: Atrocity Alert No. 503: Israel and the Occupied Palestinian Territory, Ethiopia and Afghanistan
items.blurb:
Countries: occupied Palestinian territory, Afghanistan, Eritrea, Ethiopia
Source: Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect

Atrocity Alert is a weekly publication by the Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect highlighting situations where populations are at risk of, or are enduring, mass atrocity crimes.

WINTER FLOODING BEGINS IN GAZA AMID DEVASTATION WROUGHT BY ISRAEL

As Palestinians brace for the fourth winter since the start of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, living conditions across the enclave are becoming more dire amid the onset of seasonal flooding. The first major winter storm of the season, on 6 November, resulted in the flooding of over 700,000 tents housing displaced persons in a single day. Thousands of families were left without shelter, essential services were disrupted and in the days that followed several people were killed when a sand dune collapsed onto their tent.

Noting the continued constraints to distributing essential aid ahead of winter, UN Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher has called for immediate action to end the “collective punishment” and “predictable, preventable suffering” of Palestinians in Gaza. He stressed that humanitarians had sounded the alarm for months about the need for essential winter supplies, only to be told by foreign ministers and other partners to wait for progress following Israeli elections in October.

Israel’s conduct across the enclave places Palestinians in Gaza at particular risk during winter. Over 80 percent of all structures remain damaged or destroyed, while Israel continues to deny entry of major reconstruction materials, further undermining water and sanitation, healthcare facilities, energy supplies and housing. Of the approximately 1.7 million people who remain internally displaced, some 1.4 million are living in tents or makeshift shelters, with roughly 950,000 confined to flood-prone areas, according to the World Health Organization. More than a year after the so-called ceasefire took effect, Palestinians remain unable to rebuild critical, life-sustaining infrastructure and lack even adequate temporary shelter. Israel continues to obstruct the delivery of tents, with over 150,000 awaiting entry approval just outside Gaza.

The consequences of these conditions are already evident. An infant has died from severe hypothermia, acute respiratory infections have increased by 33,000 cases compared to the same period last year and hospitals in Gaza have reported a surge in meningitis cases among children. On 12 November a joint media stakeout at the UN, led by the United Kingdom, Qatar and Jordan and involving 53 countries and international organizations, called for urgent humanitarian access to Gaza as winter nears. Earlier in the day, an Israeli airstrike hit a hospital in Gaza, killing six people and injuring 27 others.

Israel must immediately open all border crossings for Gaza, allow unimpeded access for humanitarian aid and ensure humanitarian organizations can operate freely across the enclave. States must enact concrete measures to ensure Israel upholds its obligations under international law and its responsibilities as an occupying power toward Palestinians in Gaza, including by halting arms transfers to Israel, suspending trade agreements and imposing targeted sanctions on Israeli officials.

ETHIOPIA–ERITREA BORDER CLASHES HEIGHTEN RISKS OF FURTHER ATROCITIES

Reports of clashes between Ethiopian and Eritrean forces near the long-disputed border town of Badme have heightened fears of a wider regional conflict. Between 11 and 13 November the Ethiopian National Defense Forces and Eritrean Defense Forces reportedly exchanged fire, with Ethiopian drones and Eritrean heavy artillery deployed near the border.

Badme was at the center of the devastating 1998–2000 Ethiopia-Eritrea war, which ended with the signing of the Algiers Peace Agreement in December 2000. In 2002 the independent Eritrea-Ethiopia Boundary Commission awarded Badme to Eritrea. However, Ethiopia’s refusal to implement the ruling contributed to nearly two decades of hostility between the two countries. While engagement between Ethiopia and Eritrea improved significantly following a historic rapprochement in 2018 and the countries subsequently allied during the 2020–2022 war in Ethiopia’s Tigray region, relations have since deteriorated. Notably, over the past year, tensions have mounted as the two countries have publicly exchanged statements over Ethiopia’s aspirations to secure access to a port on the Red Sea. Diplomatic relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea broke down in September amid renewed fighting in Tigray.

Amid growing regional tensions, atrocity risks are also mounting within Ethiopia. In Oromia, at least 94 Orthodox Christians were reportedly killed in a series of attacks between 20 October and 5 November. The Ethiopian Human Rights Commission attributed a 24 October attack in Sirka district to the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), documenting civilian deaths and attacks on civilian infrastructure. The OLA has rejected this finding. Attacks targeting civilians on the basis of their ethnicity may constitute the crime against humanity of persecution if committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack against a civilian population.

Violence has also escalated around Moyale since October, where clashes involving forces and militias affiliated with the Oromia and Somali regional authorities have fueled longstanding disputes over administrative boundaries, territory and resources. The violence has displaced an estimated 50,000 people into neighboring Kenya, with women and children arriving in urgent need of food, shelter and medical assistance.

Ethiopia and Eritrea must cease hostilities, resume diplomatic dialogue and protect civilians. Ethiopian authorities must safeguard vulnerable communities, investigate attacks and pursue a peaceful resolution to the Oromia-Somali border dispute. The Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect’s Horn of Africa expert, Sarah Hunter, said, “Escalating tensions across Ethiopia and its borders threaten to engulf the Horn of Africa. Without urgent action to address these interconnected crises, civilians face a growing risk of further atrocities. The international community, including the UN and African Union, must prioritize diplomacy and accountability to ensure a durable peace.”

CLOSURE OF AFGHANISTAN ICC CASE LEAVES ACCOUNTABILITY GAPS

On 12 November the International Criminal Court (ICC) Pre-Trial Chamber II ordered the formal closure of the Situation in Afghanistan I case, finding that the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP) failed to “effectively carry out any further investigative or prosecutorial activities.” Authorized in 2020, the investigation covered alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed on Afghan territory from 1 May 2003 involving United States (US) military and intelligence actors, former Afghan government forces and the Taliban, as well as the so-called Islamic State in Iraq and the Levant-Khorasan. Alleged crimes included murder, torture, deliberate attacks against civilians and unlawful detention. On 13 November the OTP filed a notice of appeal and requested a stay of the closure decision.

The decision follows a series of procedural disputes over the scope and organization of the Afghanistan investigation. In 2026 the Chamber separated the proceedings into two situations: Afghanistan II, concerning alleged crimes committed by the Taliban since the 2021 takeover, and Afghanistan I, covering the remaining aspects of the original investigation. Closing Afghanistan I consequently leaves a significant accountability gap for atrocity crimes committed by a range of actors across more than two decades of conflict.

The closure comes amid a drastic escalation in US pressure on the Court. On 9 October the US imposed institution-wide sanctions on the ICC, marking a drastic escalation in its campaign against the Court and threatening its ability to pursue accountability for the world’s gravest crimes. The US has repeatedly sought to obstruct the Court’s work, including to prevent potential prosecutions of US nationals. While the sanctions and the closure decision are distinct developments, the decision risks further narrowing the Court’s pursuit of accountability for alleged crimes involving US personnel.

While the ICC unsealed on 5 October four arrest warrants in the Afghanistan II situation against senior Taliban officials for the alleged crime against humanity of gender persecution, the closure of Afghanistan I underscores the importance of other initiatives to contribute to accountability, most notably the UN Human Rights Council-mandated Independent Investigative Mechanism for Afghanistan (IIM-A). The IIM-A is the only international investigative body mandated to collect, preserve and analyze evidence of serious violations and abuses perpetrated by all parties in Afghanistan, which may support future accountability efforts. The IIM-A’s mandate is not time-limited, meaning it can assess past, ongoing and future crimes.

The international community must ensure that the closure of one accountability pathway does not end efforts to secure justice for victims and survivors. State parties to the Rome Statute should stand firmly with the victims of atrocity crimes and support the OTP’s appeal and request for a stay of the closure decision pending the Appeals Chamber’s determination. UN member states must ensure the IIM-A is fully operationalized without delay and provided with the political, financial and technical support its mandate demands.

items.title: Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak: Democratic Republic of the Congo | Kenya | Nigeria Weekly External Situation Report 27, Data as of 15 November 2026
items.blurb:
Countries: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya, Nigeria
Source: World Health Organization

Please refer to the attached file.

Event description

The Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continues at a high and sustained level of transmission. During epidemiological week 46 (9 – 15 November 2026), 442 confirmed cases and 239 confirmed deaths were reported, compared with 458 cases and 228 deaths in week 45; the national seven-day average has remained between 62 and 65 cases per day, and a new health zone, Watsa in Haut-Uélé, reported its first confirmed cases. Over three epidemiological weeks (weeks 44 – 46 compared with weeks 41 – 43), reported cases decreased by 6.7% and deaths by 4.6%, with a decline in Ituri partly offset by continued intense transmission in Nord-Kivu, where Beni remains the health zone with the most cases, and by rising incidence in Mangala, Mambasa and Mutwanga. Deaths in treatment centres increased in week 46 and the proportion of deaths occurring in the community fell to 59% (142 of 239), its lowest weekly level since August. In Kenya, the last patient was discharged on 11 November, and all contacts have completed their follow-up; the 42-day countdown is under way, and the event has not yet been declared over. In Nigeria, all 62 contacts completed their 21-day follow-up on 13 November and no secondary case was identified; surveillance continues in both countries. Additionally, Nigeria started the 42 days countdown on 27 Oct after the case was medically evacuated to Switzerland on the 26 October 2026.

In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, insecurity in Beni, Mabalako and Bafwasende, strikes over unpaid salaries in several provinces and community resistance to safe burials continue to constrain surveillance and response operations.

items.title: Venezuela: Nuevas rutas migratorias cobran fuerza en América del Sur mientras los cruces por el Darién caen un 90 %, según la OIM
items.blurb:
Countries: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of), Brazil, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Haiti, Honduras, Panama, Uruguay, World
Source: International Organization for Migration

Ciudad de Panamá, 18 de noviembre de 2026 – La migración en América Latina y el Caribe está experimentando una transformación marcada por la consolidación de nuevas rutas migratorias en América del Sur y una disminución del 90 % en los cruces hacia el norte a través del Darién, en Panamá, en comparación con el primer semestre de 2025, según un nuevo informe de la Organización Internacional para las Migraciones (OIM).

«La marcada disminución de los cruces por el Darién es solo una parte de la realidad. La migración no se ha detenido. Las personas están encontrando nuevas rutas, desplazándose en distintas direcciones y tomando decisiones difíciles sobre dónde construir su futuro», afirmó Juan Francisco Espinosa, Director Regional de la OIM para las Américas. «Debemos adaptarnos a estos cambios para garantizar que se protejan los derechos de las personas migrantes durante sus desplazamientos».

Por primera vez, la OIM identifica la ruta del este de América del Sur como un corredor migratorio plenamente consolidado, que se extiende desde el Caribe, a través del norte de América del Sur, hasta el Brasil y el Cono Sur. Mientras disminuye el número de personas que se desplazan hacia el norte por Centroamérica, otras viajan hacia el sur, retornan a sus países de origen o se establecen en países como Brasil y Uruguay. La disminución de los movimientos tradicionales hacia el norte no significa necesariamente que haya menos personas en movimiento, sino que los patrones migratorios en la región están cambiando.

Durante los primeros cuatro meses de 2026, aproximadamente 3.000 personas cubanas ingresaron al Brasil cada mes, mientras que, en el Uruguay, se registró un saldo migratorio positivo de 5.946 personas cubanas entre enero y mayo. En conjunto, estas tendencias sugieren que América del Sur se está convirtiendo en un destino cada vez más importante para las personas migrantes, en lugar de ser únicamente una región de tránsito. La respuesta de los países, incluido el acceso a una situación migratoria regular y al empleo, determinará en gran medida las oportunidades de estas personas para contribuir a las comunidades de acogida.

La ruta recientemente identificada se suma a la ruta centroamericana y la ruta andina como uno de los tres principales corredores migratorios que configuran los movimientos en América Latina y el Caribe. Las tres rutas están experimentando cambios significativos, con personas migrantes que se desplazan cada vez más en distintas direcciones, permanecen temporalmente en otros países o deciden establecerse en nuevos destinos.

También está aumentando el número de personas migrantes que regresan a sus países de origen, aunque estas dinámicas distan de ser sencillas. Entre las personas venezolanas que viajaban hacia el sur por Guatemala, el 74 % indicó que tenía intención de retornar a la República Bolivariana de Venezuela. Otras tenían previsto continuar hacia Honduras, Colombia o Costa Rica.

A lo largo de la ruta andina, los movimientos registrados en el Ecuador se distribuyeron de forma relativamente equilibrada: el 55 % se dirigía hacia el norte y el 45 % hacia el sur. Esto refleja patrones migratorios cada vez más complejos, en los que las personas se desplazan entre países, regresan a destinos anteriores o continúan sus trayectos hacia otros lugares.

Mientras tanto, la disminución de los movimientos por las rutas tradicionales hacia el norte se extiende más allá de Panamá. Los movimientos hacia el norte por Honduras disminuyeron un 75 % en comparación con el primer semestre de 2025, lo que refuerza la evidencia de un cambio significativo en los patrones migratorios de Centroamérica.

«Estos cambios reflejan la evolución de los entornos normativos, las modificaciones en el acceso a vías migratorias regulares y las presiones económicas en toda la región», añadió Espinosa. «Las personas migrantes están tomando nuevas rutas, retornando a sus hogares o buscando oportunidades en otros lugares. Algunas quedan varadas durante el trayecto. Ante la evolución de los movimientos migratorios tanto regulares como irregulares, debemos trabajar con los gobiernos para ampliar las vías migratorias seguras y regulares y reducir los riesgos a los que se enfrentan las personas».

El informe destaca la importancia de dar seguimiento a estos cambios a medida que se producen. A través de su Matriz de Seguimiento de los Desplazamientos (DTM, por sus siglas en inglés), la OIM recopila y analiza datos sobre los movimientos migratorios, lo que permite a los gobiernos y a los socios humanitarios comprender mejor las rutas emergentes, identificar las necesidades de las personas y planificar respuestas adecuadas.

Esta información fundamentada en datos permite a los gobiernos gestionar los cambios en los movimientos migratorios de manera ordenada y previsible, al tiempo que brinda apoyo tanto a las personas migrantes como a las comunidades de acogida.

El informe completo, Tendencias Regionales de Movilidad: América Latina y el Caribe (enero-junio de 2026), está disponible en línea.

Para obtener más información, visite el Centro de Medios de la OIM.

items.title: Venezuela: New South American Migration Routes Gain Ground as Darién Crossings Plunge 90%, IOM Reports
items.blurb:
Countries: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of), Brazil, Colombia, Costa Rica, Cuba, Ecuador, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, Panama, Uruguay, World
Source: International Organization for Migration

Panama City, 18 November 2026 – Migration across Latin America and the Caribbean is being reshaped by the consolidation of new South American migration routes and a 90 per cent decline in northbound crossings through Panama’s Darién compared to the first half of 2025, according to a new report from the International Organization for Migration (IOM).

“The sharp drop in crossings through the Darién tells only part of the story. Migration hasn’t stopped. People are finding new routes, heading in different directions and making difficult decisions about where they can build a future,” said Juan Francisco Espinosa, IOM Regional Director for the Americas. “We need to keep pace with these changes so that when people move, their rights are protected.”

For the first time, IOM identifies the Eastern South American Route as a fully established migration corridor, stretching from the Caribbean through northern South America to Brazil and the Southern Cone. As fewer people travel north through Central America, others are moving south, returning to their countries of origin or settling in countries such as Brazil and Uruguay. The decline in traditional northbound movements does not necessarily mean fewer people are on the move, but rather that migration patterns across the region are changing.

Around 3,000 Cuban nationals entered Brazil each month during the first four months of 2026, while in Uruguay, Cuban arrivals outnumbered departures by nearly 6,000 between January and May. Together, these trends suggest that South America is becoming an increasingly important destination for migrants, rather than simply a region of transit. How countries respond, including through access to regular status and work, will shape what these migrants are able to contribute to the communities receiving them.

The newly identified route joins the Central American and Andean routes as one of three major migration corridors shaping movement across Latin America and the Caribbean. All three are undergoing significant changes, with migrants increasingly travelling in different directions, making temporary stops or choosing to settle in new destinations.

More migrants are also heading back towards their countries of origin, although the picture is far from straightforward. Among migrants travelling south through Guatemala, most of whom were Venezuelan, 74 per cent said they intended to return to Venezuela. Others planned to continue towards Honduras, Colombia or Costa Rica.

Along the Andean Route, movements recorded through Ecuador were almost evenly divided, with 55 per cent heading north and 45 per cent south. This reflects increasingly complex migration patterns, with people moving between countries, returning to previous destinations or continuing their journeys elsewhere.

Meanwhile, the decline in traditional northbound routes extends beyond Panama. Northbound movements through Honduras fell by 75 per cent compared to the first half of 2025, reinforcing evidence of a major shift in migration patterns across Central America.

“These changes reflect shifting policy conditions, changing access to regular migration pathways and economic pressures across the region,” Espinosa added. “Migrants are taking new routes, returning home or seeking opportunities elsewhere. Some find themselves stranded along the way. With both regular and irregular movements evolving, we must work with governments to expand safe, regular pathways and reduce the risks people face.”

The report highlights the importance of tracking these changes as they unfold. Through its Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), IOM collects and analyses data on migration movements, helping governments and humanitarian partners better understand emerging routes, identify people’s needs and plan responses. This evidence is what allows governments to manage changing movements in an orderly and predictable way, while supporting both migrants and the communities receiving them.

The full report, Latin America and the Caribbean: Regional Mobility Trends, January–June 2026, is available online.

For more information, please visit IOM’s Media Centre.

items.title: Venezuela: De nouvelles routes migratoires se consolident en Amérique du Sud alors que les traversées du Darién diminuent de 90 %, selon l’OIM
items.blurb:
Countries: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of), Brazil, Colombia, Costa Rica, Cuba, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, Panama, Uruguay, World
Source: International Organization for Migration

Panama City, 18 novembre 2026 – Les dynamiques migratoires en Amérique latine et dans les Caraïbes connaissent une profonde évolution, marquée par la consolidation de nouvelles routes migratoires en Amérique du Sud et une baisse de 90 % des traversées vers le nord à travers le Darién panaméen par rapport au premier semestre 2025, selon un nouveau rapport de l’Organisation internationale pour les migrations (OIM).

« La forte baisse des traversées du Darién ne reflète qu’une partie de la réalité. La migration ne s’est pas arrêtée. Les migrants empruntent de nouvelles routes, se dirigent vers d’autres destinations et doivent prendre des décisions difficiles quant au lieu où ils peuvent construire leur avenir », a déclaré Juan Francisco Espinosa, Directeur régional de l’OIM pour les Amériques. « Nous devons nous adapter à ces changements afin que les droits des personnes en déplacement soient protégés. »

Pour la première fois, l’OIM identifie la route migratoire de l’est de l’Amérique du Sud comme un couloir migratoire désormais bien établi, qui s’étend des Caraïbes au Cône Sud, en passant par le nord de l’Amérique du Sud et le Brésil. Alors que moins de personnes se dirigent vers le nord à travers l’Amérique centrale, d’autres prennent la direction du sud, retournent dans leur pays d’origine ou s’établissent dans des pays tels que le Brésil et l’Uruguay. Le recul des mouvements traditionnels vers le nord ne signifie pas nécessairement que moins de personnes sont en déplacement, mais plutôt que les dynamiques migratoires évoluent à l’échelle de la région.

Environ 3 000 ressortissants cubains sont entrés au Brésil chaque mois au cours des quatre premiers mois de 2026, tandis qu’en Uruguay, les arrivées de ressortissants cubains ont dépassé les départs d’environ 6 000 personnes entre janvier et mai. Ensemble, ces tendances suggèrent que l’Amérique du Sud devient une destination de plus en plus importante pour les migrants, et non plus simplement une région de transit. La manière dont les pays réagissent, notamment en facilitant l’accès à un statut migratoire régulier et à l’emploi, déterminera dans quelle mesure ces migrants pourront contribuer aux communautés qui les accueillent.

La route nouvellement identifiée vient s’ajouter aux routes centraméricaine et andine pour former trois grands couloirs migratoires qui structurent les mouvements en Amérique latine et dans les Caraïbes. Ces trois couloirs connaissent des évolutions significatives, les migrants empruntant des directions de plus en plus variées, effectuant des arrêts temporaires ou choisissant de s’établir dans de nouvelles destinations.

De plus en plus de migrants se dirigent également vers leur pays d’origine, même si la situation reste complexe. Parmi les migrants se déplaçant vers le sud à travers le Guatemala, dont la grande majorité était vénézuélienne, 74 % ont indiqué avoir l’intention de retourner au Venezuela. D’autres prévoyaient de poursuivre leur route vers le Honduras, la Colombie ou le Costa Rica.

Sur la route andine, les mouvements migratoires enregistrés en Équateur se répartissaient presque équitablement, avec 55 % des personnes se dirigeant vers le nord et 45 % vers le sud. Cette répartition témoigne de dynamiques migratoires de plus en plus complexes, caractérisées par des déplacements entre plusieurs pays, des retours vers des destinations antérieures ou la poursuite des parcours migratoires vers d’autres destinations.

Par ailleurs, le recul des mouvements migratoires traditionnels vers le nord ne se limite pas au Panama. Les mouvements vers le nord à travers le Honduras ont diminué de 75 % par rapport au premier semestre 2025, ce qui confirme l’ampleur des changements observés dans les dynamiques migratoires en Amérique centrale.

« Ces changements reflètent l’évolution des conditions politiques, des changements dans l’accès aux voies de migration régulières et des pressions économiques dans l’ensemble de la région », a ajouté M. Espinosa. « Les migrants empruntent de nouvelles routes, retournent dans leur pays d’origine ou cherchent des opportunités ailleurs. Certains se retrouvent bloqués en chemin. Alors que les mouvements réguliers et irréguliers évoluent, nous devons travailler avec les gouvernements pour élargir l’accès à des voies de migration sûres et régulières et réduire les risques auxquels les personnes sont exposées. »

Le rapport souligne l’importance de suivre ces changements au fur et à mesure qu’ils se produisent. Grâce à sa Matrice de suivi des déplacements (DTM), l’OIM collecte et analyse des données sur les mouvements migratoires, aidant les gouvernements et les partenaires humanitaires à mieux comprendre les routes émergentes, à identifier les besoins des personnes et à planifier les interventions nécessaires. Ces données permettent aux gouvernements d’anticiper et de gérer l’évolution des mouvements migratoires de manière ordonnée et prévisible, tout en apportant un soutien aux migrants et aux communautés qui les accueillent.

Le rapport complet, Amérique latine et Caraïbes : Tendances de la mobilité régionale, janvier–juin 2026, est disponible en ligne.

Pour plus d’informations, veuillez consulter le Centre médias de l’OIM.

items.title: Por primera vez, la campaña “Ilumina el Mundo” llega a Ecuador para apoyar la alimentación escolar
items.blurb:
Country: Ecuador
Source: World Food Programme

QUITO, Ecuador – Esta Navidad, la solidaridad se convierte en una oportunidad para transformar la vida de miles de niños y niñas. Por primera vez, la campaña global “Ilumina el Mundo” llega a Ecuador para movilizar a personas, familias y empresas en apoyo a una causa que abre oportunidades para el futuro: la alimentación escolar.

La iniciativa estará disponible del 19 de noviembre al 31 de diciembre a través de una máquina inteligente de donaciones ubicada en el Centro Comercial El Jardín. Mediante una experiencia simple e interactiva, las personas podrán realizar contribuciones que se transformarán en apoyo para ampliar el programa de alimentación escolar impulsado por el Programa Mundial de Alimentos, beneficiando a niños y niñas de las comunidades más vulnerables del Ecuador.

Cada aporte ayudará a fortalecer el acceso a comidas escolares nutritivas, contribuyendo no solo a una mejor alimentación, sino también al aprendizaje, el desarrollo integral y el bienestar de miles de estudiantes. Para muchos niños y niñas, una comida escolar saludable representa una oportunidad para crecer, concentrarse en sus estudios y desarrollar todo su potencial.

La llegada de “Ilumina el Mundo” a Ecuador forma parte de un movimiento solidario de alcance mundial. Desde su creación en 2017, la iniciativa ha recaudado aproximadamente US$70 millones y ha movilizado a millones de personas en distintos países para apoyar causas relacionadas con alimentación, salud, educación y bienestar. En 2026, la campaña estará presente en 28 países y cerca de 150 ubicaciones distribuidas en más de 140 ciudades de seis continentes.

Impulsada globalmente por La Iglesia de Jesucristo de los Santos de los Últimos Días, la campaña invita a celebrar la Navidad compartiendo esperanza y solidaridad con quienes más lo necesitan. En Ecuador,

esta acción se realiza en alianza con el Programa Mundial de Alimentos para fortalecer la alimentación escolar y contribuir a un futuro más saludable para miles de niños y niñas.

Porque un gesto sencillo puede hacer una gran diferencia, “Ilumina el Mundo” invita a todos los ecuatorianos a sumarse a esta iniciativa global y demostrar que, cuando una comunidad se une en torno a la nutrición y el bienestar de la niñez, es posible transformar vidas.

El Programa Mundial de Alimentos de las Naciones Unidas es la organización humanitaria más grande del mundo: salva vidas en situaciones de emergencia y utiliza la asistencia alimentaria para construir un camino hacia la paz, la estabilidad y la prosperidad de las personas que se recuperan de conflictos, desastres y los efectos de los fenómenos meteorológicos extremos.

items.title: Japan Supports Life-Saving Food Assistance for Conflict-affected Families in Yemen | World Food Programme
items.blurb:
Countries: Yemen, Japan
Source: World Food Programme

ADEN, Yemen – The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) today welcomed a USD 3 million contribution from the Government of Japan to provide life-saving food assistance to 300,000 conflict-affected people in Yemen, including families newly displaced by the recent escalation in hostilities.

Years of conflict, economic decline, climate shocks and funding shortages have left millions of people struggling to meet their basic food needs. The situation has deteriorated further since fighting escalated in September 2026, displacing [VERIFY: number of people displaced since early September 2026], including families from Taiz and areas along Yemen’s west coast.

“For families forced to flee conflict, receiving food quickly can make the difference between coping and falling deeper into crisis,” said Elkhidir Daloum, WFP Representative and Country Director in Yemen. “We are grateful to Japan for its continued support, enabling WFP to provide immediate assistance to newly displaced families and help vulnerable communities meet their food needs.”

Japan’s contribution will enable WFP to:

  • Provide life-saving food assistance to 300,000 conflict-affected people.
  • Support the inter-agency Rapid Response Mechanism to reach families in the first days following displacement with 2,500 Immediate Response Ration kits.
  • Distribute 2,995 metric tons of wheat flour to vulnerable households.

Each Immediate Response Ration kit contains ready-to-eat food sufficient for a family of seven for five days. The wheat flour will provide follow-on assistance after families receive the initial emergency ration.

The new contribution comes as many families across Yemen are increasingly resorting to harmful coping strategies as they struggle to secure enough food. Conflict-related displacement is placing further pressure on affected communities and humanitarian services.

Japan is a longstanding partner of WFP in Yemen, contributing USD 170 million since 2016 to humanitarian and development programmes that save lives, strengthen resilience and improve food security.

“This contribution will help WFP act quickly when families are displaced, while continuing to support communities already facing severe food insecurity,” said Elkhidir Daloum, WFP Representative and Country Director in Yemen. “Japan’s partnership is vital to ensuring assistance reaches people when they need it most.”

# # #

The United Nations World Food Programme is the world’s largest humanitarian organization saving lives in emergencies and using food assistance to build a pathway to peace, stability and prosperity for people recovering from conflict, disasters and the impact of weather extremes.

items.title: World: Oxfam reaction to the inadequate pledges to the Adaptation Fund High-Level Contributor Dialogue
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: Oxfam

Reacting to the inadequate pledges to the Adaptation Fund High-Level Contributor Dialogue, Nafkote Dabi, Climate Change Policy and Advocacy Lead said:

“For the third year in a row, rich countries have failed to meet the modest $300 million Adaptation Fund target, which is just 0.1 percent of the $300 billion Global South countries need to adapt to a crisis they did little to create. We’re being told there is no money, but taxing luxury carbon – from private jets to the excess profits of fossil fuel corporations – could raise over $445 billion a year. So, let’s stop pretending this is about money. It’s about political choices, priorities, and accountability. With communities from Nepal to the Sahel being battered by escalating climate disasters, the solution is simple: make rich polluters pay.”

Notes to editors

Contributors announced pledges totaling just $50 million.

The Adaptation Fund is the only UNFCCC-linked fund dedicated to providing grant-based adaptation finance to low- and middle-income OR Global South countries, which is the only fair and just method of delivering climate finance.

At COP29, a new goal was set to reach at least $300 billion per year by 2035. A year later, it was further agreed to (within the $300 billion target) triple support for adaptation by 2035. Global South countries believe the tripling must be a tripling by 2035 of the already agreed doubling by 2025 compared to 2019 levels, leading to at least $120 billion a year by 2035.

items.title: She Began Dancing at 7, Gave Birth Mid-Show & Kept Tamasha Alive: The Real Story Behind ‘Eetha’
items.blurb: Vithabai Narayangaonkar was nine months pregnant and in the middle of a Tamasha performance when her labour began. She slipped backstage, delivered her baby and cut the umbilical cord with a stone. Maharashtra's folk theatre world has told the story ever since, and it stands for a woman who gave her life to the stage and spent decades keeping the Tamasha tradition alive. The stage was her first classroom Vithabai grew up in Solapur district in a family that lived by the stage. Her father, Bhau Bapu Mang Narayangaonkar, ran a Tamasha troupe founded by her grandfather, Narayan Khude, and she grew up on Lavani, Gavlan and Bhedik, the songs and forms of Tamasha, Maharashtra's travelling folk theatre. Nine months pregnant, Vithabai slipped backstage, delivered her baby and returned to a life devoted to Tamasha. Photograph: ( Lokmat ) She followed the family trade from village to village, performing and refining her art . When the Marathi playwright Mama Varerkar saw her on stage, he was so mesmerised that he invited her to join his troupe, where she mastered techniques such as Angik, Vachik, Satvik and Abhinaya without formal drama training. Her daughter, the Tamasha artist Mangala Bansode, later recalled that Vithabai had danced since the age of 7, and that she pulled her own daughter out of school in class two to put her on the stage at 9, because the troupe needed more women. In families like theirs, song and dance were the first lessons, drilled in by parents through long hours of rehearsal, and the stage was the classroom. Such artists traditionally came from nomadic, lower-caste and Dalit communities. She won hearts, but couldn’t make ends meet Fame did not guarantee food. The family had name and recognition but little money to buy a meal, and Vithabai's songs said as much . In a Lavani she sang in the 1960s, she asked the men in the audience to keep their own sense of shame, because she was dancing for her daily living and cared for nobody else's opinion. From village performances to national honours, Vithabai made Maharashtra’s travelling folk theatre her lifelong stage. Photograph: ( Mid Day ) Fans began calling her Tamasha Samradni, or Tamasha Empress, and when the India-China war began she performed a special Tamasha at the North-East Frontier Agency border. The President of India honoured her twice, in 1957 and 1990. Even then, her work depended on contractors, who decided when a Tamasha opened or closed, and on audiences who set the terms of what artists performed. Mangala recalled dancing at a tamasha held under a tree, with no stage and the crowd pressing in, where she had to walk up to men to collect money and some pulled at her sari. Holding on to art even on the hardest days After the birth, the contractor stopped the Tamasha and the family was moved back into a dharmashala. Mangala remembered visiting her mother in hospital, where there was no food and no clothes for the newborn. When she asked the contractor for help, he told her nothing could be done until the Tamasha started again. Someone suggested pawning the harmonium for cash, but Mangala refused, calling the harmonium and ankle bells the family's wealth. She instead asked another troupe for ₹1,000 and agreed to dance for it every evening. With that money she bought food for everyone, mutton biryani for her mother and clothes for the baby. The hardship never fully lifted. Despite the honours, Vithabai and her family were never financially stable, and she died in 2002. 3 generations & a shared love for Tamasha In 2006, the Government of Maharashtra instituted the Vithabai Narayangaonkar Lifetime Achievement Award for artists working in Tamasha, the art she had dedicated much of her life to. The state has given grants to traditional folk arts, including Tamasha, Dashavatar and Shahiri, since 2008. When money ran short, her daughter protected the harmonium and ankle bells that kept their family’s art alive. Photograph: ( News24 ) Mangala carried the stage forward, calling her mother her guru and saying she was famous because of her. By 2004, she was 55 and still dancing, a Tamasgir, or troupe leader, with around 150 people depending on her for their daily survival. She called Tamasha a public service rather than a business, and said she would keep performing as long as the public wanted her. Three generations of her family had performed in Tamasha, and her son took the stage at 7. Yet Mangala said audiences were thinning as remixes and orchestras drew crowds away, and she wanted the state to do more for its traditional artists. She had the fame a stage can give and little of the security it cannot. She left behind a harmonium her daughter refused to pawn, ankle bells that kept sounding through a daughter and a grandson, and an award in her name for those who keep Tamasha alive. items.title: Exclusive: From Leaving Engineering for Music to Earning a Grammy Nod, Devan Ekambaram’s ‘Varuvaaiy’ Makes History For Tamil
items.blurb: “Uruvaai arivil olirvaai Kanna! Uyirin amudhaai pozhivaai Kanna!” Shine within my consciousness, O Kanna; pour forth as the nectar of my life. In Subramania Bharati's poetry, the imagery of devotion and love often reaches beyond the immediate moment. More than a century after his words were written, one of his compositions has found a new musical life — this time, on a global stage. But when the Grammy nominations were being announced on 16 November, the man behind that contemporary interpretation was nowhere near a television screen. Back from a project in Sri Lanka, Devan Ekambaram could not bring himself to watch the nominations unfold. He went instead to a temple. “I was too nervous to watch,” he recalls. At 6.47 pm IST, his phone lit up. A friend in Los Angeles sent him a message: “Congratulations!” His phone soon filled with 80 or 90 similar messages. “I realised what had happened and immediately broke down crying,” he says. Released independently in August 2026, Varuvaaiy became the first Tamil song nominated for a Grammy. The song that had brought him to this moment was Varuvaaiy , an independent Tamil recording he composed and produced with vocalist Subhiksha Rangarajan, known as Susha. It had been nominated for Best Global Music Performance at the 69th Grammy Awards, becoming the first Tamil song to receive a Grammy nomination. For Ekambaram, the moment carried a childhood dream: watching Michael Jackson win a Grammy for Thriller and hearing presenter Whoopi Goldberg urge young viewers to hold on to their dreams. It was also a milestone reached without a family music legacy. “I come from a family of doctors and engineers. Nobody is in the art field, and I had to embark on this journey all alone,” he says. A childhood tuned to music Growing up in New Jersey, often one of the few Indian children in his neighbourhood, Ekambaram found it difficult to fit in. Music became a source of confidence . His mother introduced him to different genres, while programmes such as American Bandstand and Solid Gold showed him performers building careers around music. He began playing guitar between the seventh and tenth grades, then joined the school choir and marching band. He learnt to listen for harmonies and how musical parts fitted together, and began recording at home. “I knew my weakness, but I found my strength,” he says. He developed his musical identity through choir, harmony and arranging. Growing up in New Jersey, Devan Ekambaram found his first musical inspiration through school choirs, guitars and American television. The Grammys entered his imagination around this time. “I remember watching Michael Jackson win for Thriller , and hearing presenter Whoopi Goldberg urge young viewers to hold on to their dreams, come what may. And that became my dream,” he says. At 19 or 20, while studying electrical engineering at the University of Illinois, he explored music opportunities during a college break in India. He eventually left engineering and moved to Chennai at 21. “I just quit my engineering degree in the US and came here with no support and no direction. It was the scariest thing because I never saw anyone do this growing up,” he says. Building a life in music — and finding the right voice Ekambaram’s move to Chennai gradually opened doors. His 1998 album Kamban Oru Kannile , made with S P Charan, caught A R Rahman’s attention and led to work on Kadhalar Dhinam . He made his playback debut with “Oh Maria” in 1999 and went on to sing on more than 500 film soundtracks, while also working as a composer, voice artist, and vocal arranger. He had contributed to Grammy-winning projects such as Winds of Samsara (2015) and Divine Tides (2022). But this time, he wanted to create something that was unmistakably his own: an independent album reimagining the poetry of Subramania Bharati through contemporary arrangements. For the first single, he had a particular voice in mind. Ekambaram had met Subhiksha Rangarajan, known as Susha, back in 2007, when they appeared on the television programme Coffee with Anu . He had wanted to collaborate with her ever since, but the opportunity never quite came together. When he began working on the Bharati project, he reached out to her again. Years after meeting vocalist Susha in 2007, Ekambaram brought her into his independent project celebrating Subramania Bharati’s poetry. Photograph: ( Instagram/@sushasings ) In June 2026, Susha arrived at his home studio with her mother, Lakshmi Rangarajan. The composition they were about to record was one Lakshmi had taught her, set to a tune by L Krishnan that was already around 40 to 50 years old. What followed was an unusually quick coming together of ideas . Ekambaram asked Susha to sing, and the recording took shape over the next two to three hours. For him, her voice brought together the musical sensibilities the song needed. Trained in Carnatic music and having studied jazz at the University of Toronto, Susha could move between the classical foundation of the composition and the contemporary sound he wanted to create. She had also been building her own independent music career, including through NEXA Music, an initiative by A R Rahman and Clinton Cerejo that selected her among 24 artistes in 2019. “Without her singing, nobody would have listened to the song,” Ekambaram says. Giving an old poem a new sound He wanted to rebuild the traditional arrangement while retaining the melody’s character. “I just gave it a makeover,” he says. “I looked at it thinking, how I would want to hear this?” He wanted to make the form inviting to a new generation of listeners unfamiliar with Carnatic music without flattening its identity. Set in raga Desh, the arrangement brings Carnatic phrasing together with piano, slide guitar, acoustic guitar, bass and tabla. Ekambaram played keyboards and produced the track. It features pianist Anil Srinivasan, slide guitarist Prakash Sontakke, guitarist Naveen Samson, bassist Joseph John and tabla player Sarvajit Krishna Mohan. Roshan Sebastian mixed and mastered it. The collaboration was largely remote: Susha recorded at Ekambaram’s home studio, while the instrumentalists sent their parts from elsewhere. “I coordinated the musicians and worked with Sebastian on the final mix. The result was a three-minute-and-26-second recording released independently on 12 August 2026,” he says. Susha’s Carnatic training and jazz influences shaped Varuvaaiy, a contemporary interpretation of a century-old Tamil composition. Susha’s contribution was central to the sound he had imagined. “Without her singing, nobody would have listened to the song,” Ekambaram says. Her Carnatic training, jazz studies at the University of Toronto and contemporary sensibility shaped the recording. In 2019, she was among 24 artistes selected for NEXA Music, an initiative by A R Rahman and Clinton Cerejo. Her debut album, Love Language , arrived in August 2026. Written more than a century ago, the poem’s exact date is unknown, though it is believed to date from Bharati’s years in Pondicherry. Its imagery calls for a force to enter human thought and dispel darkness, and has been read as a metaphor for resisting oppression and colonial rule. That purpose appealed to Ekambaram. Rather than create a new song with contemporary lyrics, he wanted to bring a poet whose words shaped Tamil public life to younger listeners. “I thought this had a purpose,” he says. He hoped a fresh musical arrangement would allow his children’s generation to encounter Bharati’s language without feeling distanced by it. A release against the clock Getting the single out in time required a difficult decision. Ekambaram says labels he approached were hesitant because the underlying work was in the public domain, and the permissions process threatened to delay the release. “With the Grammy submission deadline approaching, I chose to release the track independently and complete the distribution myself. But I never imagined how well it would work,” he recalls. Rooted in raga Desh, the recording blends Carnatic nuances with jazz influences, guitars, piano and tabla. He had submitted work before and contributed to Grammy-winning projects, but this time concentrated on Varuvaaiy , preparing its streaming links for the Best Global Music Performance category. The category had 526 submissions, he says, and seeing the names on the ballot made a nomination feel far from certain. On nomination morning, the song had around 300 YouTube views, according to Ekambaram. As the news spread, the count rose to about 35,000. Messages of appreciation came from musicians including Scott Hoying of Pentatonix and Chandrika Tandon. What comes after the nomination The recognition arrived as Ekambaram questioned what came next. He had considered continuing in Chennai or returning to the United States if work did not move forward. He wanted to build a body of work listeners could associate with him, not a film or star. He worried that short-lived online trends left less room for songs that stay with people. The February 2027 Grammy ceremony will see Varuvaaiy compete alongside recordings by internationally acclaimed musicians. “The nomination has renewed my resolve to make independent music, compose and experiment rather than rely only on past successes. To think that I almost gave up and left for L. A., but we never know when opportunities will come. Today, I’m glad I continued on the path,” he says. Ekambaram credits mentors including Madhav Das at Magnus Sound, choir director Ruth Lane McIntyre and the high-school teacher who encouraged him to sing. He wishes they could have witnessed the announcement. The larger Bharati album is now the next step. Ekambaram says it will contain 10 to 12 contemporary interpretations, with the tracks already taking shape and around two months of work remaining at the time of the interview. He is also waiting for a bilingual Tamil-Telugu film for which he composed the music to reach audiences. The ceremony is scheduled for February 2027 in Los Angeles, where Varuvaaiy will compete alongside recordings by Angélique Kidjo, Rosalía, Shakira and Burna Boy. Winning would be wonderful, he says, but the nomination has already given him something deeply valuable. For Ekambaram, the nomination is already a milestone: bringing Tamil poetry and music to a global audience. “I don’t care whether I win the category or not,” he says. “I’ve been a catalyst in placing Tamil music on the global map. That is my win.” More than a century after Bharati wrote the poem, its words have travelled into a new musical language: first through a melody passed down across generations, then through a contemporary arrangement shaped by musicians working across genres and distances. Now, listeners far beyond Tamil-speaking communities are being invited to hear it, too, today. That, perhaps, is the lasting possibility of Varuvaaiy . A poem written in another time has not been left behind in it. It has been given another voice, another audience and another chance to be understood. And somewhere, a listener encountering Bharati for the first time may follow the song back to the words that began it all.

items.title: Drones Track 36,000 Vehicles as IIT Guwahati Builds Smarter Models for Indian Roads
items.blurb: A car brakes suddenly as a two-wheeler slips into the gap ahead. An auto-rickshaw swerves to avoid a bus, while another vehicle edges into the next lane. On Indian roads, where cars, buses, three-wheelers and two-wheelers often share limited space, traffic can change its rhythm in seconds. For urban planners and traffic engineers, understanding this movement is no easy task. Many conventional traffic models assume that vehicles follow lanes and maintain relatively predictable speeds. But Indian roads rarely offer such orderly conditions. Researchers at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Guwahati are working to bridge this gap. By combining drone footage, automated vehicle tracking and machine learning, they have developed mathematical models that better account for the unpredictable ways vehicles move on Indian roads. Tracking nearly nine million vehicle positions Led by Professor Akhilesh Kumar Maurya from the Department of Civil Engineering, the research team studied traffic on an eight-lane divided highway on the outskirts of Delhi. Using drones equipped with high-resolution cameras, they recorded around five hours of daytime traffic footage in 4K resolution. The videos were then processed using DataFromSky, an automated software that extracts vehicle movements from aerial footage. Led by Professor Akhilesh Kumar Maurya, the IIT Guwahati research could help improve traffic simulations, highway planning and congestion management in India. Photograph: (IIT Guwahati) The result was a dataset of 36,818 vehicles and 8,938,920 vehicle-position data points, captured at 10 frames per second. Researchers categorised the vehicles into six groups: two-wheelers, three-wheelers, cars, buses, heavy commercial vehicles and light commercial vehicles. This gave them a detailed picture of how different vehicles moved, how closely they followed one another and how their speeds changed as traffic became denser. Explaining why India-specific data is necessary, Prof Maurya says, “Traffic conditions in India are different from those in many countries where existing traffic models have been developed. We need traffic data that represents the diversity and characteristics of Indian roads.” Drone-based data collection provides an opportunity to observe a large number of vehicles and their movements over a road section at high spatial and temporal resolution. Teaching traffic models to account for unpredictability One interesting finding was that the distance vehicles maintained from one another changed with traffic density. On relatively empty roads, vehicles kept larger gaps. As traffic increased, these gaps became smaller. However, when congestion became severe, the spacing patterns changed again. This variability is important because two vehicles travelling under seemingly similar traffic conditions may not necessarily move at the same speed. Using automated vehicle tracking and machine learning, the researchers mapped 36,818 vehicles and nearly nine million vehicle-position data points. Photograph: ( iStock ) To understand these differences, the researchers tested six mathematical traffic models, including established approaches such as Greenshields and Underwood. They also trained two machine learning models: Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) and Random Forest (RF). But perhaps the most interesting part was their development of stochastic fundamental diagrams. In simple terms, conventional traffic models generally estimate one speed for a given traffic density. Stochastic models go a step further by accounting for the range of speeds that vehicles may actually travel at under those conditions. This allows the models to represent the randomness of Indian traffic more realistically, rather than smoothing over the differences between individual vehicles. From better predictions to smarter road planning The researchers found that the Underwood model performed most consistently among the mathematical models tested, achieving an R² value of 0.86. The two machine learning models achieved approximately 0.83. The research could have practical applications in assessing highway capacity, designing intersections, estimating road speeds, and improving traffic simulations. The data could also help researchers calibrate car-following models, which study how drivers adjust their distance and speed in relation to vehicles ahead. Prof. Maurya explains, “Reliable traffic management begins with models that represent how traffic actually behaves on Indian roads. The high-resolution trajectory data generated through drones allows us to capture interactions among different vehicle types and the large variability that conventional traffic models often overlook.” Such India-specific models can support more realistic traffic simulation, better road and intersection design, congestion management, capacity assessment, and the development of intelligent traffic-management systems suited to Indian conditions. Unlike conventional traffic models, the stochastic models developed by the team account for variations in vehicle speeds and distances, even under similar traffic conditions. Photograph: ( Adobe Stock ) For anyone who has spent time on an Indian road, the challenge of predicting traffic is easy to understand. A car slows down, a two-wheeler slips into a narrow gap, an auto-rickshaw changes lanes, and the movement of hundreds of vehicles can shift in seconds. By capturing these interactions in detail, the IIT Guwahati team hopes to make traffic models better reflect what commuters experience every day. The research is a step towards understanding not just how many vehicles use a road, but how they move around one another. And that understanding could eventually help make the daily journey a little more predictable, whether someone is driving to work, taking a bus to school or navigating a crowded intersection.

items.title: Better Drains, Rainwater Harvesting and Urban Greening: Bengaluru's Plan for Five Neighbourhoods
items.blurb: Once known as the Garden City for its tree-lined avenues, blooming parks and pleasant weather, Bengaluru is now facing a growing question: How can a rapidly expanding city make room for nature while preparing for heavier rains, water shortages and rising temperatures? Now, a neighbourhood-level climate planning exercise across five wards aims to address some of these concerns through better drainage, rainwater management and urban greening. The Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) has prepared ward-level Climate Action Plans for five pilot wards across the city, identifying environmental challenges and proposing interventions suited to the conditions of each neighbourhood. The initiative is now awaiting budgetary approval from the respective city corporations before implementation can begin. The five wards selected for the pilot are Shantinagar in Central Bengaluru, Jakkur in the North, Begur in the South, Vijinapura in the East and Nalwadi Krishnaraja Wadiyar ward in the West. Developed under the GBA's Climate Action Cell, the plans aim to take climate planning beyond city-wide recommendations and identify what individual neighbourhoods need. The assessments cover energy and buildings, transportation, solid waste management, urban planning, greenery and biodiversity, water management, wastewater and stormwater management, and disaster preparedness. According to The New Indian Express, the plans were prepared following sector-wise assessments and consultations with residents, experts and other stakeholders. The exercise recognises that climate-related challenges are not uniform across Bengaluru. While some localities experience recurring flooding, others face water scarcity, declining green cover, rising temperatures or inadequate waste management. Why Bengaluru needs neighbourhood-level climate planning The city's contrasting water challenges illustrate why localised planning matters. Bengaluru experiences heavy surface runoff during the monsoon, even as several neighbourhoods face groundwater depletion and water shortages during summer. A March 18, 2026 report by Mongabay-India, which examined the ward-level planning exercise, highlighted how geography influences flood vulnerability. For instance, Shantinagar, a densely populated urban ward, lies in a downstream valley zone. Hydrological assessments by WELL Labs and Bengaluru's Climate Action Cell found that floodwater can originate beyond the ward's boundaries, making flooding a problem that cannot always be addressed through isolated drainage work within one locality. The five-ward pilot is intended to provide a model for extending climate action planning to other neighbourhoods under the GBA. Photograph: (Bengaluru Climate Action Cell-via Mongabay) Anam Husain, programme associate for Urban Water at WELL Labs, told Mongabay-India that nature-based interventions such as rain gardens, bioswales, permeable surfaces and small retention systems can help slow down rainwater runoff and improve groundwater infiltration. These interventions offer ways to manage excess rainwater closer to where it falls, while also reducing pressure on conventional drainage infrastructure. Rainwater harvesting and groundwater recharge are particularly relevant in a city where water scarcity and monsoon runoff exist side by side. Alongside improving stormwater management, wastewater reuse and stormwater reuse can contribute to longer-term water security. Bringing green infrastructure into urban planning Urban greening is another important component of Bengaluru's climate planning exercise. In neighbourhoods experiencing rising temperatures, the GBA is considering measures such as increasing green cover, using heat-reflective cool paints and establishing cool shelters. These interventions can help address the urban heat island effect , in which built-up areas with extensive concrete surfaces and limited vegetation retain more heat than surrounding areas. Bengaluru's existing Climate Action and Resilience Plan also identifies nature-based solutions as an important part of urban development. View this post on Instagram A post shared by ಬೆಂಗಳೂರು ದಕ್ಷಿಣ ನಗರ ಪಾಲಿಕೆ (Bengaluru South City Corporation) (@bscc.gba) Its sectoral recommendations include restoring the city's blue-green networks, increasing tree canopy and expanding green and permeable surfaces to help reduce flood and heat-related risks. The plan sets targets to increase the city's tree canopy by 10% from its baseline by 2030 and 20% by 2040. It also proposes increasing green cover and permeable surfaces to 40% of the city's area by 2040. From climate plans to neighbourhood-level action Public participation has also been part of the planning process. Just recently, The Better India documented how Bengaluru residents are taking small, collective steps to care for their city's shared spaces . From removing 110 kg of plastic waste around Madiwala Lake during a 75-minute plogging drive to watering hundreds of saplings at Vengaiah Lake through the Bhagiratha initiative, the report highlighted how citizen participation can complement urban conservation efforts. Read the report. Other efforts include residents in Balagere, Panathur and Varthur clearing accumulated roadside dust, and volunteers working with civic authorities to restore neglected footpaths and public spaces. The Greater Bengaluru Authority's proposed Climate Action Plans across five wards take this approach further by seeking to integrate local environmental needs into formal urban planning. The five-ward pilot is intended to provide a model for extending climate action planning to other neighbourhoods under the GBA. For Bengaluru, the next step will be translating these local assessments into funded projects that improve drainage, strengthen water management and expand green infrastructure. The effectiveness of the exercise will ultimately depend on how consistently these proposals are implemented and monitored at the neighbourhood level. Sources: ‘GBA goes micro local with ward-level climate plans’ : By Express News Service, Published on 4 November 2026 ‘Ward-level plans bring climate action closer to communities’ : By Mahima Jain, Published on 18 March 2026
