items.title: From Sanitation to Solar Power, What Should Your Village Prioritise? This IAS Officer’s 25-Point Manifesto Makes People Part of the Plan
items.blurb: When we vote in a national or state election, we often have a document to refer to: the political party’s manifesto. It tells us what the party promises to do if elected, from creating jobs and improving healthcare to building infrastructure. And once the government is in power, those promises give voters something to question it about. “But what happens when we vote for our village’s Gram Pradhan? What are the promises we can expect them to make? And, more importantly, what can we hold them accountable for once they are elected?” This is the question that IAS officer Dr Heera Lal wants to bring into village elections through a 25-point Village Manifesto. His idea is straightforward: village elections, too, should be fought on issues and written promises, giving people a clearer say in what development should look like in their communities. “Elections are contested in Parliament on manifestos. In MLA seats, on manifestos. But in the village, we do not have any manifesto,” he explains. A village's priorities could begin with a blocked drain, an unresolved land dispute or something as basic as sanitation. For him, a manifesto is essentially a written promise . If a candidate commits to addressing specific problems before being elected, villagers have something tangible to refer to afterwards. Without such a commitment, he argues, it becomes difficult for voters to question their elected representative about what they have delivered. Beyond roads, schools and drinking Water The 25-point framework tries to broaden what villages consider development. Conversations around rural progress often centre on a handful of visible needs, such as roads, schools, drinking water and electricity. But several other factors shape a village's quality of life, too. Saurabh Lall, CEO of Model Gaon, which developed the framework , says the idea emerged from recognising that a better life could not be measured through just three or four parameters. “Our first initiative was to make them understand that a better life entails a lot many other things than just having these three, four things being worked upon,” he says. The manifesto therefore looks at a wider range of issues, including health, education, sanitation, income generation, employment, access to technology, sustainability, women's empowerment, local talent, dispute resolution and proper documentation of village records. Solar power, better sanitation and access to technology feature among the 25 priorities proposed for village-level development. Some of these priorities may not immediately come to mind when people think about rural development. But they can have a direct bearing on everyday life. A village where small disputes repeatedly escalate into expensive legal cases, for instance, faces a different challenge from one where the most pressing concern is access to irrigation or employment. The framework was deliberately simplified into a one-page document so that villagers could understand and engage with it. It was also designed to be personalised. “All those 25 things could mean different things for different people. And their priorities in life would also differ based on the phase of life that they were in, the context that they were living in,” says Saurabh. The idea, then, is not to impose the same development agenda on every village. It is to give communities a framework through which they can identify what matters most to them. What should your village's manifesto actually promise? A list of 25 priorities is only a starting point . The more important exercise is deciding which of those priorities need attention first in a particular village. To do this, the process involves conversations at the ward level, where residents can raise problems they experience in their everyday lives. These meetings typically bring together around 25 to 35 people from a particular part of the village. The concerns can be remarkably specific. Saurabh recalls residents raising issues such as a drain being constructed inconveniently outside someone's home or a neighbour encroaching on a portion of their land. One recurring concern was the number of small local disputes that were escalating into court cases. Residents often had to travel to cities, spend money, and wait for lengthy legal processes to resolve issues that could potentially be addressed locally. Ward-level meetings bring 25 to 35 residents together to discuss everyday problems and decide which issues deserve attention first. “If people stop wasting time in resolving their petty disputes, they would end up either studying or working in their farms or looking for jobs,” he says. In such cases, dispute resolution could become one of the village's most important priorities, even if it might not feature prominently in another village's manifesto. The meetings also allow the Gram Pradhan to hear these concerns directly. Rather than treating the manifesto as a document prepared by an outside organisation, the aim is to make it a reflection of what residents themselves want addressed. Saurabh believes this participation is essential to meaningful development. “Unless and until the beneficiary is involved in the designing of the programme itself, it never really gets very comprehensive.” From written promises to accountability For a manifesto to mean something beyond election season, its promises must translate into action. That requires villagers to know what their priorities are, and their elected representatives to understand how to work towards them. Saurabh says the process also involves helping Gram Pradhans understand their rights, responsibilities, and the administrative procedures involved in local governance. The aim is to help them identify solutions by bringing together existing government schemes, local resources and relevant expertise. “We said that installing another system is not the solution. Galvanising the existing system is probably going to be more effective,” he says. What should a Gram Pradhan promise voters? The manifesto encourages residents to identify their most pressing local needs. This is important because a village's problems do not always require an entirely new project or a fresh allocation of funds. Sometimes, the challenge is knowing which existing resources can be brought together to address a particular need. The larger ambition is to take this framework into upcoming Gram Pradhan elections. Dr Heera Lal describes the campaign with a slogan: “Chunaav mudra se nahi, muddon pe hoga” — elections should be fought on issues, not money. The proposal is to make the village manifesto a part of the election conversation, so candidates can put their priorities in writing and voters can assess them against the needs of their communities. Ultimately, the 25-point framework raises a question that goes beyond any one organisation or development initiative: shouldn't people have a clearer say in what their elected village representatives promise to deliver? A manifesto cannot guarantee that every problem will be solved. But it can give a village something to begin with: a shared list of priorities, written commitments and a way to ask its elected representative what has been done.

items.title: It’s unfashionable to say it, but class still matters – and young people know that | Polly Toynbee
items.blurb:
From inheritance to nepotism in the workplace, social inequality is now a daily experience for many young people

This should come as no great surprise: young people are more keenly aware of the significance of social class than those who came before them. The yawning gap in life chances at birth is something they know better than complacent older generations. Class may be unfashionable in the language of politics – long damned by the right as the politics of envy, avoided by many on the left for fear of sounding chip-on-the-shoulder – yet it’s part of the daily experience for young people.

Nearly half of 16- to 34-year-olds in the UK now say class is important to their identity – and not in a good way – according to a new Ipsos poll. That’s nearly twice as many as among the over-55s. Maybe that’s because more young people are better educated at each level, so they know more, with a grounding in reasoned thinking.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

items.title: Is Donald Trump beyond caricature? Not at all – here’s his hilarious origin story
items.blurb:
Ustinov Studio, Bath
Elliot Cowan is scarily convincing as the budding Potus in Donald, a high-speed, three-actor comedy from the playwright behind The Lehman Trilogy

His manner and actions often seeming like improbable caricature, the current US president sets a challenge for satire, any comic exaggeration likely to be trumped by reality. Mike Bartlett’s play The 47th (2022), staged between Trump’s administrations, pursued wild fantasies about the politician’s future career that were soon superseded by odder events. Ali Abbasi’s movie The Apprentice (2024) more sensibly focused on the period from 1973 to 1986 in which the New York realtor developed the behavioural and verbal tics that make him probably the most ridiculed figure in modern history, though such mockery, until the recent midterms, largely consoled detractors while being ignored by supporters.

Closer to Abbasi’s approach, Donald by the Italian dramatist Stefano Massini resembles his play The Lehman Trilogy – an international hit about the banking dynasty – in being a psychological analysis played by three actors with lightning switches of character and costume. In this case, the cut-up structure reflects Massini’s seeding conceit that only about 10 minutes of any life really matter, a total of the brief sequences in which someone makes formative or destructive choices.

items.title: Ram through datacentres no one wants and hope the AI bubble never bursts: that’s the UK’s growth plan | George Monbiot
items.blurb:
The government doesn’t know what they are going to be used for, but that’s beside the point. Their real purpose is to sustain the share price of big tech

It should have the status of an economic law: the sectors a government does most to promote in the name of growth are the sectors most likely to tank the economy. In the UK and the US, deregulation was meant to turn the financial sector into a never-ending growth machine. We have not yet fully recovered from the crash it helped cause in 2008. Fossil fuels are the most heavily subsidised sector on Earth. All that public money makes us highly vulnerable to oil price shocks, the whims of autocrats and societal collapse caused by climate breakdown. As for the great growth priority of our time – AI and datacentres – well, don’t take it from me. As Anthropic’s IPO prospectus warns, advanced AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”.

One thing we learned from the US midterm elections is that the drive to build datacentres is less a function of real commercial demand than of the need to sustain the share price of the big tech companies. After citizens across the US voted for moratoria on new datacentres, tech stocks, which have become dangerously dominant, plummeted, triggering fears of wider contagion. Whether new datacentres are required or not, we must keep building them, because confidence depends on them, and without that confidence the bubble will pop. The more you build, and the more this value dependency grows, the bigger the bubble becomes.

George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

items.title: Andy Burnham is in danger of over-selling his big Brussels summit. What happens if he under-delivers? | Joël Reland
items.blurb:
In laying a trap for himself, the PM could derail his longer-term ambition of revisiting Brexit

This week’s UK-EU summit may, one day, be seen as the start of the UK’s long march back towards the EU. Andy Burnham’s much-anticipated first meeting with EU chiefs in Brussels on Friday will be used to unveil a suite of detailed agreements to improve trade and economic cooperation, before the Prime Minister kickstarts his longer term “national conversation” about a much closer form of political and economic relationship with the EU. This, as Burnham signalled in a speech on Monday night, could well culminate in Labour’s next election manifesto abandoning the party’s famous red lines, and proposing an application for EU membership.

For pro-Europeans, this must read like a fever dream. Just four months ago, when Burnham took office, such a bold offer on Europe from the Labour party seemed implausible. But while Burnham has certainly reinvigorated the Brexit debate, he will have to move carefully to avoid storing up trouble for himself down the road. There is a risk that Burnham will come to be seen as someone who over-promises and under-delivers on Europe – and, in doing so, halts the growing momentum around revisiting the troublesome Brexit question.

Joël Reland is senior researcher at the UK in a Changing Europe thinktank
